A LYRIC: An open window, where the sunbeams spread Their golden wings, A scent h nlr Of lilies, ies, like an odour shed e From sacred, hidden things; And songs of birds that sweetly wander through The windless morning and the sky of blue. And all the fresh Spring sounds, the growing green, The peace and young delight; The far rooks calling from their lacy screen, The fair dove's nearer flight; The little breath that stirs the tender leaves And tiny chirp of builders in the eaves. And in the heart a sudden faint surprise At some sweet plaining note, Whose silver strain comes thrilling from the skies, Ethereal, remote. As though some ioy renounced or counted lost Should stray again in murmurs to the ear, With dulcet touches, should the soul accost, And fade ere memory knew what thing was near. Ji3icenf: a Poem. By E. Fairfax Byrne. AT THE PARTY. Half-a-dozen children At our house ! Half-a-dozen children • Quiet as a mouse, Quiet as a moonbeam, You could hear a Pia Waiting for the party To begin. • Such a flood of flounces ! (0 dear nae !) Such a surge of sashes, Like a silken sea, Little eyes demurely Cast upon the ground, Little airs and graces All around. Up spoke a little lady Aged five ; "I've tumbled up my over-dress Sure as I'm alive ! . My dress came from Paris; We sent to Worth for it! Mother says she calls it Such a fit ! " Quick there piped another Little voice : "I didn't send for dresses, Though I had my choice; I have got a doll that Came from. Paris, too; It can walk and talk as Well as you!" Still till now, there sat one Little girl ; Simple as a snowdrop, Without a flounce or curl. Modest as a primrose Soft, plain hair brushed back, But the colour of her dress was Black—all black. Swift she glanced around with Sweet surprise; Bright and grave the look that Widened in her eyes. To entertain the party She must do her share, As if God had sent her Stood she there. Stood a minute thinking With crossed hands, How she might best meet the Company's demands. Grave and swept the purpose To the child's voice given: "/have a little brother Gone to Heaven!" ELIZABETH STUMM PHELPS. —Leeds Mercury Weekly.

When thou speakest to another, look at the eyes; when another speaketh to thee, upon the month. Heaven will pay for any toes we may suffer to gain It; but nothing can pay for the loss of heaven. If a man only saw himself occasionally as others see him, he would cut his own acquaintance on the spot. A boy who was kept after school for bad orthography excused himself to his pirents by sayilg that he was spell.

bound. "There's music in the heir," was a fond father's remark as be paced the midnight floor with his crying son in his arms. "Marriage," said an unfortunate husband," is the church- yard of love." "And you men," replied his wife, "are the grave-diggers." A French oil merchant advertises that he has a "chasm" for an apprentice. He has looked up the word "opening" in the dictionary. No one was ever corrected with a sarcasm, but oftener driven further in the wrong direction. In teaching always be kind and patient. Before marriage a girl frequently calls her intended "her treasure," but when he becomes her husband she looks upon him as her "treasurer." An exchange publishes the successful paper for a prize essay on woman. It is this: "After man came woman, and she has been after him ever since." Many a small man has never done talking about the small sacrifices he makes; but he is a great man indeed who can sacrifice everything and say nothing. Archbishop Whately, in reply to some one who remarked that a brother prelate had a wonderful command of;lan- goage, said, "No; but language has a wonderful comMand of him." Some writers collect their disjointed ideas from all the authors within their reach, just as the paper they write on is made from the tattered rags of all the stuff on earth. Preserve your conscience always soft and sensitive. If but one sin force its way into that tender part of the soul and dwell easy there, the road is paved for a thousand iniquities.— Watts. Hate idleness and curb all passions. Be true in all words and actions. Deliver not your opinion unnecessarily; but, when you do, let it be just, well-considered, and plain. Be charitable, and ever ready to forgive injuries done to your- self, and be more pleased to do good than to receive good. Morality, taken as apart from religion, is but another name for decency in sin. It is just that negative species of virtue which consists in not doing what is scandalously de- praved and wicked. But there is no heart of holy principle in it, any more than there is in the grosser sins.—Dr. Bush- nell. • There was a lady who had a canary, which was so tame I that the door of the cage was occasionally left open, that he might enjoy the freedom of the room. One day he hap- pened to alight on the mantel-shelf, whereon was a mirror. Here was a new discovery of the most profound interest. Re gazed long and curiously at himself, and came to the conclusion that he had found a mate. Going back to his cage, he selected a seed from his box, and brought it in his bill as an offering to the stranger. In vain the canary exerted himself to make his new found friend partake, and becoming weary of that, tried another tack. Stepping back a few inches from the glass, he poured forth his sweetest notes, pausing now and then for a reply. None came; moody and disgusted, he flew back to his perch, hanging his head in shame and silence for the rest of the day; and although the door was repeatedly left open, refused to come Out again. TRYING IT ON.—tinder the title of "Trying it on; or, Reviving the Mummy," our contemporary _Punch,devotes his cartoon this week to the topic of Mitigated Free Trade. On the right of the picture a figure wearing a belt labelled "Durham" is strenuously working at a huge electrical ma- chine bearing the inscription," Fair Trade," while another, labelled in like manner "Lincolnshire," is exclaiming "Let's give him a shock," and is manipulating a powerful battery whence wires are connected with the head and feet of a mummy, tightly enveloped in the usual bandages. Mean- while, the subject of these vigorous operations exhibits little sign of moving, but he is so far aroused as to be able to wink one eye with an air of rather enjoying the joke. This latter circumstance manifestly escapes the attention of Sir Stafford Northcote, who, peeping with extreme caution from behind a curtain, is concentrating his attention on the two operators, while he mutters, "Dangerous experiment! Wonder how it'll answer." The cartoon bears the familiar initials of John Tenniel.—ln connection with the same sub- ject we may give here a letter which Mr. Bright has sent, replying to an invitation to attend a Liberal meeting near Sheffield. He writes:—" As to reciprocity and the rubbish which is disturbing some minds, I do not think we need trouble ourselves much about it. The jingo cry has died out, and the Tory party must have something to say for themselves and against us. It is pleasant to think they are so hard up for a topic. Whatsoever there is of sense and honesty amongst them must revolt against the old weapon they have picked up. Three hundred farmers in Aberdeen- shire have just denounced Protection as heartily as you or I could have done it. The cry may do some mischief at a single election, but I think it will be dead enough before a general election is upon us." Crta_Nox IN THE PUNISHMENT OF C'2IMINALS.—Any one who can throw his recollections back some sixty or seventy years, must, on considering the change of times, be struck with the manner in which criminals are now dealt with, in comparison with the way they were treated in his early days. It would be hazardous to say whether the change was, in all points of view, for the better. There is now far more leniency and humane consideration of circumstances ' than formerly, which, in the main can only be spoken of with approval. But, on the other ;land, the leniency is often carried to lengths so irrational and absurd as to be little better than a public scandal. The more remarkable pecu- liarity of the present day is the small amount of capital punishment, which at least indicates a certain improved tone of feeling. In old times, the gallows was in constant requisition, often for offences of a comparatively trivial character. Occasionally, at Newgate, a dozen or more poor wretches were hanged on a Monday morning. Every large 1 town had an executioner as one of its salaried officers. 1 Public executions were a favourite eight for vast crowds of spectators, among whom were boys, women, and children, who flocked to the sight as they would do to a performance rf horsemanship. No boy would stay away from an execu- tion if he could at all help it. We have the painful recollec- tion of seeing a young man banged for a highway robbery of toor•and-sixpence, or some such small sum • and of ing another youth, a post office clerk, hangeefor taking se ea. in w five-pound note from a letter that was pass gtah3roaunghthhis hands. People at large did not think there wrong in these cruel severities. Magistrates looked' viengry coolly on the proceedings. It was necessary to make an example. And there was all the moan that was made.— Chambers's Journal.

------------- EXPERIMENTS it FEEDING Hoes.—An lowa fanner put up twenty one-year-old bogs, and for the first twenty-eight days fed them on dry shelled corn, of which they ate 82 bushels and gained 8371 b.-over 101 b. to the bushel of corn. He then fed the same hogs for fourteen days on dry corn meal, buring which time they consumed 47 bushels, and gained 5531b5., or 11/lbs. to the bushel. The same ' hogs were then fed fourteen days on corn meal and water mixed, consumed 55± bushels of corn, and gained 7311b5, or 13 1-6th lbs. to the bushel of corn. He then fed them four- teen days on corn meal cooked, and, after consuming 45 bushels of the cooked meal, they had gained 7991b5., or very nearly 151bs. to the bushel of meill. ENSILAOR.—The following objections to ensilage were made by Harris Lewis, of New York,. in a recent address be- fore a dairymen's association in Canada :—" Its value must depend on one thing—its preservation. If preserved pro- perly it will be advantageous, and will do away with the necessity of feeding roots during the winter in connection with dry good. The feeding of a cow with one class of food, however, is a doubtful thing. It does not constitute a well-balanced food, and hence I should be afraid to use it. If I fed ensilage I should only do so once a day, and feed something else the rest of the time. That might make it valuable. The farmer who proclaims the great success of the system is shrewd enough to feed with the ensilage some good food, hence his cows come out well. But it he would feed it alone for three months they would come out the wrong end of the horn ; or the horns will come off, the hide shrink up, and fall in wrinkles over them. I have played the fool for a whole township, but I have never gone into pie and cake for the dairy cow. That ensilage should have swept this country like a tornado is not surprising. There was a time when men said a dollar could be saved by stew. lug the cow's food; but you may go about the country now and find almost any number of steamers laid up to dry. The farmers found out that it did not pay. The fact was that on it cows could not be kept healthy three months at a time, and I believe that this ensilage will turn out the same way." FEED Dams Cows LIBER&LLY.—WO believe the dairy- man should study how he may produce all the food neces- sary for his cows upon his own farm, and that he should make all the provision that an intelligent foresight can do; but he should never suffer his herd to go with deficient food, even for one week, for this he cannot afford to do. And that we may encourage him to be liberal, even when his pasture is short, and he has no extra 'green food to give them, let us compare the cost of nutriment in some by-pro- duct, such as bran, cottonseed meal, linseed meal, corn meal, &c., some one of which the dairyman may always find near at hand, with pasture grass. Pasture grass has about 80 per cent. of water, and the nutriment in 1001bs of it is sup- posed to be worth 21 cents. The nutriment in 191bs. of fine bran is just equal to 1001bs. of pasture grass; 101bs. of cottonseed meal, 121bs. of linseed meal, or 191bs. of corn meal, is equal to 1001bs. of grass. Now 1001bs. of pasture grass is a ration for an ordinary-sized cow per day. If the pasture, tlaen,is short one-third, or one-half, or in any other proportion, it is easy to make up this deficiency by feeding some one or several of these foods, which are so easily handled. It is seldom that more than one-third would have to be fed to make a full ration on short pasture. Let us suppose the dairyman to be feeding 71bs. of fine bran; this, at &lois. per ton, would cost 2.8 cents per day, or about 19 cents per week. Now the extra milk per week produced by this bran would much more than pay the cost. If he should feed, instead of bran, 41bs of linseed meal, it would cost him about 28 cents per week ; or if 311bs. of cottonseed meal, it would cost 22 cents per week; Of Vbs of corn meal, it would coat from 20 to 35 cents per cow per week. If he has command of these, let him make up a ration nearly as follows: --41b5. bran, P. linseed meal, and lilbs. corn meal to each cow per day, which will in most cases cost only 20 cents per week, and will keep up a generous flow of milk till the fall rains renew the pasture and then the extra food can be discontinued. We have known many who have used an extra ration similar to this during short pasture, and never found one who reported it unprofitable. The ration may be varied to suit all circumsances. Corn meal will be found cheap in some localities; but it is always best to mix some bran with It; and, in most parts of our broad dairy belt, bran will be found the cheapest extra food to make up for short pasture.—National Live Stock Journal, Chi-

that the qualities of the great gipsy race of the South Sea, the Polynesians upon New Zealand have been developed to the highest degree they can attain." Surrounded by ocean, it is not surprising that the Maoris (the word Maori signi- fies native or indigenous to New Zealand) should display a natural fondness for the sea, that they should become ex- pert swimmers, fishers, or canoeists, or that their legend of creation should be a wonderful sea story. According to this legend, "Maui," their traditional hero, a mythic Heroules who achieved great exploits, their instructor in boat and house building, the inventor of flax spinning, the destroyer of the sea monster Tunarua, the lord of fire and water, air and sky—fished up New Zealand out of the sea with the jaw bone of one of his enemies. The North Island, strange to say, does somewhat resemble the shape of a fish, and the natives call it " Te Ilka a Mani,' the fish of" Mani," finding, as they think,a comparison between its various geo- graphical points and the head, tail, fins, gills, Sze., of a fish. No sooner, says the legend, was the fish above water than the brothers of Mani fell upon and cut it up, thus forming the mountains, valleys, and irregularities of the surface. The Maori mythology, of which this is a specimen, contains also wonderful explanations of the origin of the sun, moon, and of the discovery and peopling of New Zealand. All the native traditions relating to the first immigration in New Zealand agree that the original settlers came from a place called Hawaiki, situated to the east or north-east, but where this Hawaiki is, or was, seems very difficult to determine. Some think it refers to "Hamai," in the Sandwich group; again, " Sawai," in the Samoan group, is held to be the place; whilst another authority regards these traditions as mythical, and interprets " Hawaiki" in its literal sense— viz., lying beneath, and as denoting the lower regions, the realms of the dead, and that the natives mean that they came from the place their fathers came from, and to which the souls of the departed return. As Mani raised the earth out of Hawaiki, so the first immigrants hailed from Hawaika. To these mythical founders and heroes each tribe seeks to trace its descent, and on this supposed connection lays claim to this or that heritage of land. These Mani myths extend over the whole of Polynesia, and this fact is justly regarded by Dr. Hockstetter as proving the original unity of the Polynesian race, as certainly as does the conformity of their language. It is supposed that as the Polynesian race is dispersed over islands remote from each other, migra- tions must have taken place, since these true " gipsies of the sea" are to this day characterised by a love of wander- ing; but when and in what direction these migrations first took place, and what the original starting point of the whole race, are problems for the solution of which we are entirely without evidence. A distinct and peculiar people, without any trace of the admixture of foreign elements in their lan- guage, mythys, or ,social habits, we must conclude with Dr. Hochstetter that the Polynesians had their own sphere of creation.

--The history of the Maoris is as obscure as their origin. All agree that the North Island was first inhabited, and the South gradually colonised. Tasman, the first historian of New Zealand, describes the natives as a brown-skinned race, of gigantic stature, their jet black hair tucked up in a bob behind, after the Japanese fashion, and in it a large white feather. They ferociously attacked the boat's crew sent to shore by Tasman, killing three of their number and mor- tally wounding a fourth, deciding Tasman to forsake such an inhospitable shore, and to name it "Massacre Bay." It lies on the north coast of the South Island, and is now called "Golden Bay." To Tasman belongs the honour of first discovering and naming New Zealand, but he did not land on her shores, and merely reported his discovery to the civilised world, characterising the natives as monsters of cruelty and barbarism. It remained for our own famous navigator, Captain Cook, rather more than a century later (1769), not only to touch the shores, but to discover the in- sular character of New Zealand, and by the aid of his Ta- hitian interpreter to gain our first reliable information of its inhabitants. Captain Cook's first experience confirmed the report of their hostile and ferocious disposition, and after several skirmishes, finding friendly intercourse and the sup- ply of provisions impossible, he called the luckles spot "Poverty Bay," and sailed south, discovering the strait which bears his name. Happily Cook found the natives on other parts of the coast less hostile, and more open to inter- course and barter, but he describes them as savages in every sense of the word, their mechanical art, displayed in carved woodwork, in cutting and carving out of the solid trunk of a tree elegant and swift going canoes, and in making hunt- ing, fishing, and fighting weapons; their agriculture, to the growing of two esculent roots—the taro or sweet potato and the kamera, similar in size, but more like an English chest- uut in taste—and these, with fern roots, fish, wild fowl, rats, and human flesh made up their dietary. Their religion was similar to that commonly found in the infancy of nations, a kihd of polytheism or worship of elemen- tary spirits and deified monsters, yet without idols or temples. They also believed in a future state, and in the immortality of the soul. But their chief boast and delight was in war, and the various tribes were frequently engaged in deadly struggles, in which all the cunning, endurance audacity, and ferocity of the race were nurtured and developed. • The most menial work was put upon the women, but they were companions in council and often.in actual war, and it may well be doubted whether the stigma cast upon the character of Maori women is in any degree true or deserved at the period to which we now refer, although it is said that female infanticide was not unknown. Cannibalism, which began most probably in ne- cessity, and then became the utmost triumph of war, throws over all this Maori life a lurid glare, under which the Maori character has appeared and has been painted in wholly un- natural colours. Dr. Hochstetter, however, credits the Maoris with a degree of intelligence and social order scarcely to be expected from cannibals. They lived in vil- lages protected by ditches and pallisades, and surrounded by plantations. They were governed by families of chiefs, after the patriarchial system. Property was common to the whole tribe. Education and character were disciplined after a Spartan fashion. Bravery, cunning, self-command, revenge, and udurance were virtues most esteemed. The boy belonging to the tribe, was never subjected to corporal punishment, for he must grow up brave and independent, not cowardly and submissive; his days spent in learning the art of hnnting and fishing, in games, dancing, and wrest- ling. The sons of chiefs, however, had to learn the tradi- tions, laws, and rites of the people, to be orator and poet, I statesman and warrior, farmer and seaman, hunter and fish- erman, in one person. [For fuller details of the primitive I life of the Maoris, vide Manning's "Old and New Zealand ;" Hochstetter's "New Zealand ;" and a volume in Knight's Library, entitled "New Zealand."] Following Captain „Cook came the occasional visit of a whaler or of a trading ship, and then missionary enterprise, with its civilising influence, social, educational, and reli- gious. Cannibalism, which probably originated in neces- sity, with the introduction of pigs, potatoes, grain, and the influence of Christianity, passed away, and tattooing I became limited to the chiefs and their families. Without at I present entering into the history of European settlement, it I may be remarked that within a quarter of a century the Maoris were outnumbered by the settlers, and the dispro- portion has constantly increased; indeed, the diminution of the Maoris is the saddest and one of the most striking facts of their history. It is believed that only twenty years ago they numbered one hundred thousand, now they are sup- posed to be less than forty-five thousand, residing (all but some two thousand in the South or Middle Island) in this North Island. The European population, on the other hand, now numbers probably between six and seven hundred thousand, and is rapidly increasing. You may ask—Why so fine and robust a race as the Maoris should so perceptibly and rapidly decline ? The answer may not at first sight ap- pear. It has been frequently said and written that the Maoris had already reached their meridian, and had in fact begun to decline when Europeans first settled in these islands; and that their decay was inevitable and could be premised from their inter-tribal fighting and from their sexual habits. I have come to think there is very little truth in this. Maori wars would, of course, like any others, retard the growth of population, but less in proportion when victory depended on physical qualities alone or chiefly, and nothing like to the extent here supposed. The assertion as to the absence of female virtue is, I believe, ac- cording to the testimony of old missionaries, a libel upon Maori character and habits. No, I think the cause of this rapid dwindling of the Maori race is to be sought elsewhere. Suppose we were to reckon up the number of cases of suicide, of fatal accidents, of insanity, and of premature death resulting directly or indirectly, during the last twenty years, from alcoholic drinks, no one would expect the brewers and the publicans for a moment to admit that they or their legitimate traffic were responsible for, or, in- deed, even connected with this hecatomb of victims? Vould not these estimable people assert and argue the undeniable public benefits of their vocation? Would they not, in case of an august national inquest over these prematurely slain, point the jury to the wishes and habits of the de- ceased multitude, to their folly and want of self- control ? Suppose the victims to be these 60,000 Maori's, and substitute the word "drink" by that of "civi- lisation," as embodied in our nation, end I think the decline of the Maoris is no longer a mystery, but merely one on that black roll of extinct or decaying races withered and consumed, not by the true spirit but by the vices of civilisa- tion. Dr. Hochstetter does, I know, represent civilisation as an Angel of Life, summoning the Maori race to a nobler manhood and to higher enjoyments, but if they do not, or cannot accept this higher life, dooming them to extinction. The principle, the soul of civilisation, may indeed be thus imaged as an Angel of Life, for it is the bright, unfettered, and incorruptible intelligence of man ; but civilisation, as the colonising, annexing, commercial, wealth-making spirit of modern times, flaps the air with dark, heavy, vulture-like wings, and to bewildered aboriginal tribes is—the Angel of Death. "Richly endowed by Nature with intellectual and physical powers," writes Dr. Hochstetter, of a lively tem- per, energetic and open :minded, and with T, atn ral wit, the Maori is fully aware of his progress in moral improvement and culture, yet he is not capable of attaining the full height of a Christian civilised life, and it is from this very incompetence that his race is doomed to gradual extinction!' These measured words are not equally true. In some respects of morality and moral perception, the Maori charac- ter may have improved, but not I believe in others; and if in some of the highest qualities of moral character they have improved (although this is questionable), it is not from the transforming beauty of European example, but from the discipline of suffering and adversity. Had "the full height t of a Christian civilised life" been pre-eminently visible o the Maori race, they would have been changed into its image from sheer sympathy and admiration. Only on Friday last, a petition was presented to the House, now sitting at Wel- lington, by one of the native representatives from the Ngatioa Natives, praying for their land to exempted from a proposed rate, on the grounds of their poverty and "the injustice to which they. had been subd'ected by the action of successive Governments in regard to their lands." A simi- lar petition, based on similar grounds, was also prest4ed

div.p: THE EX.MINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 24, 1881.

cago. A NEW COWMILKER.—The American Dairyman describes Durand's cowmilker as a coming success. The use of it, not by hand but by power, is preferred; and we doubt not that the coming American farmer will put his milch cows, per- haps half-a-dozen at a time, on one of his so-called horse- power revolving footbeards—making them thus provide the force necessary, not only to milk themselves, but work the cream separator, churn, and butter-worker as the milking ' proceeds. Not so far off even now as "Utopia" or " Weiss- nicht-wo " is the ideal farm where automatic dairying and artificial harvesting and electric ploughing, threshing and, chaff-cutting will be the ordinary experience of the tenant farmer. Meanwhile we may give the following short account of the new machine, which proceeds on the basis of Colvin's patent, adopting the principle of suction. A hand carries four diaphragm exhaust pumps, and above each pump is a teat-cup. These cups are made of rings of hard rubber, and can be slipped over the outside of teats of un- equal size, and arranged to do their work whether the teats are far apart or close together. When adjusted to the udder the fly-wheel is started, the pumps act, and the milk is drawn intermittently, like calf-sucking and hand-milking, from one teat or more, two on a side, two across, or all four at once. The milk from the four pumps flows into a single flexible tube, which passes along under the arm and enters a large can set in the floor near the foot of the post sup- porting the milker. The can is closed ; no air comes in contact with the milk. The udder being well cleaned to begin with, a more cleanly process of milking is impossible. The editor adds," Having known Mr. D. for over ten years, and being familiar with his business qualifications, we feel satisfied that when he puts his cowmilker upon the market it will meet the approval of all who use it." SOME EFFECTS OF HEAT AND LIMIT ON VEGETATION. I —A curious modification of the normal structure of plant stems has been observed by M. Prillieux on making the tem- perature of the ground about the plant higher than th4t of the air above. Beans and pumpkins gave the best results. The seeds were placed in earth in a large dish, in which was inserted part of a brass rod bent at a right angle, and having a gas flame applied to its horizontal end. The chamber was moist and cool. The seeds germinated well; but on coming above ground the plants acquired a peculiar shape; they grew but little in length, and became unusually thick, the latter growth involving much tension in the surface layers, so that deep rifts before long appeared (mostly transverse), and made further growth impossible. M. Prilliens found the enlargement traceable mainly to an increase, not of the number, but of the volume of cells in the interior (cells of the cortical tissue and, the pith). The excessive growth of these cases occurred not only in the cell walls, but in the nucleus, which was often multiplied. The excess of tem- perature of the ground over the air was about 10 deg. Again, the view adopted by the older botanists that light is either without effect in germination, or has an adverse effect, fails to harmonise with some results lately arrived at by Herr Stabler, in the case of many seeds of agricultural importance, such as varieties of meadow grass (poa), the I germination of which he finds to be favoured considerably more by light than by heat. Thus, with two groups of 400 seeds each of Pea memoralis, in one experiment, there ger- minated in light a per cent., and in darkness 3 per cent. Similarly with Poapratensis— in light, 59 per cent.; in dark- ness, 7 per cent, and so on. Sunlight being a very variable force, difficult of determination, experiments were further made with gaslight, and with the same result—that light favours the germination of certain seeds, especially grasses, ' and that these germinate either not at all, or very scantily, in darkness. The fact was verified by Herr Stebler in quite a series of seeds, Festuca, Cyaosurus, Alopecurus, &c. In the case of seeds that germinate quickly and easily, such as clover, beans, or peas, he thinks light is probably not ad- vantageous.—Times. STORING POTATOES.—A little more than a month ago the lifting of early potatoes was referred to, and all that had attained their fall size we advised should be taken up, whe- ther the haulm was green or not. That this was good ad- vice all will have proved who adopted the practice recom- mended, as they will now have sound tubers, whereas it is more than probable that those left to ripen in the ground have been overtaken by the disease. Long experience has proved that if potatoes are dug when the foliage is quite , green and unspotted by the fungus that the tubers will keep well, even if the skins are so loose as to slip off by being handled ; and it has been further proved that such tubers .not only form fresh skins when thinly stored, but they make the best of sets for planting, and afford at least as early produce and as good crops as tabers do that have been left in the ground to ripen (or rot) in the orthodox manner. Such unripe potatoes are, of course, not good for eating as soon as they are taken up ; but it is a rather singular fact that they in time develop starch, becoming mealy and of good table quality. Early ripening and early lifting of potatoes are the only certain means of evading the disease, except as regards such very strong growers as the Cham- pion, and these, it will be found out by-and-bye, are great soil exhansters, growing as they do for two months after the early sorts may be lifted. Potatoes that are taken up early must be stored thin, dry, and cool. This is of great import- ance for retarding their growth. The chief reason why some potatoes that are planted in the autumn afford a bet- ter return than others planted in the spring is because the whole vitality of the former has been retained in the tubers, whereas the vitality of the latter has been impaired by pre- mature growth and removal or injury of the first sprouts. It is rather amusing to those cultivators who have made potatoes their special study, to read of the advocacy of autumn planting as a new or tentative practice. It is sixty years since it was first adopted, and it is certain that him,' dreds of trials have been made by careful men under vari- ous circumstances. The result is, that the most skilled cultivators now find it advantageous to prepare the seed in- telligently, and plant in the spring.. So firmly established is this practice that it is almost certain that not half a dozen, and probably not one, of the thousands of dishes of the best produce of Great Britain that will be exhibited at the Na- tional Potato Show this month will be the result of autumn planting. By thin storing and careful preparation of the seed far better crops may be had, and are produced every year, than those that have Anen recorded lately from autumn-planted seed.-211a4e:Aane Express. .firr. Cocoa, deprived of the superfluous oil, and guaranteed absolutely pure, is a most soothing, sustaining, and refreshing beverage. THE LAD QUESTION. The Land Question should rise above the level ot party politics, for it is of, national importance, and in the worda of a leading Metropolitan Journal is "the great question of the immediate future." Public opinion is becoming alive to its magnitude and pressing character, and when public opinion is thoroughly educated on the subject, the Reform of our Land Laws will speedily come "within the rang (Apse- ics."

tical It is essentially a landlord's question. A retired Man- chester merchant now resident in the south of England re- cently wrote to the Manchester Guardian :—" In most coun- ties from 20,000 to 40,000 acres are either without tenants, or shortly will be, or are being only half-worked by nearly bankrupt tenants, or by the landlords themselves. In this county there are many persona who have received no tithe, and many more landlords have had little or no rent during the last twelve months." Again, a local journal in one of the southern countieein September last contained upwards. of 100 advertisements of auction sales of farming stock within its own district, embracing 55,000 acres of land given op by the tenants, some of which had been re-let'at a great reduction of rent, but most remained on the owners' hands. It is a farmers' question as the foregoing plainly shows. According to a competent authority in many districts the money loss per acre during the last two or three seasons, I cannot hate been averaged much less than a on arable lands, and probably as much on most of the grazing and pasture lands if loss of sheep and cattle be taken into con- sideration, and doubtless would amount to a total for Eng- land alone of over one hundred millions sterling, of which about two-thirds is estimated to have come out of the pockets of the farmers. The latter, however, have other and stronger grievances than temporary bad seasons, which were briefly alluded to by Professor Fawcett in his speech at Manchestei in January last, when he asked the manu- facturers present what chance they would have of being able to hold their position against foreign competition if they had to rent their mills on such an uncertain tenure that for every piece of improved machinery which they put into their mills, and for every change in the manufactures which they carried out they had first to consider whether or not at the expiration of their lease their rent would not be raised in exact proportion to the extent to which their profits had been increased, and increased too by their own capital, their own energy, and their own skill. Such has been the reward of many an enterprising farmer. It is a working man's question, affecting as it does his food, beef, mutton, bread and cheese, butter and bacon, milk, eggs, poultry, and vegatables. All these products are , affected and increased in price if the land is under a system 1 which tends to limit the quantity, and consequently in- crease the price. The writer does not propose to advance his own unsup- ported opinions on the various subjects touched on in these articles, but intends to quote well-known public men, whose views should carry great weight. He, therefore, cannot do better than give the opinion of the Marquis of Hartiogt n on our present Land System. As heir of the Duke of revon- shire if he ;survives 'his father, he will succeed to nearly 200,000 acres, situated in 14 counties, with an estimatad rental of nearly £200,000, irrespectide of any property in London. He is certainly not open to the charge of being , "a crazy Radical," and yet in the House of Commons he spoke of our "Land System" as "a system under which' the land is divided into large estates, and where the pro- prietors though wealthy men are often not complete masters of their own property, and not able to deal with it as they may desire. It is a system under which the cultivation of the soil is carried on by a class of men (the farmers) who are not the owners of the soil, and under whom the actual cul- tivators of the soil (the labourers) are never and can never hope to become its owners. It is a system under which the land is cultivated by men (the labourers) who have this one claim upon it, that in case of old age or absolute destitu- tion they should be supported without expense, and almost without labour on the land. Such is the land system of this country, and as I have said it is one which prevails in no other country in the world." In other words the great balk of the 40,000,000 acres constituting England and Wales is divided into big estates, which do not really belong to their nominal owners, who have no power to sell or deal with them in the most benefi- cial manner for themselves, the estates, the tenants, or the country. The business of farming is subjected to the tram- mels of injurious laws, and the farmers tied down by strin- gent leases, or have no leases at all, being simply. tenants at will, while the labourers have been aptly described as "leading a life of toil down hill, with the workhouse at the bottom ;" while another writer, referring to them, says "111-housed, ill-clothed, and ill-fed from childhood to old age, they toil in the fields that others may reap the fruits of their labour, for the workhouse pittance is their reward in the end." What are the practical effects of this marvellous system to which by habit we are accustomed? 1. Anyone who knows much oragricultnre will admit at once that there is very great room for better farming, and that if improved methods were adopted by the application of capital to the soil we should produce a large quantity of the food which we now have to purchase from abroad, and thereby keep that amount of money in the country to the improvement of the home trade. The Earl of Leicester, a nobleman who made agriculture his study, writes," I have [travelled through much of England and through parts of Scotland, and taking into consideration the whole of the land I have seen under cultivation I think I may safely say that the produce might be nearly doubled under a more per- feet system of agriculture." The late Mr. Mechi, also a great authority on agriculture, wrote, "There are many millions of acres of exhausted grass lands and poor stiff clays which now bind the tenant in poverty and discontent that would be rendered profitable by an investment of from £2O to £35 per acre," in improvements, which be specified, and. so on the evidence of others might be given were it t. We are suffering at the present time from a glut of capital, much of which is lying comparatively unproductive, vrhile Railway Companies and Municipal Corporations can have as' mach money as they' like at n per cent., and no safe investment can be got which will pay more than 4 per cent, and yet it is estimated that if the area at present under cultivation were thoroughly drained and otherwise put in a condition to bring forth the best possible crops, the expenditure, and very profitable expenditure too, would be at least 500 millions sterling, to say nothing of the cost of reclaiming waste lands. This would furnish a vast field of labour for many who now have to emigrate, but being thus employed would increase the home market for manufac- tured and other goods resulting in better trade. 3. In the face of all this indifferent cultivation and com- parative unproductiveness of the soil of the country, arising from the want of the application of that capital, waiting investment, what do we find as to our imports of food from abroad, food of a kind which wa can produce ourselves? The following is a list for 1879 :- 1 Quantity. Value Oxen—Bulls, Cows, and Calves ...No. 247,768 ... £4,639,431 Sheep and Lambs 944,888 ... 2,252,824 Bacon and Hams cwt. 4,917,631 ... 8,880,223 Beef Butter Cheese 8,824,017 t Corn—Wheat „ 59,591,795 ... 31,468,171 „ Other kinds Flour—Wheat Other kinds Eggs No. 766,707,840 ... 2,295,720 Lard cwt. 840,819 ... 1,420,881 Meat—Fresh or salted 153,384 ... 440,726 Otherwise preserved ,, 567,877 ... 1,690,020 Pork—Fresh Potatoes

Total £102,410,484 To put it in another form, Mr. Caird estimates that in 1877 the value per head of the population of the foreign food imported into the United Kingdom was nearly £3, or, in other words, every householder (taking each family at five) paid in that year at least £1.5 to foreign countries for the necessaries and simplest luxuries of life. What is the remedy for the state of things briefly re- ferred to above? The Reform of "The Land Laws," as follows : Abolition of the Law of Primogeniture. Gradual Extinction of Entail and Life Estates. Easy and Cheap Transfer of Land and Registration of Titles.

div.head: NEW ZEALAND: THE MAORIS.
div.p: NEW ZEALAND: THE MAORIS.

Free Land. Security to the Tenant for Improvements. Greater Freedom of Cultivation. Abolition of Game Laws. Abolition of Law of Distress as to Farm Tenancies. Re-adjustment of Land Tax. Reform of Tithes. The cultivation of all land capable of it, or, stated in more general terms, the Reform of the Land Laws of this country, should include the removal of the restrictions im- posed by the existing laws of Primogeniture, Entail, and Settlement, and the adjustment of the relations between Landlord and Tenant, so as to protect the property and in- terest alike of owner and occupier ; and, further, it should facilitate the sale and transfer of land, and afford oppor- tunity for the gradual acquirement by the agricultural population of some portion of the soil they cultivate. There are those in this country who, having neither read or thought much on the subject, regard any interference with the Land Question as almost "profanity and sacrilege." On suggesting Reforms, their prejudice and want of know- ledge prevent their inquiring into the reasonable or neces- sity of such Reforms, and cause them to act something like the men of Ephesus who refused to hear Paul, and "all with one voice, about the space of two hours, cried out, • Great is Diana of the Ephesians.' " Their leaders, how- ever, who are interested in or prefer the continuance of the present system, do not hesitate to denounce alike Reforms and Reformers in unmeasured terms, charging them with Socialism, Communism, and the like, but we may answer, in the profound words of Lord Chancellor Selborne, when defending, in August, the Irish Land Bill in the House of Lords 1—" He felt as strongly as any of their Lordships that the laws of a country which governed the tenure of property ought not to be lightly altered- But all the laws of property and tenure were made for men, and they must be changed and adjusted when the pressure of circumstances required it, and the safety of the State made it necessary; and such adjustments, however apt men might be to de- nounce them as unjust, and revolutionary, and with all the other words furnished by the dictionary of vituperation, would appear both just and beneficial, and not to one class only, but to all the classes concerned in them, when they were zhade to maintain the substance of right and wrong without altering their conditions and their form. Still more when they were made so as to place the enjoyment of rights upon a more secure basis.

No fewer than 328,000 immigrants have landed at New York this year, and it is expected that the arrivals next month will be unprecedentedly large. . The rite of baptism by immersion was administered on the 11th instant by the vicar of Gwyddelwern, near Corwen, to two candidates for confirmation who had never been bap- tized, and whose parents were Baptists. The ceremony took place in a brook near the church, and was witnessed by crowds of people. A DIAMOND WEDDING.—Last week Mr. and Mrs., Wyatt, of Bryngwynant, Carnarvonshire, celebrated the sixtieth anniversary of their wedding-day, generally known as a diamond wedding. There were present on the occasion all the seven children, and the company included representatives of four generations. The Shrewsbury Board of Guardians on Monday passed a resolution requesting unions throughout the country to adopt a memorial to Parliament urging immediate legisla- tion on the subject of vagrancy. The Board were of opinion that the only remedy for the present state of things lies in increasing the period of detention in the vagrant wards. 1 Sir Henry Brand (the speaker) addressed a meeting at Glynde harvest home, Sussex, on Saturday. Whatever might be said to the contrary, he thought the present prices were fair as between producer and consumer. The taxation I placed on the farmer was somewhat unfair, and this was a matter deserving the attention of Parliament. He ridiculed the idea of returning to protection when the consumption of necessaries so greatly exceeded the production. The land agitation in the north of Scotland is assuming prominence. A meeting of tenant farmers throughout Aber- deenshire, Banffshire, and the adjoining counties, have already arranged for holding demonstrations, at which reso- lutions will be submitted with the object of petitioning the Government to take into consideration the depressed state of agriculture with a view to its amelioration as far as pos- sible by legislation. On Saturday, on the Bradford Borough Police Court assembling, the Mayor (Alderman Angus Holden,) upon taking his seat, was presented by the magistrates' clerk with a pair of white gloves, there being neither prisoners to deal with nor summonses to hear. This is the second time within three months that a maiden sitting of the Police Cburt has occurred; and this fact, remembering that the population of the borough is over 200,000, was remarked upon by the Mayor. One of the agricultural joarnals, in its weekly review of the British corn trade, says the •great improvement in the weather, the brilliant sunshine, and the general advance in temperature augur well for the completion of the harvest in the later districts, where no doubt better results will be obtained than in the earlier districts. Although the weather has been finer and thrashing more frequent, the de- liveries of home-grown produce have not increased to any extent. The members of the Batley Liberal Association, while on a ttip on Monday, with a number of their friends to Hanel] den, were briefly addressed by Mr. Gladstone, who come upon the party as he was going for a drive in the park. He observed that he had been obliged from reasons of public utility to make it a rule that no more addresses should be made by him in that park. He was the less pained at feeling it necessary to avoid speaking at auy length to them because he would shortly have an opportunity of meeting many of them in Yorkshire in chcumstances when he would not be placed under any such THE SPEAKER ON SHEEP BREEDING—Sir Henry Brand presided on Monday at a luncheon at Beddingham, near Lewes, on a farm forming part of his estate, which was for- merly the home of the celebrated Southdown breed of sheep. The 'flock offered for sale numbered over 1,000 head. Pre- vious to the sale Sir Henry proposed the health of the re- tiring tenant, and, alluding to sheep breeding, said his experience of farming in recent years was that the flock was the only satisfactory part of the business. As the price of mutton was sure to advance, the sale offered a good oppor- tunity for investment. England, he said, contained at the present time a million less sheep than it did three years ago. PROPOSED PEACE CONFERENCE AT LEEDS.—At a prelim- inary meeting on this subject held in Leeds, under the presidency of the Mayor, the following resolution was pro- posed by Mr. Thomas Harvey, seconded by the Rev. W. Thomas, and unanimously adopted:—" That this meet- ing considers it desirable that a conference of ministers of religion and other influential persons of the northern counties should be held about the middle of November in Leeds to consider—M.) the anti-Christian nature and leni- ency of war; (2) the best means of solving international difficulties without resorting to war; (3) the enormous evils of military establishments and standing armies."—lt is pro- posed that short papers on these questions, to be prepared by members of different denominations, shall form the basis of the deliberations at the Conference. A crafty licensed victualler at Glossop, being visited the other night by the police at an hour when his house ought to have been closed, adopted the ingenious idea of putting to bed the one man in the house, who being a tradesman resident in the town was reasonably open to suspicion of illicit drinking. The police after some delay were admitted and saw this man in bed. They recognised him, and being equal to the emergency waited outside. After their patience had been exercised for half an hour the gentleman who had been in bed emerged from the house and walked home. The consequence was the appearance of the crest-fallen inn- keeper before the justices on Monday, and a conviction cvith a 40s. penalty attached to it. A CLUB SCANDAL.—At a certain foreign club noted for high play a member was suspected of cheating. This man, who wore dark-coloured, glasses, was closely watched, and although his winnings were ascribed to something more than a run of luck, nothing could be proved against him. When he left the cards were always strictly examined and scrutinized under a magnifying-glass, but no clue to the mystery could be obtained. One night the secretary had occasion to go to to the drawer of his desk, in which the cards had been put away. His candle went out, and feeling in the draw he saw some luminous dots. The secret was , out. The cards were marked with phosphorous, and thanks ' to the dark-coloured spectacles, the dots were visible to the wearer of them alone.—Society. Lord Randolph Churchill M.P., spoke on Saturday at a meeting in connection with the Oldham Conservative Working Men's League. He urged that the remedy for the depression in trade was to be found in restoring to the agricultural interest some measure of its former prosperity: "in other words, in building up again with much care, t.nd even with some temporary sacrifice, that home market on which we must for the future chiefly rely for the sale of our goods." A safe and expeditious way of attaining this result would be to take off a large portion of the burdens upon land, which should be assumed by the State, the rev- enue for this being obtained by imposing taxes which would fall upon the foreigner. He likened foreign markets to oysters. To open an oyster they did not tickle it with a feather, but used a strong-bladed knife. Mr. Chamberlain and Mr. Bright were trying to tickle foreign markets into opening themselves with the feathers of theory and entreaty. Let the Government use the strong-bladed knife of increased Customs duties, and they would make a sensible impresion upon those markets. DEATH OF THE ORIGINATOR OF MOTHERS' MEETINGS?' —The death of Mrs. Mary Chadderton, who was the originator, and has for the past thirty years been the conduc- tor of mothers' meetings, is announced. The deceased lady was born at Blackburn in 1820. At the age of twelve she went to reside in the district of Bury. In 1846 she was ntarried to Mr. Samuel Chadderton, of Bury. Both Mrs. Chadderton and her husband were members of the Wes- leyan body. They came to reside in Manchester in 1849. Two years later she commenced the mothers meetings, which have continued with unabated success to the present time. The meetings are now held in Walker-street, Old- ham-road, with an average attendance of 250. A great feature in summer time is the annual trip, at which there is an attendance varying from 300 to 500 persons. The trip this summer was to Morecambe. The day was wet and chilly, and his supposed Mrs. Chadderton caught a cold, which re- sulted in her death, on Friday last, at her residence, 43, Queen's-road, Queen's Park. Mothers' meetings on the principles she adopted have since been formed in many towns. During her ministrations she had endeared to her a large circle of friends, who deeply feel the loss they have sustained. THO METHODIST CECUMBNICIL CONFERENCE—This con- fer ence was brought to a close in London on Monday. The Bev. R. Chew (Methodist Free Church) was president. The subject for discussion was " Foreign Missions." The first paper was read by the Rev. Wyman H. Potter, up. (Metho- dist Episcopal Church), on the establishment and support of training schools for native converts and native ministers in the foreign field. He contended that it was of the utmost importance that Methodist seeels :.uuld exist for the pur- pose of the training of coutverl 5 preachers. He urged that the Church should support. Reel schools liberally, because, beside the provision of nati preachers, the existence of such institutions in the midst or the people whence the con- verts came must have a beneficial effect. 'The Rev. John Kilner, of the British Wesleyan Methodist Church, argued that every organised mission of the people should have some training institution, carried on under the very best supervision. The Rev. Dr. Clarke, of 'Georgia, urged that training colleges should be supported by the whole of the Methodists. The Rev. J. Calvert said that in Fiji they had 23,000 Church members and 5,000 on trial for Chinch mem- bership. Mr. E. Lumley, of Halifax, who was attending the conference, died suddenly in the morning. A WELSH VICAR AND ins TITHES.—A jircular issued by the Rev. Owen A. Nares, vicar of Kerry, Melntgomeryshire, and Vice-Chairman of Newtown and Llanidloes Board of Guardians has created a sensation in the neighbourhood. It is as follows: "Regulation for the collection of vicarial tithes in the parish of Kerry. The tithes becoming due on the Ist Jan. and Ist July will be collected during the first seven days of the months of February and August respectively in each year. Whoever shall neglect to pay the full amounts of tithe due before the 7th February and August respectively, shall receive a notice to distress at the expiration of ten days for the recovery of the whole, or such part of the tithe as may remain unpaid, as the law directs. For the conveni-, ence of tithepayers who may he in arrear, the vicar will suspend the distress in the event of such payers signing an agreement (to be provided at their own cost) that they will pay the amount in arrear within a period of six months, together with interest thereon at the rate of 5 per cent, per annum, and the cost of notice, the interest to be calculated , from the let January and the let July, as the case may be. (Signed), OWEN A. NAMES." An endorsement on the circular, by the the vicar's agent, says:—" I am authorised to add that notice of distress will be issued at the expiration of ten days from date on those tithe-payers who shall not have previously settled their tithes, or have signed the on (Ii

I do not profess to know the Maoris ; they can only be known by those who live amongst them, and that I have had neither the pleasure nor discomfort of doing. I say pleasure, because there must be a bracing hilarity and a tonic jest in natural outdoor pursuits mid wood and sea, with hospitable, vivacious, and sharp-witted companions, adepts at sport. I say discomfort, because Englishmen hardly relish spending the night, wet or fine, under the canopy of heaven, rolled up in a blanket ; nor would they enjoy spending it inside a " whare," or native mud hut, in contact with that world of minute animal life which is said always to surround a Maori and to vivify his dwelling. Few Europeans have shared that life for any length of tone, and fewer still have shared it long who have been capable of resisting its lower tendencies, and also capable of precisely delineating its features and presenting a faithful portrait to the English public. Perhaps the portrait cannot be exactly true or complete until touched and finished by the hand of a Maori himself. Do we expect a foreigner to write the truest and most reliable history of English social, political, and religious life? The Maoris have their pro- phets and their poets; who knows but some day they will have their Carlyle or their Mottley, whose pen, like iron upon the flinty rock, scattering burning words, shall "ring out the false, and ring in the true" of Maori history ? This at least is certain—the Maoris are a singular race, with great force of character, with many natural endowments, and deserve to be faithfully represented. Such at least is my first impression, and first impressions are all I can venture to give. Once for all, allow me to admit that it is difficult, perhaps impossible, for a young Colonist to avoid falling into occasional error, or of being misinformed ; and to this rule I am myself no exception ; but one assurance I can .give, and that is, an earnest wish to know the truth upon any subject which has formed part of this correspondence. I may also add that for the most part, it has (before being , posted) been read to one of the best informed and most intelligent critics it is possible to find throughout New Zealand. An impression still lingers that the proximity of the Maoris, who have often been described as a race of fighting cannibals, is a standing danger to European settlers in the I colony. t is, however, very possible to reside a lifetime in a New Zealand town, and beyond the occasional sight of a Maori passing down the street, or staring with childish wonder into a shop window, or calling at the door to sell a basket of peaches, or being dragged in ki state of sleepy drunkenness to the lock-up, or lounging about the Supreme Court when a native case is going on, know nothing and become oblivious of the fact that around us, scattered espe- cially over the North Island, a distinct and remarkable race of people, once its sole occupiers, is silently and rapidly dwindling in numbers and importance, and destined ere long from conquering and decaying influences within and with- out to become as historical as our ancient Britons. The other day a Maori lady, gaudily dressed, with large ear- rings, came into my room, carrying in her arms a bonnie boy, about twelve months old. She had the sacred but very ugly tattoo marks from the outer edge of the lower lip down the chin, betokening her rank as a Princess. She was accompanied by a gentle Maori girl, about twenty years old, shy and refined, who, having been tattood, had also .the public schools could speak English more purely than many of our Lancashire girls of the same age, and acted as inter- preter. The only English word the Princess could utter was " fightened,' pointing to a sadly decayed molar which she wished to retain. Her teeth were beautiful, pearly white in colour and embedded in perfectly healthy mem- branes and process. Her complexion was lighter than is usual among the Maoris, and her eyes glistened large and dirk like those of an English gipsy. Both the Princess and her interpreter I found had lost several teeth, and that the Maoris who live in or near the towns frequently suffer from toothache, but those who live in the "bush" do not. To gain a good look at the Maori's it is necessary to go to one ot their settlements, say, to the small one at Oraki Bay, on the western side of the Waitemata waters, and some six miles from Auckland. A little time ago there was a Maori Parliament," as it is called, at Oraki, that is a gathering of natives to discuss Maori affairs, particularly in reference to the land, its ownership and boundaries, and to disputes with Europeats concerning the same. The speech- making and feasting continue for several days; the natives then separate to their various localities. Wishing to see something of this Oraki gathering, I walked, under a hot sun, following a road winding round bay after bay until suddenly, on a flat blot of ground close to the rolling music of toe Wairelnata tide-waves and begirt with a rocky coast and hilly in land scenery, .1. came upon the settlement, or what, but for the few houses, I could have supposed to be a large gipsy encampment. To nearly every tree a wiry look- ing pig was fastened by a rope; a number of dogs (the Maoris are fond of dogs and refuse to pay the dog-register tax) were lying on the pathway, whilst squatted on the grass a group of women hard by smoked in silent gravity the cahnet of peace, pausing for an instant to utter with sharp metallic voice the greeting word, " Tena-koe." A four-roomed cottage, boasting a bay window, the residence of Paul the Chief, with a few smaller cottages and a school- house made up the habitations; but there was in addition a long low shed witn partitions, very similar to a row of dog kennels seen at agricultural shows, in which lay huddled the newly-arrived Maoris, who had marched- many miles with their carpet bags to attend the Parliament, and now lay smoking and. chatting, but by their expression resenting the curiosity of the " Pakeha." Unusual activity pervaded the settlement. Here, a stout Maori woman was cooking fish in a large hole apparently full of stones, the fish being underneath; in an adjoining cottage, lithe and good-natured young men were busy making an English plum pudding; outside, laughing young Maori girls and men bandied joke and repartee, and an air of important business on hand sat upon the earnest faces of the elders. Drying in the sun were scores of sharks and a host of small fry, and heaps of potatoes lay ready for the feast; and children of all ages skip and glide with elastic step, erect and happy. Pre- sently we are told that one of the orators is speaking, and proceeding to a low white-washed building, its door Posts carved with hideous heads, we stoop down and peep inside. In the right corner of the room sits an old man with fine features and lofty forehead, his arm spasmodically beating the air, as in a strange but not unmusical tongue he persistently declaimed against the survey and acquisition of land by the " Pakehas ' in the district of Waikato. The orator squatted on the floor like a tailor, but his bearers lay at full length in regular order, women and men, and lis- tened in patient silence or closed their eyes in sleepy medi- tation. In the middle of the room were placed small heaps of food, fish and potatoes, for what. object I could not di- vine. The Maoris are not as a rule given to hurry, and cer- tainly this venerable orator with his grey closely cut hair and bronzed face was in no haste, but continued his dis- course for hours, revolving this one topic, the land griev- ance. Outside stood a good-natured Maori, who interpreted to us a portion of the oration. Look at this man, he is a typical better-class Maori, with broad face, regular, strong, and compact features, full of power and expression, with abundance of black hair, and large, dark, glittering eyes rolling in a yellow sea, a large, broad, mobile nose, thick lips, splendid 'teeth, and powerful maxillw. Mightily did he laugh when I said to him, "The Maoris have good teeth," for he thought I made a sly allusion to their capa- city for eating. He stands 51 t. Pin. in height, broad and thickly bullt, and would not be a pleasant man to struggle with. The women, too, are broad and powerful, but they are not beautiful (save to Maori eyes), and have usually broad, mobile features, the lips are full and collapse; the young carry a merry face, and when they laugh their teeth almoe shine out upon you; but upon the elderly rests a seda'.eness, a settled, sad, thoughtfulness, a depth and re- serve of feeling in harmony with the raven tresses of their flowing hair, and with the quiet gaze of their dark, lustrous, arid impenetrable eyes. As to dress, the Maoris exhibit a medley of tastes. Now you see a stalwart figure loosely surrounded by a blanket; another with dirty-white trousers and a checked red woollen shawl thrown round his ehoul- ders ; a third appears in the costume of an English workman. Diversity of taste also reigns among the women. Some ap- pear in plain and badly-fitting dresses, others in a short petticoat and a shawl (somewhat after our common Lan- cashire fashion), whilst now and again a Maori lady of rank parades in gaudy and costly attire, but fails amusingly to look elegant or ladylike. Yet it is impossible not to feel an interest in this people, —impossible to listen to their vivacious prattle, to watch the long and springy stride of their lithe and muscular forms, to smile with the laughing faces of their young men and women, and to mark the resigned, self-controlled ex- pression of elderly Maoris, without asking who and what they are, what their history and condition, and why they should be swept away into the limbo of defunct nationali- ties, whether by innate weakness or from the dubious and bewildering influences of a civilisation they are unable to resist.

The numerous islands scattered over the Pacific Ocean are inhabited by two diverse races. The South-Western region, comprising New Guinea, New Ireland, Solomon Islands, Fiji, Sze., is occupied by a race very dark, almost black in complexion, ungainly in figure' of low intelligence, and scarcely capable of civilisation. They are called Melane- sians or Papnas, and are closely akin to the Aborigines of Australia and Tasmania. The second race is distributed over the islands extending from the Pelew group on the west to Easter Island east, including in particular the Sand- wich Islands in the north and New Zealand in the south. They are lighter in complexion than the former race, in all the shades of brown, much finer in physique, and of higher intelligence, and are akin to the Malay tribes inhabiting the peninsula of Malacca, Borneo, Celebes, Szc. They are de- signated the Malay Polynesian race. These again are divided into Mikronesians and Polynesians proper, the former comprising the Western Islands from the Kingmill groupfrom staomtohae aPnedl e Tw olnsgl aan da ss, t fareh as late Et ear ttehr Ea aans tde,r nt algs leatnhde rs with-the Sandwich Islands and New Zealand. European ideas, and rank much higher in the scale of civilisation than the Melanesians or Mikronesians. Of the Polynesian family the natives of New Zealand form the most important branch, both as to numbaerreindencdoowparmeinstsn. div.head: DEATH OF PRESIDENT GARFIgLD.
div.p: DEATH OF PRESIDENT GARFIgLD.

The suspense which since thei commencement of July has existed as to the fate of General Garfield is now at an end. ' The wounded President experienced a most alarming relapse on Saturday, and on Monday evening was telegraphed from LOng Branch the sorrowful but not unexpected news that he was dead. Saturday's history was a peculiar one. In the morning the President's condition was so favourable that everybody was encouraged. At noon the startling announce- ment was made that the President bad had a rigour, lasting half an hour, during which the pulse reached 137. Panic followed. The general belief was that the end had come. The chill was taken as evidence that an abscess had been formed in the lung. A few minutes later came the state- tnent that the President was vomiting. Then the most sanguine abandoned hope. Towards night the news became less alarming. The fatal attack commenced at half-past eight o'clock on Monday morning, when the President, 'though he had previously passed a comfortable night, bad another very severe rigour lasting twenty minutes. Dr. Bliss said that if the chills continued during the next 48 hours the President could not live, and it was possible that he might die in one of them. At eleven o'clock• Dr. Agnew said the situation was decidedly gloomy, the President not having rallied from the effects of the rigour. Much excite- ment prevailed, and the worst fears were entertained. The physicians' bulletin issued 12-30 stated that the chill lasted for 15 minutes, and was followed by a febrile rise in the temperature and by sweating. The President had slept for some time, but his condition was not materially changed. Pulse, 104; temperature, 982; respiration, 20. He after the morning dressing of his wound called for a hand glass, and after looking in it said; "I cannot understand why lam so weak when I look so well." His voice was not so hoarse as when the parotid gland was inflamed. At three o'clock in the afternoon there was no-change. Dr. Agnew expressed grave apprehension. The President was sleeping. At six o'clock the following official bulletin was issned:"Although the gravity of the President's condition continues, there has been no aggravation of the symptoms since noon. He has slept most of the time, coughing but little and with ease. The sputa remains uncl-ainged. Sufficient nourishmenthas been taken and retained. Pulse, 102; temperature, 984; respiration, Ri." The following official telegram was des- patched from Longbranch between 10 and 10-30, just before the death:—" The President had another chill of considerable severity this morning, which, following so soon after the chill of last evening, left him very weak. Indeed his pulse became more frequent and feeble than at any time since he recovered from the immediate shock of the wound, and his general condition was more alarming. During the day his symptom has reacted to some extent, and he passed the after- noon and evening comfortably. At this hour he is resting quietly, and no disturbance is expected during the night. There has been, however, no gain whatever in strength, and there is therefore no decrease of anxiety.--51'VE50u." A few minutes after the receipt of this telegram in London came the following:—" The President has just' died.— WAYNE MTELOII." The intelligence was received through- out England with mournful interest In this, as as other districts, flags were: hoisted half mast high on the public buildings, and the latest telegrams that were ex- hibited were read with great eagerness. Telegrams have beed received from the Queen and the Princess of Wales ex- pressing profound sympathy with Mrs. Garfield at her irre- parable loss. The Queen's message to Mr. Lowell states:— It is with deep regret that I and my children have learned the sad but not unexpected news of the fatal termination of the sufferings of the President. His loss is a great misfor- tune. The Prince of Wales's message says :—The Princess of Wales and myself beg to offer our sincere condolence to Mrs. Garfield. GENERAL GARFIELD'S CAREER. From a biographical sketch recently published the follow- ing particulars as to the career of the deceased President are quoted :—James Abram Garfield was born on the 19th November. 1831, in Ohio. His father, who was of Massa- chussetta stock, together with his wife, the future Presi- dent's mother, a native of New Hampshire, settled in the Ohio forest in January, 1830. Here Abram Garfield, a man of remarkable energy, purchased a tract of heavily wooded land, built a small house of logs, and began his struggle of life. Unhaviily, while still plodding his way upward, the father was carried off by inflammation of the throat, leaving behind him, most scantily provided for, a widow and four children. The future President was then only an infant. During the ten years which followed the father's death the family endured great hardships and privations. Mrs. Gar- field toiled and laboured to keep her children together under a like children's clothing own eye and care. In some way the fields were ploughed ande planted and the scanty harvests gathered. She made h g with her own bands, and performed ike service for the family of a neighbouring shoemaker, in return for which he made rude but substantial shoes for the little Garfields. During the winters, while the country was covered with snow, and all farm work except cutting wo oci and caring for the cattle necessarily suspended, the children, as soon as they were old enough, attended the neighbouring district school, and there, as well as from the teachings of his mother, the future President received his first taste of book-lore, which in later years was to inspire him with the passionate ambition of scholarship. From three years of age until ten the boy attended the daily ses- sions of that primitive school. Thenceforward, he was com- pelled during part of each year to share somewhat in the labour of the farm. He was from childhood phenomenally precocious, both physically and mentally. When eight years Of age he had read all the books that his poor Mother could provide, and began borrowing from the scanty libra- ries of the neighbours. At the age of 16 he made a contract with his cousin to cut one hundred cords of wood for the sum of twenty-five dollars. The task was performed in a tract of high woodland which commanded a view of Lake Erie, upon whose blue waters he could see the steamers and sailing vessels entering and leaving the port of Cleveland. The young Viking had resolved to become a sailor, and he began as a canal driver, not because be had any liking for the business, but because it gave him employment by which money could be earned and something learned of navigation. He would take his first degree, he thought, on the canal, and then push for the blue sea and the ships that sail to distant lands. At the end of three months of canal driving he was carried to his mother's home in Orange, delirious with ma- larial fever. That illness gave his mother the opportunity for which she had prayed, and during the five months of slow convalescence through which she nursed him back to health, she planted in his mind the seeds of a new and higher ambition. When her books had all been read to him and her words of counsel exhausted, the schoolmaster was called in to add his scholarly advice. Thus persuaded, young James, on his recovery, went to the Geauga Seminarv, 14 miles distant, and' with but 17 do'lars is his pocket enrolled himself as a student, and began the study of Latin, Greek, and mathematics. While at the Geauga Seminary he had embraced religion, and joined a religious body known as the "Disciples of Christ," the same who have been otherwise called " Camp- hellites." The creed of the " Disciples " is simply a belief in the New Testament, the divinity Gf Christ and His atone- ment, in baptism by immersion, and, for the rest, "protest against imposing as a condition of church membership any human formula of divine truth." The progress of the "Disciples" in Northern Ohio led to the establishment of an academical school in the village of Hiram, thirty miles from Cleveland. Here the future ministers and elders of the church were educated. To this "school of the prophets" young Garfield went, first as a scholar, next as a tutor, and finally as a teacher. His progress was marked, and in a short time he was qualified to enter Williams College, one of the oldest and most advanced of all the institutions of learn- ing in New England. President Hopkins took kindly to the young Western student, whose gigantic size made him as conspicuous as his proficiency in Greek and Latin made him distinguished. After two years at Williams College he went back to Hiram seminary as professor of ancient lan- guages and English literature, and at the end of a year he became president of the institution. He was now (1857) twenty-six years of age, and, while fell of energy himself, had a happy way of imparting that energy to all, who came under his influence. There were three hundred students in the institution at that time, and no one could be indifferent to the great aims and purposes of education who listened to his lectures. The early morning assembly, which usually extended over an hour, was a good start for the day. Pro- ceedings commenced with prayer in the chapel, then a chapter of the Bible was read, followed by an extempora- neous address, sometimes upon a Scripture subject, some- times Cu some recent political event, or some scientific subject, or upon a new book. Once, it is said, he took the newspaper report of the tragic death of Hugh Miller, setting forth the lessons of his noble life in words which made a profound impression. Manliness was one distinguishing feature of his character, and he strove to inspire the young exercises, football men of the institution with like habits, as also of self- reliance and courage.and cricketT hey beingwe r were the encouragedgam esi h in athletic h e excelled, efforts He and in which he personally euperintended their alsaeid, drew them tbhoZ of iretco;anridtsionhim; :o single that, wasonolnferoomf them has him, seas to me an inspiration." Into " these discussions Garfield threw his strength, and in the ex- tension and triumphs of the party and its cause he boreaconspicuous part. In 1859, when he was only 28 years old, he was elected a State senator for Ohio. Soon after this the !mouldering embers of rebellion in the Southern slave-hold- ing States broke out into flame. Garfield had already
