become one of the acknowledged leaders of the Radical branch of the Republican party, forming with J. 0. Cox (afterwards Governor of Ohio), and Professor Muncre, of Oberlin College, tha "Radical Triumvirate." They saw the storm coming, but hoped it would pass ever without a general war, or, at least, without a conflict of so destructive and bitter a character as ensued. The disaster at Bull Run I dispelled all such hopes. Seven days after Senator. Garfield accepted a commission as lieutenant-colonel of a regiment then organising at Camp Chase. His con- duct in the war and his election to the Congress by his native State are still fresh in memory, and after his elevation to the White House as President he won golden opinions not only amongst his own countrymen but in Europe.where his death is widely lamented. A writer in Scribner's Monthly, speaking of General Gar- field just before the assassination, said :—Never within our memory has so brilliant a man as General Garfield occupied the presidential office. A man of splendid gifts, of thorough education, of wide and long familiarity with public life, of intimate practical acquainance with the public business, of first-class oratorical power, he is altogether an exceptional man. Of the long list of Presidents since John Quincey Adams, no map but Martin Van Buren could be compared with General Garfield in native gifts and public culture. As a scholar and an orator he is much above what Lincoln was at his beat, and much above Hayes. A genial man, a manly man, a courageous Man, who is used to meeting and acting upon men, who through a legislative experience of many years has become familiar with all public business, and whose habit during all this period has been that of battling for the right, as he in judgment and conscience apprehended it—a man equipped with talent of the best, with wide learn- ing held safely and serviceable in a marvellous memory, and with oratorical powers of great readiness and brillia:ncy, this is Garfield, the President-elect. THE CAUSE OF DEATH. THE POST-MORTEM EXAMINATION. _ LONG BRLNCH, SEPT. 21.—1 t is officially stated that at I the post-mortem examination made yesterday afternoon, it I was found that the ball, after fracturing the eleventh rib on the right side, had passed through the spinal column in front of the spinal canal, fracturing the body of the first I lumbar vertebra, and driving a number of small fragments of bone into the adjacent soft parts, finally lodging below the pancreas, about two inches and a half to the left of the spine, and behind the peritoneum, where it had become completely encysted. The Immediate cause ot death was secondary hemorrhage from one of the mesenterie arteries adjoining the track of the ball, the blood rupturing the peritoneum, and nearly a pint escaping into the abdominal cavity. This hemorrhage is believed to have been the cause of the severe pain in the lower part of the chest which the President complained of just before his (death. An abscess cavity, six inches long by four wide Was found in the vicinity of the gall bladder, between be liver and the trans- verse colon, which were strongly adherent. It did not involve the substance of the liver, and no communication was found between it and the wound. A !ono. suppurating channel extended from the external wound' between the muscles of the loin and the right kidney almost as far as the right groin. This channel is now known to have been due to the burrowing of pus from the wound, and was supposed. during the life of the President, to have been the track of the ball. On examination of the organs of the chest evid- ences of severe bronchitis were found on both sides, with hroncho pnuernonia of the lower portion of the right lung, and also of the left, though to a much less extent. The lungs contained no abscesses, and the heart no clots of blood. The liver was large and fatty, but free from abscesses, nor were any found in any other organ except in the left kidney, which contained, near to its surface, a small abscess about one-third of an inch in diameter. In ie viewing the history Of the case in cofineetion with the autopsy, it is quite evident that the different suppurating surfaces, and especially the fracture and spongy tissue of the vertebra, furnish significant explanations of the septic condition

which existed. SYMPATHY WITH MRS. GARFIELD. Mrs. Garfield has received the following telegram from Queen Victoria Words cannot express the deep sym- pathy I fe6l with you at this terrible moment. May God support and comfort you as Be alone can." The Queen telegraphed to the 'American Legation as fol- lows :—lt is with deep grief tiiit I and my children have learned the serif but not unexprcted news of the fatal ter- mination of the sufferings of the President. His loss is a

great misfortune." A telegram was also received from the Prince of Wales, as follows:—"It is with deep sorrow that we learn that the the President has passed away. The Princess and myself beg you to offer our sincere condolence to Mrs. Garfield." Telegrams expressing sympathy have also been sent by Earl Granville and Mr. Gladstone. Every day fresh expressions of sympathy are recorded, and so great is the feeling in this country that it would scarcely be an exaggeration to say that only the death of the Queen, or the Heir Apparent, or the Prime Minister, could be expected to elicit like manifestations of intense sorrow and sympathy.

REMOVAL TO WASHINGTON. Wasmsterrox, September 21, Evening.—General Garfield's remains having been encased in an unpretentious casket covered with black cloth, lay this morning in the cottage at Elberon, where for an hour the public were admitted to view them, hundreds availing themselves of the opportunity. The late President's features were much changed, and he could hardly be recognised. At 9-30 a.m. the public were excluded, and a brief religious service was held in the presence of Mrs. Garfield and family and the attendant members of the Cabinet. The avenue in front of the cottage was crowded with a silent mass of pecple, and the scene was most impressive. At 10 a.m., a train, consisting of four carriages heavily draped, arrived over a temporarily- constructed railway. The casket was placed in the first carriage, and the others were occupied by the members of the family and the Cabinet. The train slowly moved through Elberon, amid the deepest silence, and was met by a special train from New York bringing President Arthur and General Grant, who entered the funeral train, which then proceeded on its way to Washington. The Governor of New Jersey and his staff were present at the departure. At every city, town, and village along the route the people gathered in large numbers and witnessed the train passing in mournful silence. No other demonstrations were made. The train travelled rapidly, making but few stoppages, and arrived in Washington at 4-41. TOUCHING DEMONSTRATION AT WASHINGTON. MOURNFUL PROCESSION TO THE CAPITOL. One hundred and thirty officers of the army and navy formed a single rank on the left, facing the train. As it rolled slowly into the station every head upon the platform was uncovered, and stillness pervaded the throng. Mrs. Garfield was escorted to a carriage by Treasurer Blaine and her son Harry. The entire party, including President Arthur, General Grant, and the members of the Cabinet, also took carriages. The ladies of the party did not go to the Capitol. Eight soldiers bore the casket to the hearse, the band meanwhile playing "Nearer, my God, to Thee." while every head was bowed, and many eyes were dimmed with tears. The casket having been placed in the hearse, President Arthur's carriage followed immediately after it. The carriage containing Mrs. Garfield and her daughter was 'driven to the residence of Mr. McVeagh, whose guest she will be during her stay in • Washington. The precession started to the Capitol consisted of detach- ments of police and militia, several companies of regular troops, numerous military veterans and marines, and the Knight Templar Society, and was interspersed with bands of music. The hearse followed, flanked on either side by a single line consisting of the chief officers of the army and navy, including General Sherman. The cortege moved slowly up the avenue of the dense mass of people lining the side of the walks all the way. As the procession moved scarcely a sound was heard save the feet of the moving men and horses. All hats were removed and heads bowed down. At the east front of the Capitol a vast crowd had assem- bled. At the foot of the steps a double file of senators and members of the Rouse of Representatives, headed by the officers of the respective houses, was in waiting to escort the body to the Rotunda. When the cortege arrived a hush came over the multitude, and all heads were reverently un- covered as the casket was removed from the hearse. The band again played the same hymm as the remains were borne to the Rotunda and placed in the catafalque. The senators and representatives preceded the body, and ranged themselves on each side of the dais. Close behind the casket walked President Arthur and Mr. BlaMe, who were followed by Messrs. Waite, Windom, Hunt, Lincoln, MTeagh, Kirkwood, James, General Grant, and others. The casket was opened, and President Arthur and Mr. Blaine approached, and after looking upon the deceased President slowly retired. The other persons present also advanced and gazed upon the President's face, which was greatly emaciated and somewhat discoloured. The public at large were then admitted. Forty members of the army of Cumberland tendered their services as a guard of honour, and their services were accepted. Mrs. Garfield to-day expressed a sincere desire that she might not again see the White House, where she has passed so many days of Sorrow and anxiety, and she will conse- quently not visit the Executive Mansion while here. At a meeting to-day, which was attended by such members of the Senate and House of Representatives as are at present in Washington, it was decided that all the members of the Forty-Seventh Congress should be notified in due coarse of the place of interment, and be requested to attend the ceremony The remains of the deceased President will be open to view both day and night. Reports from every city and town in the Union shows the uriiversal mourning which prevails. The authorities of several cities, of many organizations, have appointed delegates to attend the funeral of the late Preeident Meetings to express the people's sense of their loss areheing held everywhere in the South as well as in the North. The Governors of many States have issued proclamations fixing Monday as a day of fasting and prayer; and in many cities it has already been resolved to observe the day by religions meetings and processions in memory of the deceased. Tllere are also indications that business will be entirely suspended throughout the country on the day of the funeral. The sympathyorganisationws itohf leivresr Gkairnfideldar eandpastshi the g larteesolpurteisoindSon! to,of family. Extensive arrangements are in progress for the funeral at Cleveland. A proposal has been made that a national subscription should be raised for erecting a monu- ment to the late President. Meetings have been held in most of the large towns throughout the United Kingdom to express sympathy with Mrs. Garfield and family. THE NEW PRESIDENT. General Chester A. Arthur, who now succeeds to the chief magistracy of the United States was barn in Albany in 1831, and is consequently in his fiftieth year, precisely the age of the President He was educated in Union College, Schenectardy, where be excelled in all branches of study. AAfitbera'n his graduation in the University, he entered the y Law School, which is a branch of the college, and

(was admitted to the bar at an early age.- Mr. Arthur always took an active part in politics, his political life beginning when, as a boy of 14, he proclaimed himself a member of the Whig party. During the Polk-Clay canvass party feeling in favour of Henry Clay and against him rose so high that few were exempt from its influence. Mr. Arthur commenced his business life by becoming a partner with Mr. E. D. Culver as a lawyer in New York, and afterwards obtained considerable legal celebrity by his connection with the Lemmon Stone case. He was a Republican from the time of the organisation of the party. He was Quarter- master-General of the State of New York during the war, and afterwards retiring into private life, he formed a law partner- ship with Mr. Ransom. Mr. Philips, the District Attorney of New York, was added to the firm, and General Arthur now stands at the head of the firm of Arthur, Philips, Knevals, and Ransom. He always took a leading part in state and city politics. He was appointed collector of the port of New York by President Grant, November 21, 1872, to succeed Thomas Murphy, holding the office until July 20, 1878, when he was removed by President Hayes because he was accused of being in the way of the success of the reform of the civil service. • Being a warm personal friend of Senator Conkling's, he has managed much of the senator's political business in New York State and city. He is a member of the Union League Club.

President Arthur will make no declaration of his policy until after the funeral of the late President. He is reported to have said that he would gladly change 'places with General Garfield rather than owe the Presidency to the act of an assassin. The Democrats promise to afford him sup- port. Mr. Bayard, the leader of the Democrats in the Senate, and who will probably be chosen Vice-President, says that his party wish President Arthur success and will assist him in everything they believe to be right and just. The Cabinet will formally tender their resignations, and the decision which Mr. Arthur will then be called upon to make will afford a trustworthy indication of his policy.

The important task of framing the rules and forming the procedure under the new Land Law is nearly completed. We believe the commissioners have already received appli- cations from tenantry in the county of Monaghan for the exercise of the jurisdiction of the Court to preserve their in- terests in farms now under seizure to suit the landlord. It is not intended, we understand, to have the sitting of the Chief Commissioner's Court in Dublin to correspond with the sittings of the High Court of Justice as to dates and dura- tion. but according as cases are entered arrangements will be made for promptly hearing and deciding them. The same practice will be followed by the Courts of the Assist- ant Commissioners held throughout the country.—Fee-

_ EXTRAORDINARY SCENE IN SLIGO. An extraordinary scene occurred on Sunday, at Dromore, Sligo. The Rev. Mr. Conway, parish priest of the district, had been renloved by the Bishop, and the people felt in- dignant. In the expectation of a disturbance resulting 100 police were sent to Skreen and 50 to Dromore. When the curate arrived at the chapel in the latter place to say mass, he found the church surrounded by a multitude of people, who declared their intention to allow no one to say mass, except their parish priest. They had nailed up the door of 1 the church. The curate, and an American priest, who wasl with him, entreated them to allow either to celebrate mass, but the people refused to listen to the remonstrances of the rev, gentleman, and so threatening was the attitude of the congregation that the police considered it inadvisable to break in the chapel doors and effect forcible entrance, and the two clergymen drove away. The people knelt down outside the chapel, and recited aloud the rosary, praying in particular for their pastor, who lytd incurred the censure of the Bishop. There was no demonstration at Skreen.

extraordinary; and ifis stated in the minutes that..you are

not to raise any levels without the sanction of the com- mittee. What I want you to do is to keep yourself right with the committee, and the committee with the Council.— Mr. HART said that on account of some alterations to a public-house called the " Noggs," it was necessary it should be done.—The CHAIRMAN : No doubt it was necessary, but you should have an order.—Mr. HART: Well, will you pass an order now ?—The CHAIRMAN : Oh, yes, for it must be done. Mr. HART : As it was it was positively dangerous for anyone driving down there at night.—The Chairman: And you have now got the footpath below the level of the road in some places ? Mr. Hart: Never disturbed the footpath.--,The Chairman: Why you have raised the level of the road near Mr. McKenzie's in Church-street, and now one aide of the street is much below the other.—Mr. Hart: But you cannct lay a tramway as if you were dealing with a colliery siding. —The Chairman : Now, I think that is a poor comparison. about the colliery siding.—Mr. HART: But when you come to lay down rails you must alter one side or the other.—The CHAIRMAN: You will have all the water on the footpath when it rains.—Mr. HART: I will undertake to say there is not an inclination of one in twenty.—The CHAIRMAN: But I say you have raised it higher than it was before.—Mr. HART: You cannot possibly lay two miles of tramway with- out making some alterations in the outline or general level of the road. In Bridge-street, for instance, where the pro- perty is built without any regard to regularity, you would have some difficulty.—The CHAIRMAN: But why raise the road; if you had taken some off it would have been better than putting some on. Some time ago, in the Council, there was a proposition for spending some hundreds for the pur- pose of taking some off. Have you not noticed that in some portions of the tramway there are great holes filled with water ?—Mr. HART : Oh, yes; it will have to be done over again.—The CHAIRMAN : It is of the utmost importance that the paving be watched, because we have spent some money, and it ought to be done well.—Mr. HART: It has been watched carefully. I hope in another three months the tramways will be finished, for lam sick of it. I am kept upset.—Mr. WILCOCK drew the Surveyor's attention to the bac.l condition of several crossings in the town, par- ticularly in Church-street, and also to the disgraceful state of the bridge in Dunriding-lane.—The SURVEYOR promised his attention to the former, and was ordered to repair the latter.

MEETING AT HUYTON. On Thusday a meeting in connection with the above society was held in the Congregational • Church, Huyton, when Mr. Richard Butchard, the district secretary, delivered an address. There was only a moderate attendance. From the eighty-second annual report of the society it appears that there had been issued during the year 627 new publi- cations, of which 137 were tracts. The total circulation from the home depot, including books, tracts, &c., had reached 69,089,460, of which 24,515,140 were tracts, being an increase on the previous year of 3,472,770. The issues from the foreign depOts might be safely stated at 12,000,000, making a total circulation of 81,089,460, aud of 2,012,047,900 since the formation of the society. The total amount received from sales, missionary receipts, and all sources, including last year's balance, was £193,560 10s. 2d. The total expenditure in both trade and grant departments, including balance of investments was £189,042 14s. 4d., leaving a balance in favour of the society of £4,537 15s. 10d. Missionary Funds.—The total amount received from subscriptions and other contributions, &c., was. £33,373 Os. lid., the whole of this sum being available for the missionary objects of the society. The expenditure amounted to £46,625 15s. 2d., and consisted of foreign money grants of paper electrotypes, and publications, grants to emigrants, domestic applicants for tracts, circulating libraries, school libraries, itc. The grants exceed those of last year by the sum of £6,552 16s. 9d. The excess of grants over the missionary receipts, amounting to £13,252 141. 3d. had been:supplied from the trade funds which had also borne the entire cost of manag- ement both of the business and missionary depart- ments.—The Rev. J. W. Walker, pastor, occupied the chair, and stated that during last year over £50,000 was devoted to the glorious missionary work of the society. Mr. Walker then introduced Mr. Butchard, who, he remarked, had come from Bury to be with them that evening. Mr. Butchard then gave an address, alike interest- ing and instructive, descriptive of the home and foreign work of the above society. He dwelt at great length upon the literature disseminated by the society, both at home and abroad, literature which was good and wholesome. As instances he quoted the "Boys' Own Paper" and the " Girls' Own Paper," which he contended had accomplished un- calculable good in the mind of the young, and had driven out of existence some of those papers the contents of which were likely to lead boys and girls into the wrong path.— Mr. E. S. Eccles also addressed the meeting, after which the company separated.

It is mentioned, as an indication of approaching severe weather, that wild ducks have already made their appear- ance on the east coast, and that some have been shot by sportsmen. At the Westminster Registration Court, on Wednesday, the name of Mr. Henry Broadhurst, M.P., was struck off the list of voters, on the ground that the overseers had neglected to put upon the register his new address in Buckingham- street, Strand. A proposal that the Court of Common Council of the City of London should present a complimentary address to Mr. Gladstone and ask the rigbt hon gentleman to sit for a marble bust for the Guildhall led to a scene on Thursday. 51r. Cox moved the resolution for carrying out the proposal, and it was seconded oy Alderman Stone, who said the sug- gested honour was entirely separated from the question of politics. Mr. Philips, a Conservative, opposed the motion amid cries of " Shame " asked why the Council should "pander to a contemptible Government," and declared that ta 'y were "trying to buy Mr. Gladstone." The Lord Mayor cai!ea Mr. Phillips to order, and he had to withdraw the offensive language. Mr. Shaw said the attempt to sever the name of Mr. Gladstone from polities was ridiculous. They had no -ight to assume to speak in this matter for " the citizens of London," and he proposed that for these words they should substitute the words "Corporation of London." Alderman Sir Thomas Dakin said the words objected to were! used In the case of Lord Beaconsfield. After an •_; fited, discussion the original motion was adopted by 104 votqs to 14.

div.head: "COTTON CORNER."
div.p: THE "COTTON CORNER."

Several more Blackburn mills were stopped on Saturday, and it is estimated that there have been thrown out of em- ployment temporarily, by the action of the employers in a conflict with the brokers, about 10,000 operatives—a third of the totE.l number employed in the town. Messrs. Hodg- kinson and Codling, and Messrs. Harrison and Co., have stopped their weavers as well as the spinners. It is pro- bable that there will be a great increase in the number of weavers idle in the course of the week, as there is a strong feeling amongst the manufacturers in favour of the adoption of short time to avoid the effect which the stoppage of spindles would have on the weaving branch of the trade. Of the eleven spinning concerns in Darwen, nine are at present stopped in compliance with the resolution passed at the meeting of the trade in Manchester last week. The proprietors of about 600,000 spindles in Preston are stopping their mills. The secretary of the Masters' Asso- ciation has sent out circulars asking them if they are wil- ling to stop their machinery three days a week for a month, provided the proprietors of two-thirds of the looms in the district would do the same. The weavers are in favour of short time. Thirteen mills in Ashton-under-Lyne, representing 600,000 spindles, closed on Saturday for a week. The other menu- ' factories in the town will continue working as they are not materially affected by the "corner." In several churches in Manchester and elsewhere in the cotton trade districts references were made on Sunday to the hardships likely to be inflicted on the operatives by the stoppage of the mills and the consequent loss of wages. Occasion was taken in many instances for a sermon on com- mercial morality, the speculative and gambling spirit of the age being strongly denounced. In one Liverpool church a well-known local clergyman somewhat surprised his congre- gation by preaching on the "corner," or rather on the heart- less and cruel action of those millowners who had availed themselves of the " corner " as an excuse for closing their factories, and thus depriving their employes of their means of livelihood. The rev, gentleman went so far as to suggest that the bankers of such millowners should cease to have further dealings with them. THE LIVERPOOL " Corrox CORNER."—An adjourned meeting of the manufacturers of North and North-East Lancashire was held on Tuesday, in the Royal Exchange, to receive the answers to the circular sent out a few days ago with regard to the question of working short time. The Chairman (Mr. Greenwood) stated that the replies were not sufficiently numerous to justify the adoption of any resolu- tion on the subject. Many firms had not thought it worth while to reply to the circular, and consequently it was deemed advisable to adjourn the meeting sine die. At a meeting of the Committee of the• Cotton Spinners' Association held on Thursday, notice was given of the following resolution, to be proposed at a meeting of the committee on Friday :—" That the proprietors of mills be recommended to stop their mills for a further period of six days during the next fortnight, and that a general meeting of spinners be held in the Manchester Town Hall on Tues- day next to consider the adoption of such recommendation." A meeting of the Yorkshire spinners and doublers has been summoned for Saturday afternoon, to consider the question of a general stoppage or the adoption of short time in the Yorkshire district, in order to assist in the breaking down of the Liverpool " corner."

div.head: TRADE NOTES.
div.p: TRADE NOTES.

The Fife and Clackmannan Miners' Association has resolved to demand from the coalrnasters an advance of 61. per day, the men considering that the present state of trade justifies this action on their part. The Cleveland ironmasters have unanimously adopted the recommendation of the recent Carlisle meeting, to reduce the production of iron by 12i per cent. The decision has, it is stated, already stiffened the prices of pig iron at Middlesborough. A mass meeting of puddlers, rollers, and other iron workers in North Staffordshire, on Monday resolved to unite with the iron workers of South Staffordshire, in their agitation for an increase in wages at the rate of 10 per cent., and pledged itself to take every legitimate means for securing the same.

At a meeting of Scotch and Cleveland iron masters' held at Carlisle on Monday, it was resolved to recommend each district to reduce the make of pigiron to the extent of 121 per cent. for six months. At a large representative meeting of Miners held at the Miners' Hall, Wigan, on Monday, it was unanimously resolved to ask throughout the whole of South-west Lanca- shire for an advance of wages equal to 15 per cent. The meeting was adjourned until Saturday next, when all districts or pit sets of men are expected to send delegates, and it is anticipated the resolution will be confirmed and sent to the masters. LOCE-OIIT IN THE NIIT AND BOLT TRADE.—The operatives employed in the nut and bolt trade, Darlaston, Staffordshire, were locked out on Monday, having refused to continue work at the prices regulated by the list prepared by Mr. Chamberlain three years ago. A large number of men were sent to Birmingham, w.bere work will be provided for them. At a meeting of Scotch ironworkers, held in Hamilton on Thursday, a letter was read from Mr. Macdonald, M.P., re- commending the men to counteract the movement made by ironmasters to blow out a number of their furnaces by re- ducing their production, otherwise the anomaly of iron rising in price and wages tailing would occur. The meeting unanimously agreed that unless sixpence advance be con- ceded by the Ist of October, all miners should work four days per week and eight hours daily.

Mr. HART submitted his estimate of the cost of managing the department for the ensuing year (but not in detail), which amounted in the aggregate to £6,744. The estimate for the past year was £8,674, and the actual cost of carrying on the department was £5,956 15s. 11d. The estimate and actual cost of the various items of last year just ended is as follows, the first figures representing the estimate, and the latter the actual cost :—£2,683 for wages, £1,747; £960 for team labour, £433; £2,152 fpr materials, £1,362; £135 carting establish- ment, £132; £785 for street sweeping, £905; £57 for watering streets, £l3B, the excess this year being on account of the keep of the horses; £245 for steam roller, £l7l 9s. 5d., not much material put in the road; salaries £825, actual £827; miscellaneous matters £235, cost £237, proposed im- provement not yet effected £6OO. The amount of highway rtes collected in March, 1881, £2,933 6s. 7d.; September, 4,54; total, £8,747.—1t was decided to recommend the Council to reduce the highway rate one penny in the pound, making it Bd. in the pound.—lt was remarked that a saving of about £2,000 had been effected during the year.

div.head: !CASSELL, PETTER, AND GALRIN'S
div.p: !CASSELL, PETTER, AND GALRIN'S
PUBLICATIONS.

A profoJnd appreciation of Flaxman's Career and works Is shown in "Toe Magazine of Art," in an article by E S. Roscoe. He is said to be distinguished for classical purity, united with intense imagination, and withal, for an "abounding feeling for humanity, shown in his adaptation of his art to illustrate the kindly deeds of the rich, the teachings of the wise, and the sorrows of the poor." The following passage shows the spirit of the article :—"Two examples of Flaxman's religions creations may serve to show some of his most unique characteristics as a sculptor. We mean the two reliefs illustrative of, or rather suggested by, the Lord's Prayer—the "Deliver us from Evil" and the "Lead us not into Temptation," the former of which forms part of the Baring monument in Micheldever Church. Suspended in mid-air is a mortal, an angel of light clings to him, looks above for help, and while endeavouring to draw him upwards is yet hardly successful against the evil spirit, who grasping the man's lower limbs would drag him down. To the observer's left hand another angel, fresh to the strife, darts downwards and invincibly subdues another evil spirit who is aiding his companion. The first angel seeks to de. live; the mortal who is in danger from evil, and it may be assumed from his every attitude that the struggling spirit of good is crying, as he looks up for aid, "Deliver as from evil." Here we have a subject which can by no possibility be considered other than a purely modern one, but we have it treated with all the beauty and vigour, yet moderation, of the antique. It is full of force, the grouping is very fine, and the modelling or the limbs most powerful, yet there is all this strength without any exaggeration, nor is the attention drawn to any particular detail from the feeling for the group as a whole. The "Lead us not into Tempta- tion" is equally striking, but in a different style—there is here the force of irresistible persuasion rather than of struggling might. The person led from temptation is de- picted by the beautiful form of a woman, who though she moves forward yet looks hack towards an evil spirit, who holds out to her a crown, concealing what his other hand contains behind his back, whilst at his feet crouches a hideous beast. But a guardian ang,ei,ou a higher level than the woman, enfolds her tenderly with her right arm, but irresistibly presses her forward, whilst above her another spirit points upwards and onwards. It is a group which should be viewed and considered together with the other illustration of the Lord's Prayer, for the contrast brings out the peculiar excellencies of each. The one is illustrative of Flaxman's power in the delineation of the human form in its most vigorous motion; the other shows us his power over tenderer but still forcible subjects in quieter moments, and his management of drapery; both prove that he can blend all the various elements into a perfect harmony. For to take only one point, the assistance is rendered to the man by the strong might of spirits in the form of men, that to the woman by the gentle persuasion and the tender affection of spirits in the forms of those whom they are aiding." Michael Munkacsy, the Hungarian artist, forms the subject of "Oar Living Artists." A powerful picture of his, "The last day of a condemned prisoner" is given as the frontis- piece. The motions exhibited by the various visitants to the prison cell are very varied, but well pourtrayed, from the idle, yet awed boyish curiosity of the school lads, to the bitter grief of the wife. The interior of the "New Natu-0.1 History Museum" is described by E. I. Kell, and several illustrations of the decoration, are given. Amongst the most noticeable engravings is one by Max Volkhart. It is entitled "The Duet." It represents the court fool sitting by a table on which is "a great flask of rich red wine, the fames of which are already at work on his brain, and have inspired him to throw a music lesson to a dog, whose howl of discord is naturally expressed in the animal's attitude, and in the irresistible puckering of the musician's featuret as he sweeps the strings of his guitar to drown it."

The "International Portrait Gallery" contains a portrait and biography of one of the most variously gifted men in the United States—Oliver Wendell Holmes. Born in 1809, Dr. Holmes graduated at Harvard in 1829, and four years later he visited Europe. Here he determined to relinquish the study of the law, in which he had been engaged, and adopted the profession of medicine. Before his European sojourn, which lasted for two years, be had established his claim to belong to the poetic fraternity,and shortly after his return he added to his fame by the poem entitled "Poetry : a Metrical Essay." In poetry and medicine he made equal advances, having published several more works before he was appointed professor in the medical department at Har- vard in 1847. It was ten years later than this, however, that he made a lasting reputation by his papers in the then new Atlantic Monthly. His "Autocrat of the Breakfast Table," original, sparkling, and powerful, made the new magazine— though it bothered the critics. "The Professor" followed, and after that his inimitable tale of New England Life, "Elsie Venner," to which he gave a sequel, "The Guardian Angel," in 1867. During the Civil War he published a volume of songs and hymns, and also wrote professionally at all times. The conclusion of his magazine articles ap- peared in 1873, when he published "The Poet at the Break- fast Table" Hie work during the last few years has in- cluded many poems, and a Life of Motley, the Historian. Such, in a few lines, has been the life of Dr. Holmes, whose fine, oval face, wrinkled and less fresh than in healthy Eng- lish age, but with bright eyes and snowy hair, is pourtrayed before us. Hood is sometimes mentioned as his compeer, but the biographer considers him wider in culture, superior in learning, and robrister in intellect, while less pathetic and less rich in humour than Hood.

Part 72 concludes Vol. VI. of " Cassell's History of Eng- land." In it are descriptions of the progress of law, religion, and literature in the reign of George 111. Goldsmith, Johnston, Crabbe, Cowper, Scott, and Moore, have each their place assigned in the literature of the time. Of Cowper it is said "He combined in his verge the polish of Pope with the freedom and force of Churchill. He possessed the satirical strength of Churchill, and a more Christian spirit. In Cowper broke forth the strongest clearest sense which had distinguished any writer in prose or verse for genera- tions. He painted nature like a lover, but with the truth of a great artist, and he flagellated the vice of society in the very highest quarters with unshrinking boldness; at the same time with equal intrepidity he advanced the assertions of a perfect faith in the religion of the Gospel, in the face of the hardest and most disdainful sceptickm of the age. To the diplomatists, who vainly imagined that they guided human affairs, he demonstrated a higher and a more real Director :

They trust in navies, and their navies fail— God's curse can east away ten thousand sail They trust in armies, and their courage dies: In wisdom, wealth, in fortune, and in lies; But all they trust in withers, and it must, When He commands in whom they place no trust. Burns, the Lake School—Wordsworth, Coleridge, Southey— and the many others are likewise discussed; and the progress of the age in Physical science, &c.' estimated. The next volume will commence the reign of George IV. "OLD elm NEW EDINBURGH " has now reached its tenth part. The chapters in this month's instalment deal with some of the new streets which modern improvements have made; St. Mary's Wynd, Leith Wynd, and The West Bow. "No part of Edinburgh," it is said, 'was so rich in quaint old houses as the sanctified bends of the Bow " singular edifices, many of them of vast and unknown ad- tiquity, and all more or less irregular, with stone gables and dovecot gablets, timberlgalleries, outshots, and strange pro- jections, the dormer windows, patches and additions made in the succession of centuries, overhanging the narrow and tortuous street, which took the windings of the zig-zag road that led of old from the wooded waste to Duneden, the fort on the slope, at the gates of which King David dispensed justice to his people, and his queen daily distributed bread to the poor. Among the last charters of David 11. is one to Thomas Webster, of "ace land in the West Bow." Its antique tenements, covered with heraldic carvings and quaint dates, half hidden by sign-boards or sordid rags dry- ing on poles, it nooks, crooks, trap-doors, and gloomy cham- bers, abounded with old memories, with heroic stories of ancient martial families, and with grim legends and grand- mother's tales of ghosts and of diablerie ; but to those who see it now, or all that remains of it, where it abuts on the Grass Market, cut asunder by Victoria-terrace' replaced in one part by a flight of stairs, in another by the Free Church of St. John, and sloping away eastward into Victoria-street, it is impossible to realise what the old West Bow, which served as a connecting link between the High and the Low Town, the Lawnmarket and the Grassmarket, really was. The pencil of the artist alone may reproduce its features." Amongst the score of articles in CASSELL'S FAMILY MAGAZINE may be mentioned an article on "The Comet of 1881," in which several engravings of photographs of the recent visitant to our corner of the heavens are given, as well as a history of its appearance, and information as to kindred objects. We have "more about the Drawing-room" in "Artistic Furnishing for Modern Houses ;" and a Family Doctor discourses on "Watering-places as Health Resorts." The miscellaneous items will find enjoyment for many an odd moment during the month.—For Sunday reading, THE QUIVER is not easily approachable. "Short Arrows" con- tinue to prove their usefulness. Amongst other serials, Lirryn FOLES must not be Imp- gotten, as by acclamation it is put at the head of juvenile -nagazines ; EUROPEAN FERNS contains some carefully 31ed illustrations. Other issues of the firm are THE NEW TESTAMENT COMMENTARY, OLD AND NEW LONDON, CAS- SELL'S POPULAR EDUCATOR, NATURAL HISTORY, and, if "last not least," KNIGHT'S DICTIONARY OF MECHANICS.

ST. HELENS CONSERVATIVES.—About 700 people went to Belle Vue Zoological Gardens by the Conservative annual excursion, on Saturday.

MISSIONARY MEETING AT ST. HELEITS.—On Monday, the Rev. J. P. Ellwood, formerly a missionary stationed at Lucknow, in the East Indies, delivered an address in the girl's schoolroom, near to the Parish Church, on his work in India. The Rev. Canon Carr presided, and the room was fairly filled. The rev. gentleman referred to the labours of the Misses Mulvaney, of St. Helens, in India, and he was sure if St. Helens would only send them more like those ladies a great good would be accomplished. One of the ladies was at present in Calcutta, another lady was shortly going out there; and he trusted that their example would ' spread the interest in the foreign mission work amongst them. Mr. Ellwood then spoke of the difficulties which bad to be overcome by missionaries and described the manners and habits of the people. He afterwards sang a few English hymns in Hindostanee, and spoke of the difficulty mis- sionaries had in combatting the religious superstitions of the people, and establishing the true Christian religion.—ffit. Wm. Gamble read the statement of accounts during the past year, from which it appeared the receipts had been £54 Is. 2d., and the expenditure £l, leaving a balance of £53 is. 2d. to be handed over to the Central Association. This showed a very large falling off on previous years, mainly in conse- quence of the missionary tree having been held in St. Thomas's parish, and subscribers leaving the parish. He himself was also to blame for not having collected some subscriptions, but he hoped to get the arrears in 90011.-A collection was made at the close of the meeting, which realised £5 12s. 4d., the largest the chairman could remem- ber. This together with the collections on Sunday, made a total of £07:4 4s. lad.
By Mr. EDWARD EDWARDSON.
By Messrs. WILLIAM WILSON 4. SON.

next show of the Cheshire Agricultural Society here is certainly very [strange. There cannot be any doubt that these exhibitions have a humanising in- fluence, and shou'd be encouraged for that reason, but they also give a considerable impetus to the trade of the town in which the show is held, and by at- tracting a large number of visitors, all, of whom spend money in the town, confer benefits upon all sections of the community. The influence of a large body of people causing the expenditure of perhaps from £x,ooo to £2,000 in the town would be such an advantage to Runcorn that we are only surprised that the public meeting last Monday, which was con- vened by the Chairman of the Board of Commis- sioners, insteid of being but meagrely attended was not crowded to overflowing. There is surely sr(fi- dent public spirit in the enterprising trades- people of this town to cause them to meet together to take the necessary steps to secure the holding of the show here next year, seeing that it is a movement that cannot fail to be of very great advantage to them all. As the meet- ing on Monday could not be considered a represen- tative one, it has been adjourned to give the promoters en opportunity of making those likely to be interested in the subject acquainted with it, and it is to be hoped ,that at the adjor-ned meeting we shall see a much larger attendance of persons who will take the matter up with spirit, give the society an invitation, and work with a will to make the show such a decided success as will reflect creel upon the town at large, and the result cannot fail to be beneficial in many ways.

LOCAL NOTES.

At a recent meeting of the Runcorn Board of Commis- sioners, Mr. Thomas Norman complained, and with great justness, that the Local Government Board auditor had sur- charged him and Mr. Philip Speakman thirty shillings each in the case of expenses connected with a visit to London upon a matter vitally affecting the interests of every rate- payer in the town. A country which possesses such a court as that of Chancery, so ably satirised by Dickens, must ex- pect to find a great amount of nonsensical red tapeism about every government office; and the Local Government auditor who visits this district has of late distinguished himself by causing an infinitude of trouble in the way of correspondence relating to several matters which he, in his wisdom, has now decided to surcharge various commissioners, though be has never done so in past years. I believe that it is the same gentleman who has been making the most of his "little brief authority" in connection with the Wigan Union. In the matter affecting Messrs. Norman and Speakman it ap- pears that they received a telegram to meet the general manager of the London and North-Western Railway at Euston, in order to have an interview with him in respect to the high fares charged between Liverpool and Runcorn, the brilliant men who managed the local matters of the town at the time when the bridge which spans the Mersey was made, not having had the requisite amount of common sense to obtain concessions from the company, on condition that that they did not oppose the passing of the Bid for the construction of the bridge through the House of Commons ! I What a fine body of men must have ruled the town in those days ! It is a blessing they have been gathered to their fathers, and that some one else reigns in their stead, or poor Runcorn would still have been the Sleepy Hollow kind of place it was when its air was considered so conducive to the restoration of vale- tudinarians. The railway company granted the two gentle- men a pass, so that their journey to the metropolis did not cost any ratepayer a farthing. They were successful in ob- taining an important concession from the London and North- Western, in the shape of a reduction-upon every third class return ticket to Liverpool of threepence which must save the people of the town some hundreds of pounds per year. The deputation charged 30s. each as expenses—and we. must not forget to notice that their work included an all-night Journey to London—which the Local Government auditor seems to have looked upon as a terrible piece of cool as- surance on their part, and he declined to allow it because, gentlemenment l obtusenesswn wait until o fan in eoyffihcai forsooth, the Board had not sanctioned the expenditure by a formal resolution. Here is a splendid illustration of the daLcalledliae meetingwould hoa fv Commis- sioners before taking the • journey and thus have missed keeping ehadthe the appointment with the general manager, which want of courtesy would no doubt have irritated him, and rendered him altogether disinclined to make the concession asked for ! In conclusion I may notice a matter which, to my intellect, seems a little obscure, and I may put it in the form of a sort of conundrum—Why did Mr. Lyon, who did net go to London, have to pay the secoed 30s. instead of Mr. Philip Speakman, who had that pleasure?
I hear that the claim sent in to the London and North- Westarn by the Treacy family is fixed at £4,000.

The "Flower Queen" performance of the friends con- nected with Bethesda Congregational Chapel, Runcorn, proved a splendid success. Last year some of the people connected with the affair were a little irritated at the descrip- tion given of the gentleman who took the part of the Recluse, but they did not fail on this occasion to follow out the hint then given and make Mr. Pierpoint as much like a dweller in a "secluded dell" as they could. In fact, he was I so metamorphised that on being introduced to a particular friend as a gentleman from Manchester the person did not know him, and the incident caused much merriment. Mr. Rhodes deserves great praise for the splendid manner in which the decorations were carried out; and, indeed, I hear encomiums upon nearly all concerned,:from the conductor downwards. Even amongst the straitest religionists there is a fondness for dramatic representation, and it is.much to be regretted that elocutionary and histrionic talents which often lie buried cannot be more frequently made of use. There is no doubt that most people have some power of mimicry, some telling scale in their voice, some oratorical I power, and we should not so often hear interesting speeches utterly spoiled, owing to being delivered in a monotonous manner, if a persevering 'attempt was made to cultivate the graces of utterance, whether in the way of singing or speech. God always helps those who help fhemselves,and the hearty manner in which the church and congregation at Bethesda have gone into the work of prepar- fng for this cantata deserves the highest commendation. If a church is to be free from those unpleasantnesses which occasionally mar ecclesiastical life of nearly all des- criptions, from that of the cathedral with its solemn arches down to the smallest little Zoar belonging to some Hyper- Calvinist, each member must be found something to do. If one is particularly obstreperous, be must, as Dr. Parker, of the City Temple, says in his Ad Clerum, be given a resolu- tion to propose, or put at the head of some department which will require all his surplus energy. Ardent workers are generally too busy to be good critics or unfair fault finders. Certainly matters have gone on swimmingly at the church since the advent of Mr. Thomas, who must have capital powers as an administrator. - - -

The ratepayers of Runcorn are certainly to be congratulated on the lightness of their poor rates at a time when the people in other unions are feeling the burden to be very heavy. The old members and others interested in the Runcorn Parliamentary Debating Society will meet in Bethesda school-room next Tuesday evening, at eight o'clock, to consider the desirability of having a winter session and an opening soiree. The society has been very successful in the past, and I have no doubt that several of the sur- rounding towns started their miniature St. Stephen's on its pattern. It is pleasant to know that in ' this particular matter the young gentlemen of Runcorn took the lead in the surrounding district. The association of a similar character which was commenced in Widnes did not meet with much success during its brief existence, and has, I believe, been dissolved. There is a general conviction amongst the inhabitants of Runcorn that the Parliamentary Debating Society has done much to culti- vate the speaking abilities of the young men of the town, and as many of the brightest ornaments of the British House , of Commons first developed their speaking talents in con- nection with societies of a like nature at their respective universities—the glorious Pitt being a notable example— who knows but in the future the local historian may be able to point with pride to the fact that: some great legis- lator, or eloquent orator, first tried his wings within the precincts of Bethesda schoolroom. We are warned not to despise the day of small things.

SOUTH-WEST LANCASHIRE COUNTY REVISION.—Mr. G. H. Powell, the Liberal agent for South-West Lancashire, has written the following letter to a contemporary :—" The following notice has been issued to Liberal voters and claimants who have been objected to by the Tory party 'l3, Binns'-road, West Derby, Sept. 16, 1881.—Sir,—I much regret that, by an error, your name has been objected to for the South-Western Division of the county of Lancas- ter. I take the earliest opportunity of withdrawing my ob- jection, and enclose duplicate notice as proof thereof. You need not now attend the Revision Court, unless objected to by Mr. John Wilson (the Liberal objector), in which case you might kindly inform me, and notice shall be sent to you when to appear.—' am, sir, your obedient servant, JOHN GREEN BALES.'—I may say, for the guidance of voters and claimants in this division of the county, that Mr. John Wilson has been dead some months, and has not objected to anyone, so that no voter or claimant will have received notice of objection from Mr. John Wilson. Rather than any person, Liberal or Conservative, should be prevented (on the grounds stated in the circular) from attending the Re- vision Court to substantiate their claims, I beg to state that the objectors are for the Liberals Richard Salisbury,' and for the Conservatives John Green Bales.' The introduc- tion of Mr. John Wilson's name in the circular is, therefore, misleading, and may prevent some persons from attending to prove their qualifications before the revising barrister."

SERIOUS ROBBERY AT FARNWORTH POST OFFICE.— On Sunday night, the Farnworth post office was broken into by thieves, who obtained entrance by breaking a pane In the back kitchen window. They took the keys of the cash-box from the unmentionables of the postmaster, which were in the bedroom in which be was sleeping, broke open the box, and purloined £47 belonging to the post office, and £2B 16s. 6d. the money of the postmaster.
GOLBONE.

ANNIVERSARY SERVICES—On Sunday last the annual services on behalf of the day and Sunday schools in connec- tion with St. Thomas's church were held. The Rev. Henry S. Byrth, M.A., vicar of Bardsley, preached in the morning and afternoon, and in the evening the Rev. Wm. Bernard Swam, BA., curate of St. Peter's, Newton. There were good congregations at each service. For many years the presence and interest of the school children have not been overlooked, and Sunday was no exception, special hymns being provided for them at each service, the whole of which were given in a very pleasing manner. Mr. Caunce for the labours bestowed upon them. The choir's selection of anthems in- cluded "Make a joyful noise unto the Lord " and "I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills," two favourite compositions of Dr. Clarke Whitfield. The evening anthem was Smart's "0 be joyful in God." In the rendering of the quartette, Mrs. and Dr. Mapei Miss Pennington. and Mr. Caunce were heard to advantage. The singing and Mr. Duddle's services at Om organ were much appreciated. The collections realised £44 18s., which will probably be made into £5O, a result which is all the more satisfactory when it is remem- bered over £5O was raised only a few weeks ago on behalf of the organ restoration fund. GOLBORNE PAROCHIAL COMMITTEE.—Lighting and Water Committee.—A meeting of this committee was held on the 7th inst.—Mr. Bennie reported that he was unable to obtain payment of water rates from some consumers. The com- mittee therefore recommended that preceedings be taken against them if not paid after a few days further notice.—Mr. Winnard made an application for an alteration in the posi- tion of a lamp pillar near his workshop, in Church-street, which request, after due consideration, was granted.-- Highway Sewerage Committee.—A nteeting.was held on the above date.—The Surveyor reported that many complaints had been made to him respecting the inconvenience and annoyance to the public by people wheeling coal trucks and barrows along the parapets.—The committee instructed the surveyor to comtnunicare with Superintendent Weir, and ask him to deal with the matter.—The monthly meeting of the Parochial Committee was held at Messrs. Brewis's Office, on Thursdry, the 15th inst. Present, Messrs. W. Mitchell (in the chair), John Fearns, R. Fairhurst, Thomas Pierpoint, John Low, Joseph Howard, and the Surveyor.— The minutes of the last meeting, and also the meetings of the various committees, held at the Surveyor's office, on the 7th inst., were read and confirmed.—Mr. Fears moved, and Mr. Howard seconded, that the surveyor write to the county roads surveyor with reference to the application made some time ago to the county authorities, desiring them to adopt the road from Golborne Dale to the boundary of Abram as a main road, and to enquire what they proposed to do in the matter.—Resolved that the necessary work required at the sewerage tanks be attended to. ---The Township's Watert— The surveyor submitted a copy of Dr. Hall's report on sam- ples of water analyzed by him.—lt was resolved to deal with the persons to whom the condemned water belonged after the analysis of the wells within the township were completed.

HASTE TO THE RESCUE LODGE, 1..0.G.T., VirrracEs. —At the uSual weekly meeting of this lodge on Tuesday evening, the chairs were taken by the members of the Star of Widnes lodge. Brother Thomas Bold delivered an ad dress on temperance topics, and the evening was pleasantly spent with songs, recitations, and other similar diversions. There were 38 members present. The usual vote of thanks to the chairman, Mr. G. Turton, brought the proceedings to a close.

_ —8.A.120318 r RuNconN.—Mr: Barger appeared at the Public Hall, Runcorn, on Tuesday evening, in his musical, mimical, and ventriloquial entertainment, and was well patronised. There was a good house, which received the entertainer in a right hearty fashion. The impersonation of I Miss Florence Dashington was splendidly given, and the exhibition of Mr. Barger's powers of ventriloquism was specially deserviag of notice. There is not the slightest doubt that this gentleman's popularity will grow greater year by year, and that in him Mr. Maccalv has found a foenaan worthy of his steel.

THE LANCASHIRE ENGINEERING TRADES.—For the pre- sent the agitation which was commenced a short time back for an advance of wages in the engineering trades of the Manchester district seems to be hen in suspense. The em- ployers have not seen their way to return to the rate of wages ruling prior to the reduction made about two years ago, and the men have not felt justified in resorting to a strike with the view of enforcing compliance with their re- quest. So far as the actual condition of trade in the district is concerned, the last returns from the various local branches of the Amalgamated Society of Engineers describe it as moderate throughout Manchester, Oldham, and this im- mediate neighbourhood, with an improvement recorded in some cases, and the number of men out of employment con- tinues to steadily decrease. In many of the Lancashire districts, however, the condition of affairs is not so satis- factory; Liverpool, Bolton, Blackburn, Burnley, Heywood, Rochdale, Stalybridge, St. Helens, and Wigan being returned as either only moderate, declining, or bad; and the only Lancashire district in which trade is reported as actually good is that of Barrow-in-Furness, where the shipbuilding yards are being kept very busy. Throughout the kingdom the returns show a decrease of about 80 in the number of the society's members who are in receipt of donations in consequence of the want of employment. TEMPERANCE MISSION LODGE, I.O.G.T.—The mind' anni- versary of the Temperance Mission Lodge of Good Templars was held in the Mission Room, Academy-street, Warrington, en Wednesday, when a large number of members and friends partook of an excellent tea. After tea Mr. Hall presided, and, in opening the meeting, pointed out the dangers of yielding to the temptations of the drinking cus- toms of society.—The Rev. Joseph Morton thought the appearance of things showed that there was health and vigour in the lodge, which, if only developed, would doubt- less prove a blessing to the locality. Ile said that be thought it would be an advantage if all church members could allow the total abstinence principle to become part of their Christianity. He referred to the losses they had to mourn in consequence of drink from the ranks of ministers, local preachers, Sunday school teachers, church workers, and Sunday scholars. If they could throw around them- selves the safeguard of temperance they would be in a measure independent in a sense that many in these days are not independent, and bid defiance to strong drink. He pointed out the advantages of total abstinence, and how it would benefit those who adopted the principle.—Mrs. M. E. Green, of Liverpool, Right Worthy Grand Superintendent of the Juvenile Temple, said that some years ago she thought that the platform was not a place for a lady, but that was before she went into many of the miserable homes caused by strong drink. Now, having seen the great evils of intemperance, she could not help availing herself of the opportunity of speaking from the platform against the di ink traffic. (Applause.) She referred to the important work now being accomplished in Liverpool by a Mr. Booth, of America, the Gospel temperance missionary, and said she had been induced to help him in that work by the fact that Mr. Booth told those who signed the pledge that they would need to seek for strength from God to enable them to keep the temperance pledge. In eloquent strains she depicted the great contrast which existed between those who were led away by temptations to drink and those who were trained in Good Templar and Juvenile Templar lodges to continue total abstainers from strong drink. She dwelt upon the shame of young attractive maidens being engaged as barmaids in alluring men to indulge in intoxicating drinks, and urged all who had taken the plege to work harder to persuade others to become total abstainers' and concluded by imploring those who were moderate drinkers to give up their habits in order to put down the drink traffic. (Applause.)—Mr. David Horton, president of the Catholic League of the Cross, said he believed that everyone belonging to the temperance organisa- tions amongst all religious bodies ought to join hand in hand to oppose the ravages of strong drink. (Hear, hear.) Although Warrington was not very large there is poverty as deep as in any town in England, and the sad scenes that were frequently to be seen were enough to make their hearts bleed. He referred to the dangers of moderation, and said that the League of the Cross was progressing well. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. J. W. Hall, who presided at the latter part of the proceedings, referred to the progress made by the lodge during the last seven years. The last return showed 71 members, and during the present quarter they had increased to 86. (Applause.) Messrs. Thornley, J. Mercer, R. Alcock, and Misses E. Barton and Fanny Richardson con- tributed to the enjoyment of the evening by recitations and songs, which were heartily appreciated. STAR OF WIDNES LODGE I.O.G.T.—This lodge held its usual session on Thursday week, when, after being opened in its usual form, the chairs were taken by the mem- bers of the Widnes Samaritan Lodge, who were paying a fraternal visit to the Star Lodge. Bro. Whitley delivered an address on temperance topics, pointing out the evils which ensued from drunkenness, and urging his hearers to hearty and unremitting work in the cause of temperance. The visitors entertained the lodge by a miscellaneous programme of songs, tecitations, &c., all of which were well rendered and heartily applauded. BOWLING AT HILTON.—RuNOGRN F. Alluding to the "Fair Trade" agitation, he observed that those who took part in it did not avow that their object was protection, but endeavoured to conceal their designs by the use of such words as "reciprocity " and " a policy of retaliation." A man who had aliases was generally a man of bad character ; and the fact that Protection was skulking about the country under the aliases of " Reciprocity " and " Retaliation" ought to be enough to put people on their guard against it. RUNCORN AND THE CHESHIRE AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY.

On Monday a public meeting of ratepayers, called by Dr. Steele, the chairman of the Board of Commissioners,was held at the Runcorn Town Hall, for the purpose of con- sidering the desirability of inviting the Cheshire Agricul- tural Society to hold their mxt meeting at that town. There were present Dr. Steele, Messrs. McDougall, Taylor, Norman, Handley, Hazleburst, Williams, J. J. Speakman (Commis- sioners), and the following belonging to the general public Messrs. J. R. Frith, W. Whittaker, William Fisher, J. J Steward (secretary to the Tarpsrley Agricultural Society) and William Brookes.

On the motion of Mr. NORMAN, seconded by Mr. TAYLOR, Dr. Steele,chairman of the Commissioners, was unanimously requested to preside.—LTbe CHAIRMAN said he was sorry to see such a small attendance of the inhabitants of Runcorn at the meeting. It certsinly did not appear as if they were very anxious about the Cheshire Agricultural Society hold- ing their next show in the town. By way of commencing the proceedings, he first read the communication from the secretary to the Cheshire Agricultural Society' dated the 2nd 1 inst., (which has already appeared in our colunlns), stating that since the defeat in November last there had been a strong and growing feeling amongst the members that if desired by the Runcorn people, their next year's show ought to be at Runcorn. He was quite sure there would be no difficulty at their next general meeting in securing a majority ef votes in favour of the show for 1882 being held in Runcorn, if sufficient funds could be raised by a local committee to guarantee a big show for two days.—Mr. W. BECKETT (the secretary), added that he wrote as a private member'of the society. In replying to this communication, the chairman stated that he had no doubt but that sufficient funds would easily be raised, and he should have great pleasure in doing all he could to forward that end. He had also received the following letter from the hon. secretary to the Tarporley Agricultural Society :—" Grosvenor Chambers, Chester, September 14th, 1881. Sir,—At a committee meet- ing of the Tarporley Agricultural Society, held on Saturday last, a wish was expressed that the society should extend its ground in the direction of Frodsham and Runcorn, and I was requested to write to your Commissioners, stating that if it should be their wish, the society would be pleased to hold their annual show at Runcorn next year. I have much pleasure in enclosing you complimentary invitation tic- ket, and to state that the society would be pleased to welcome a deputation of your Commissioners at their annual show to be held at Tattenhall on Thursday, September 22nd. I shall be glad at any time to meet your Commissioners to make arrangements and talk over matters connected with the show.—l am sir, your obedient servant, Jonw JAMES STEWARD, Hon. Secretary." He wrote, in reply, to this letter, stating that an informal meeting of the Commissioners was to be held on the subjec' on the following Monday, and asking the Secretary to kindl, state what they were expected to do, in the way of provid- ing a field, or guaranteeing any sum. He next referred to the public meeting which was to take place on the same day to consider the desirability of asking the Cheshire Agricul- tural Society to bold their show at Runcorn next year. Re likewise expressed the opinion that two shows in Runcorn in the same year would not answer; and it would, therefore, be for the public meeting to decide if both societies, or which, should be invited. Mr. J. J. Steward replied that if the Tarporley society held their next annual meeting at Runcorn, they would like to leave the matter to the local committee to find a field of about ten acres near to the station, to guarantee them £lOO, and to get up a dog, poultry, and flower shots'. In conclusion, Dr. Steele re- marked that the inhabitants had not been invited to discuss at that meeting the question of inviting the Tarporley Agricultural Society to hold their next gatheringat Runcorn. Certainly, judging from the sparse attendance, it did not seem as if the ratepayers wished the Cheshire Agricultural Society to visit the town. Perhaps it would be well to adjourn in order that they might get a fuller meeting, whey the question could be decided. Dr. McDotroALL remarked that it seemed to him they had hardly got a representative meeting there that day. It appeared to him a most unfortunate circumstance that the Runcorn people, who ought to take a little interest in an institution like the Cheshire Agricultural Society, did not think it worth their while to put in an appearance there that day. As those present were almost exclusively Com- missioners, it would scarcely be wise of them to settle that day what course should be adopted. No doubt some of the Commissioners who had received complimentary tickets for the Tarporley show would make it their duty and pleasure to attend, when they would see how far it would be expedient to have the show held at Runcorn next year. He did not know whether invitations had been sent out tc farmers, but, if this were so, it was somewhat remarkable that they did not consider it worth their while to attend. Although the humanizTng influence of shows no doubt had an effect upon commer al centres, there was no doubt that they were of much greater advantage to agricultural dis- tricts. _ _ .

Mr. HANDLEY pointed out that the Commissioners had not taken the same steps to secure an attendance at the meeting as they did last year, when they sent out circulars - to the farmers which ensured their attendance. This year they had not done anything of the sort; but if their pro- ceedings were reported, then at an adjourned meeting he thought they could count on a larger attendance. After some further discussion,

Mr. STEWARD remarked that he was the honorary secre- tary for the Tarporley Agricultural Society; and if the Commissioners thought fit to give them an invitation, they would at once censent to hold their show at Runcorn. There was no " perhaps" with them, but it was a certainty. The Tarporley show included a radius of fifteen miles. Runcorn was included in that ; and if it was the wish f the rate- payers, the society would hold their show once in every two or three years at Runcorn. Dr. McDougall's remarks seemed to point out that the show would only benefit the agriculturists. It was quite true that the main motive of the society was to improve agriculture, but they must not
I lose sight of the fact that if a two days' show was held in , Runcorn, at least £l,OOO would be spent in the town, so that not only would farmers reap a benefit, but the town also.
The Castomarr : Is the Tarporley show held on two days?

Mr. STEWARD: We have held a two days' show, azul if you wish it could do so again. Mr. HANDLEY : Would the cost of a dog and tOetry show be in addition to the guarantee of £100? • Mr. STEWARD : Yes; my letter points out what the so- ciety would like, and in studying our interests you are studying your own also. It was resolved on the motion of Mr. NORMAN' seconded by Mr. TAYLOR, to adjourn the meeting to Thursday, the fith of October, and Mr. Brooks, secretary to the Commis- sioners, was instructed to issue circulars to farmers and others in the district.

WINSFORD TowN Mrssiox.—On Friday evening, a meet- ing of this charitable undertaking was held in the Board schools, when Mr. E. Leigh occupied the chair. The Rev. W. J. Hopper informed the meeting that the collections at the Free Methodist Chapel, for the mission, amounted to £3 65., and the Rev. C. Cay reported subscriptions from Mr. Dudley ,£l, Rev. W. Finch El, Mrs. A. Dudley £l, Mr. Noden's box 55., and card ss. 9d. The secretary, Mr. T. R. Cooke, stated that the amount paid into the bank during this year is £7l 2s. 9d., also that £24 17s. Gd. was yet due, but , promised, and which would raise the amount to £96 Os. 31 It was resolved to remit the balance due to the Ist inst. £59, also the sum of £lO toward last year's debt, to the Manches- ter society, which sends out the town missionary. After prayer by the Rev. C. Cay, the meeting terminated. OVER ONION FAIII.—This annual fair was held on Wed- nesday, when, though the beginning of the day was wet, and militated much against it, there was a fair assemblage of stock, and more buyers and sellers, than could have been expected. The afternoon turned out very favourable, which caused a considerable influx of visitors for the evening when the real business of the fair was over. Onions, one of the chief staple commodities of the autumn fair, were plentiful, and as cheap as usual. The success of the'alteration from the beginning to the middle of the week, is best seen in the improved way in which the Sunday is kept, compared witli what it was under the old regime. But the fair on the whole is more orderly, though the police have still certainly to look after those who fight, or drink to excess, and become unruly, or forget the distinctions between mine and thine.
