L1t3131 CRICKET CLUB —This club concluded its season on Saturday by playing Knutsford at Knutsford. The scores were: Knutsford, 102; Lymm, 36 for two wickets. Lymm have played 21 matches, of which they won eleven, lost four, and drawn six. The season has thus been a suc- cessful one.

THE CONGREGATIONAL SUNDAY SCHOOL—The anniver- sary sermons in connection with this school were preached on Sunday by the Rev. Frederick Carter, of Northwich. There was a good attendance at each service. In the after- noon a special service for parents and children was held, when an eloquent address was delivered by Mr. James Boyd, of Wilmslow. During the service appropriate hymns were sung by the scholars. The collections at the close of each service amounted to upwards of £2O, which will be I added to the school funds. 'The annual statement shows that there has been a considerable increase in the numbers attending the school during the past year. There are on the books 213 scholars, with an average attendance of 41 in the morning and 151 in the afternoon.

THE REV. T. BRACKENBITRY, Wesleyan minister, of War- rington, leaves to-day for Redhill, Surrey, in accordance with the decision of conference. Mr. Brackenbury leaves with the best wishes for his future prosperity of the numer- ous friends he has made during his residence here.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

The Hon. Robert White yesterd.sy personally posted writs and notices on Bantry estate for non-payment of rent. Last night's Gazette contains the declaration prolonging the French Commercial Treaty three months. The appointments of. the Rev. Hugh Pearson, as deputy clerk of the closet to her Majesty, and the Rev. Teignmonth Shore as ordinary chaplain to the Queen are gazetted. Colonel Jervis, who represented Harwich in the Conser- vative interest until last election, died at his residence at Felixtowe last night. The Conservatives of Northamptonshire, meeting at Ket- tering yesterday, selected the Hon. Leopold Powys to con- test the division with Lord Burghley at the general election. The man Frank Brockwell, who was arrested in connec- tion with the murder of the policeman at Kingston Hill, has been discharged, the evidence against him not being suffi- cient to warrant his detention. Mr. Healy proceeds to Cork to take up test cases for the Land Court, and intends especially to give attention to the estates of the Duke of Devonshire, Marquis of Waterford, Earl Kenmare, Mr. King Harman, and Mr. Bence Jones. Mr. Peter O'Leary has had an interview with the Bishop of Ross, who has just returned to Ireland after visiting, with the Archbishop of Cashel, Michael Divett in Portland. The prisoner, who is in excellent health, learnt for the first time of the passing of the Land Act, and the release of Mr. Dillon. He is diligently studying several languages giving special attention to the Irish.

Another serious riot is reported from Ireland. A large crowd gathered in the square at Tubbermarry to welcome home a released suspect, and they came into collision with the police. The head constable was struck to the ground, and the constabnlarly then fired on the mob. It is believed that several persons have been seriously injured, but parti- culars have not yet been ascertained. Twelve men were charged at Limerick yesterday with being concerned in the recent riot in the city. The con- stables who gave evidence described the riot as being one .of the most fearful ever witnessed, sad that if the police had not fired none of them ever would have seen the barracks again. Eleven of the prisoners were committed for trial. Great excitement prevails. Mr. Lowther, M.P., took occasion to correct at the West.. naorland Agricultural Show, on Thursday, the libellous statement that he bad described himself as an out-and-out Free Trader. So far from being anything of the kind, Mr. Lowther boldly proclaims the opinion that Free Trade has proved to be a mistake, and that not only should articles of luxury be taxed but an impost ought to be placed upon all imported cattle. Mr. Lowther admits that the time for pro.. tection on corn has departed "for ever." He does not think that the country could not stand such a tax, but he is strongly of opinion that it would not. - Lord Combermere and Mr. W. F. Tollemache, M.P., at- tended the annual show of the Tarporley Agricultural So- ciety on Thursday, and spoke at a luncheon on the show ground. Lord Combermere, taking a cheerful view of the future, said that the English farmers occupied the proud position of having the best stock in the world. Their cattle, their horses, and their sheep were largely sought for by every other country, and, if he took heart, the British farmer had no need to fear foreign competition. Mr. Tollemache con- gratulated the farmers on the condition of the potato and root crops generally, and on the good prices which cheese is realising.

THE SrmERLAND Snip Yam) STRlKE.—Yesterday after- noon a large crowd of helpers on strike proceeded to the yard of Messrs. Doxford and Sons, where some of the strange hands were working, and broke down one of the doers which had been barricaded, and rushed in. They were met by a handful of policemen and several of the men at work, but these were quite insufficient to stand the assault. Stones, clinkers, and other missiles were freely thrown, and many serious injuries were received. Intelligence was at once conveyed to the police station and a reinforce- ment of Sunderland and Newcastle constables was speedily on the spot, but had to drive their assailants up a steep bank before reaching the yard. After a sharp encounter the mob fell back. The supposed intent of the men on strike was to take possession of the yard and drive the strangers out. They were only successful, however, in breaking down a portion of the boarding. The mob, which numbered about a thousand men, had previously visited Mr. Laing's yard, but created no disturbance.

div.head: SCARLET FEVER AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: SCARLET FEVER AT WARRINGTON.

ANOTHER REMOVAL ORDER REFUSED. Mr. J. L. Whittle, deputy town clerk, applied to Mr. Peter Stabs, at the Borough Court, on Tuesday, for an order for he removal to the Hospital of Jane, daughter of Mr. James Hill, 24, Ashton-street, who is suffering from scarlet fever. Having read the section of the Act respecting the removal of infectious cases, he contended that it was imperative for the magistrate to make the order asked for, but after discussion, Mr. Stubs said the common sense of the matter seemed to him that there should be discretionary power.—The Magis- trates' Clerk (Mr. E. J. Nicholson) said the point was a difficult one, and one upon which a decision might be sought. from a superior court, but as no decision had been sought he thought the best course would be to follow the practice hitherto.—Mr. Whittle then went on to say that scarletfever was now assuming a more malignant character. The child was 6 years old, and the father and mother were living in the house.—Mr. Moore (who opposed the application) said no one was in the house except the nurse and child.—Mr. Whittle stated when Mr. Gornall went there he found two women in the house, one supposed to be the nurse and the other a charwoman. Two of Mr. Hill's children were taken ill on Friday night, and one died at 8 o'clock the following morning. He handed in the certificate of the Medical Officer of Health to the effect that the children was suffer- ing from scarlet fever and was not properly isolated.—Mr. Moore stated that while Mr. Hill was at the funeral of the child that died the Corporation sent their ambulance to take the other child from its mother, and called Dr. Huson- More who said the house contained four rooms and a scullery. The child was attended to by its aunt, and there was no one else in the house save at times thee* going with food. The child was suffering from a very bad type of scarlet fever, and he would resist the removal with every legal power, in the interest of the child and the other patients of the hospital. Removal would decidedly en- danger the child's life. There was sufficient isolation for the child where it was.—Dr. Cannel] confirmed the evidence of the last witness, and said the isolation was as complete as possible.—Mr. Gornall said he believed the removal could be effected without the slightest danger to the child. It was his opinion that the child could not be properly isolated in the house. His experience of the treatment of fever cases by the working class convinced him that he ought to recommend the removal to the hospital, as he be- lieved it to be the best form of isolation to be obtained.— Witness, replying to Mr. Stubs, said there had not to his knowledge been any Oaths caused by removal.—Mr. Stubs said he felt as the matter was before him, and without the law was general ordering all cases to the Infectious Diseases Hospital, he could not make the order asked for. At the same time he felt very strongly indeed, and knew from his own experience the risks of keeping patients suffering from infectious disease were exceedingly great; and he wished to impress upon the father of the child the necessity of watchfulness in the case. It was for him to be very careful indeed for the sake of himself and his wife, and for the sake of the whole community, that every precaution that could be suggested by the doctors was taken for the perfect isola- tion of the case.
Si. HELENS BICYCLE CLIII3.—The championship and ether races are advertised in another column to take place to-day !Saturday), on the ground of the Sutton Cricket Club.

DEA.7II OF Mns. Cormrssr.—Our readers will regret to learn that Mrs. Coleman, wife of the Rev. E. 0. Cole- man, late superintendent of the Warrington Wesleyan circuit, died on Wednesday last, at Brighton, whither the family had removed for the benefit of Mrs. Coleman's health. No doubt the numerous friends of Mr. Coleman in Warrtngton will sympathise with him in his deep sorrow, more especially as the deceased lady has left nine children to mourn her death.

RESIGNATION OF TUE VICAR OF STOCKTON HEATR. —We hear that the Rev. Richard Greensll, vicar of St. Thomas's Church, Stockton Heath, has resigned, being about to retire from the ministry of the Church of England. The reverend gentleman, who is a lover of temperance, has made himself very popular in the parish, and it is with very great regret that his con- gregation learn of his determination to leave. We are given to understand that Mr. Greened" has resolved to betake him- self to agricultural pursuits in the beautiful county of Devon, and we are sure that on his removal he will carry With him the best wishes of all who have had the Pleasure of his acquaintance.

In 1851 we were told that English art workmanship was everywhere out- stripped by France and Italy, and that anything that par- took of an attempt to produce an artistic piece of furniture was a failure in England. The great exhibition of 1851 was held, and from that time schools of art and design were established and their earnest work throughout the country had improved the general taste. There was no doubt that ' that had done so. But to show what effect this had on the general trade of the country, in 1880 the French Minister of Education in speaking on education to a large audience in France, said that England no longer was behind in art work- manship, but was in advance of the whole world, as evidencPd in the exhibition in France. (Applause.) He recommended to the French manufacturers that if they wished to hold their own with the competition of England, they must adopt some means of teaching their workmen the principles of art. That was exactly what Was wanted in all our manufactures to-day. We wanted to depart from the old rule of thumb method and proceed on scientific principles. It was no use talking of proceeding on scientific principles unless they understood the first simple principles of science. These classes offered them a chance of learning those first simple principles, and the committee earnestly begged them to take advantage of them. (Ap- plause.) Tip Chairman then introduced Mr. Percy to deliver his lecture on "The early history ef the steam engine." The LECTURER, who was cordially received, said any- thing connected with the rise and progress of the steam engine, the most wonderful mechanical arrangement the world had ever seen, was full of interest to a practical com- munity, and especially to one like Warrington. To the rise of steam we owed almost everything so far as material pros- perity was concerned. By its aid the various towns and counties in our own and other countries were brought into close proximity ; under its influence our mighty vessels ploughed the ocean wave, and the distance between the various continents were as little to us now as between neigh- bouring villages 100 or 200 years ago. It was to the power of steam that we owed the means of raising from the bowels \ of the earth that mineral wealth which was the source of the greatness of our great country ; and to which Warrington owed the ability of manufacturing on such an exteusive scale the iron which was sent to all parts of the world. Without the use of that immense power not only aviould many industries that were now in existence never have been known, but other industries handed down to us from olden times could not have been developed to anything like the extent they had ; and were it not for the immense power which this wonderful agent placed at our disposal we might

"FAIR TRADE, ALIAS PROTECTION, VERSUS FREE TRADE." Sir,—Mr. Disraeli, speaking at Aylesbury thirty years ago, said: "The protectionist system could never be brought back." Mr. Mclver, in the House of Commons, recently advocated "the imposition of customs ditties upon all foreign importations that come into unfair competition with the in- dustries of Great Britain." Lord R. Churchill, speaking this week at Oldham, refers to "hair-brained and moon- struck free traders," and advocates a wholesale system of protection. Sir Michael H. Beach, speaking at Gloucester, refers to protection in a very guarded and careful manner, says we tax tea, and because w.-2 do this we ought to do something for the peer down-trodden landlord. Lord BeaconstiAd's latest utterance on the question was, "Protection is dead." So we see the eminent statesman, after thirty years' experience, wenld have none of it. Sir Michael is careful, and it is also noticeable that in their latest utterances Sir Stafford North. cots and Sir Richard A. Cross take care not to compromise themselves. So we find we have but the rank and file rush- ing in where better men fear to tread. The working- men, through their Trades Congress, have also ref used to entertain the question. Sampson Lloyd, Captain Bedford Pym, and James Lowther are therefore left to do battle in favour of poor land lords like the Marlborough pensioners. These worthies assure us that England is going down, that trade is leaving us, and that agriculture is being gradually destroyed, all in consequence of free trade. Nay, we have a celestial Doctor of our own who has set up shop, and while forgetting that he lives in a glass house, throws stones at free trade and begs the working men of Warrington to have faith in his seraphic intelligence. Now, sir, if our trade is leaving us where is it going to? Cotton may be taken as our staple trade. Parliamentary documents give it as 321 per cent. of our whole export trade. In 1872 France exported 68 millien francs worth of manufactured cotton. In 1879 she extorted 63 million francs' worth. A falling off of 5 millions. Evidently France has not taken our cotton trade. In 1872 Germany exported 17 million marks' worth of manufactured cottons, and in 1870 only 15 million marks' worth. It is not gone to Germany. America in 1872 exported over 35 re'llion dollars' worth of manufactured cotton, in 1879 20 millions, 15 millions erf a loss in consequence of the great aid to trade, protection. Let us now look at metals, and it may be remarked that the figures given include everything under the head of metal wares. In 1872 the export of these from France amounted to 91 million francs. In 1879 it had fallen to 671 million, so that in this set of articles France has not taken our trade. Of Germany nothing can be said, as in the German returns money value is not given. It may be said that quantities have increased, but altogether the metal and machine trade of the German Empire is only 735,000 tons; whilst our trade is 3,792,993 tons in iron and steel, to which has to be added for machinery and telegraph Wire 1.0-.12- millions sterling. He not only received rents; or, to put it plainly, he not only taxes all the farmer produces, but he also taxes all that I comes out of the mountain side, and also all that comes oet of the pit mouth. THEFT FROM A PAWNSHOP.—EIIen Eckford, a married woman, of Whiston, was committed to prison for a month for stealing two pairs of boots and two vests, value 14s. 6d., from the pawnshop of Mr. Morton, Eccleston-street, Prescot.

The monthly meeting of this Board was held on Mon- day. There were present—Messrs. W. L. Evans (chair- man), J. Johnson Brown, W. Goldsworth, J. Wycherley, C. Spencely, John Sanders, and T. P. Hewitt; with Mr. J. Cowherd (assistant clerk). SCARLET FEVER AND THE ATTENDANCE AT THE SCHOOLS. Miss DUKE, mistress of the Girls' School, reported that the average attendance last week was 83, as compared with 74 in the corresponding week of last year.—ln answer to the Chairman, Miss DUKE said several of her scholars were away owing to scarlet fever. It was very prevalent.—Miss MCGREGOR, mistress of the infant school, stated that the average attendance in her department last week was 66 as against 101 in the corresponding week of last year.—The CHAIRMAN observed that fever was so prevalent he did not wonder the attendance at the infant school was low.—Miss MCGREGOR remarked that a nnmber of her pupils were ab- sent in consequence of the fever. She also reported that a sister of the pupil teacher in the infant school (Miss Guy) was suffering from scarlet fever, and that the teacher came to school on that day but was sent back again. Both of Miss Guy's brothers went to school at St. Helens that morn- ing.—After some discussion it was resolved that Miss Guy, the pupil teacher, be requested to leave her home at Rain- hill and reside in Prescot for a few days, and not to go near her home or the schools in the meantime.—Mr. P. LIGHT- I FOOT, master of the boys' school, said the average attendance last week was 161, as compared with 146 in the correspond- ing week of last year.—The ATTENDANCE OFFICER, in reply to the Chairman, said there was a great deal of scarlet fever in the town, and there were a great number of cases which had not been attended by medical men. Dr. Hall ordered four children of one family to go out of school in the pre- vious week—Mr. Bncoivis said there must be some local cause for that scarlet fever. He was told, but he had not endeavoured to ascertain whether it was correct or not, that there was a great hotbed of disease producing power behind Mr. Goldsworth's old offices, in Warrington-road, in the shape of a ditch that had never been connected with any- thing to drain it. Mr. Goldsworth did not consider that ditch had mach to do with the prevalence of scarlet fever in the town. Typhoid fever arose from defective privies, ditches, Src. Scarlet fever was very infectious and could be carried about in the clothes. A child affected with the disease, if not properly looked after, could carry it through the town in a short time. ATTENDANCE OFFICER'S REPORT. Mr. Wm. LLOYD, the school attendance officer, reported that since the last meeting he had visited the several schoolsl in his district together with the Huyton-and-Roby and Whiston schools. He had served notices on 42 Parents, re- presenting 74 children, who had been irregular in their at- tendance at school and he had also visited the parents of 202 children, whose names had been handed in. In several cases the parents had been warned. The summons which stood adjourned to the 16th inst., as per last report, was dis- posed of on that day and the usual fine inflicted.

THE SUBSCRIPTION PRIZES.

The competition for the prizes annually given by friends of the corps in St. Helens, and Widnes and neighbourhood, and called the Subscription Prizes, took place on Saturday. The weather was not favourable, rain commencing while at 500 yards; and at GOO, what with the very bad light and rain, the targets and discs were barely discernible. The shooting, therefore, under the conditions, was very good. The following were the winners :

A CORN MILL BURNT DOWN NEAR ST. HELENS. On Tuesday morning the Stanley Corn Mill, at Black- brook, St. Helens, was discovered to be on fire. Mrs. Battersby, who resides with her husband a few yards from the mill, awoke about three o'clock and remarked to her husband that something was on fire, there being a strong smell in the room. She could not account for the existence of the smell in any other way than that some chips about the hearth had caught fire, and her husband went downstairs to prove the fallacy or otherwise of that theory. After an ex- amination of the house and receiving no enlightenment, he opened the door and to his astonishment saw the corn mill" on fire. He at once awoke Mr. Maitland, who has the mill in lease from the London and North-Western Railway Com- pany, and who lodges with him the greater part of the week, and in a short time the whole of the inhabitants in the neigh- bourhood were at the scene of the fire. A man was at once des- patched to the fire office at St. Helens and several willing hands were employed in fetching buckets of water from an adjoining brook, but their efforts proved of little use. The building, which is a three storey one, was filled with machinery, and several rooms were stocked with oats and other grain which had been bought from the farmers within the last two or three weeks. On the door of the building being opeaed the place was found to be in one blaze of fire. About half-past four the fire engine and brigade arrived on the scene; and there being a brook a few yards distant, and the canal thirty yards from the building, a good supply of water was poured on the building. The fire had, however, got too firm a hold to allow its instantaneous extinction, and it was half-past eight before the brigade made their way back to St. Helens without having saved any grain or any of the mill furniture ; although their services were willingly given and energetically put forth to the saving of the property. Seeing that the case was a hopeless one their efforts were directed principally to preventing the adjoining buildings being injured; and this was done although, as the superin- tendent of the brigade says, a strong wind was blowing at the time. Some of the cottagers fearing that such a catas- trophe might ensue packed up their "goods and chattels," and made preparations for leaving their houses. At the time our representative visited the place, the roof had fallen in, the windows were completely burnt out, and the building was gutted, the lower portion being filled with the Mris of machinery, timber, and other material. The fire appears to have broken out at that part nearest the cottages, but the cause has not yet been ascertgined. The damage to the building and stock is very great, being about £1,600 alto- gether. The building formerly belonged to Lord Gerard, who sold it to the railway company. It is insured. Mr. Maitland is quite a young man, and is a resident of Liverpool. The Stanley Corn Mill was his first place if business.
PRESCOT ADJOURNED LICENSING SESSIONS.

The adjourned licensing sessions for the Prescot Division was held at the Court House, Derby-street, on Thursday, the magistrates present being Messrs. W. L. Evans and T. Pilkington.—Jacob McMullen, Huyton, applied for a license to sell spirits, wine, and beer off the premises. The applicant had already made a similar application, but he now applied for it under the old Licensing Act in order to do away with the wholesale dealer's license.—Granted.--- The license to the Eagle and Child, Warrington-road, Prescot, was renewed, it being stated that the old tenant, Paul Hunt, who had been convicted for permitting drunken- ness, had left the house, and that it had been taken by Moak Kellet, to whom a temporary authority to sell until the newt i transfer day had been granted.

div.head: PRESCOT POLICE INTELLIGENCE.
div.p: PRESCOT POLICE INTELLIGENCE.

FRlDAY.—Before Mr. F. W. Earle. HOUSEBREAKING AT WAVERTREE.—Thomas Howard, a young man, was charged with breaking and entering the dwelling-house of Michael McMahon, No. 2, Cambridge- street, Wavertree, and stealing an overcoat, silver guard, set of gold-plated studs, boy's watch and chain, and other articles.—Elizabeth McMahon, prosecutor's wife, said that on the 2nd August they were residing at 2, Cambridge- street. They retired to rest about balf-past nine that night leaving the doors and windows of the house secure. About seven o'clock the following morning her son got up and went downstairs to light a fire. From something he told told her shortly afterwards she got up and went downstairs. She found a pane of glass two feet long by eighteen inches broad had been taken out of the scullery window and placed at the far end of the yard, the putty having been removed with a white-hafted knife, which was lying on the window- sill. The window was wide open. Two small boxes and several drawers in the kitchen had been troken open, and the contents strewn about the room. On making an exami- nation she missed a silver guard, boy's watch and chain, set of gold-plated studs, an overcoat, and other articles. The articles, altogether, were worth about £2 105. Infor- mation of the robbery was then given to the police.— William Henry McMahon, son of the last witness, said that when he came downstairs on the morning of the 3rd August he discovered that the house had been entered by the scullery window, from which a pane of glass had been re- moved.—ln answer to Mr. Blackwell (assistant magistrates' clerk), Mrs. McMahon said her son was the first person to get up and go downstairs that morning.—William Edward Green said he was an auctioneer, residing at 87, Great Homer-street, Liverpool. On the 3rd August he was an assistant pawnbroker to William Joseph Hughes, 116, Brownlow-hill, and about half-past ten on that morning the prisoner pledged the coat produced at Mr. Hughes's shop, and received 4s. upon it. Witness asked prisoner if the coat was his, and he replied that it was. Prisoner gave the name of John Murphy, Gill-street, Liverpool. Witness had not the slightest doubt that the prisoner was the man who pawned the coat.—P.C. McCracken deposed that he received the prisoner into custody on the 7th inst., and took him to Wavertree police station, where he charged him with committing the offence. Prisoner replied, "I know nothing about them."—David Heron, watchman in the employ of the Liverpool Corporation and residing in No. 4 Court, Pembroke-st., Liverpool, said that on Tuesday night, the 2nd August, he was on duty at the new tramway works at Wavertree Bridge (the city boundary), which was about 200 yards from Mr. McMahon 's house. The prisoner came to his watch-fire about half-past ten o'clock, and remained till about half-past eleven. Prisoner told him that he did not want to go through Wavertree till all the shops were closed.--Superintendent Barker: When prisoner left your watch-fire did he go in the direction of Cambridge-street? Witness: Yes, sir.—ln answer to the charge, Use prisoner replied "All I have to say is that I know nothing about the affair at all."—Committed for trial at Kirkdale Quarter Sessions. ALLEGED ASSAULT AND HIGHWAY ROBBERY.—Robert Ridley, a middle-aged man, was charged with having, at Wavertree, on the 3rd-instant, assaulted a boy named Arthur William Lowe, and also with having stolen from him the sum of 16s. 10d., a purse, and a pawnticket.—Arthur Wm. Lowe said he was nine years of age, and resided with his parents at 161, Stephenson-street, Wavertree. His father was a cab-driver in the employ of Mr. Dilworth, High-street, Wavertree. On Saturday, the 3rd instant, about one o'clock in the afternoon, his mother gave him a purse and instructed him to go to Mr. Dilworth's to fetch his father's wages. He went, and saw his father put his wages (18s. Id.) into the purse, which he handed to him. He kept the purse in his hand and put the latter in his jacket pocket. On the way home be called at Taylor's breadshop and purchased a loaf. He offered a 25. piece in payment and received 10d. change. Before going into the shop he noticed the prisoner and several other men lounging about a public-house in the vicinity. He placed the change he had received in his purse, and again started on his way home along Wavertree- road. On the way he passed the prisoner and another man, both of whom followed him across the road and eventually overtook him. Prisoner's companion struck him across the arm and jerked the purse out of his band. Prisoner tried to catch it but failed, and the other man picked it up. Both men then ran away in the direction of Liverpool. He followed but lost sight of them near the railway bridge. He went back to Taylor's breadshop and from what he was told there he again went towards the railway bridge. When he got on the bridge be saw the prisoner and his companion standing together. One man was giving the other some- thing, but he could not see what it was.—ln answer to Superintendent Barker, witness stated that the man not in cus- tody was giving the prisoner something. He went home and told his parents and information was given to the police.— Prisoner: Where did you see me? Witness: Aside of the public-house.—Prisoner : What man was that whom you said was with me? Witness: I don't know his name; but I should know him again if I saw him.—William Lowe, father of the last witness, corroborated the first portion of his son's evidence.—William Jepson, watchman in the employ of the Liverpool Tramway Company, said that on the 3rd instant, about half-past two o'clock, he saw the prisoner and another man near his box. He heard this man say to the prisoner that he had better get home and change his clothes as soon as he could. Prisoner went away in the direction of Liver- pool and the other man went towards Wavertree. When the prisoner and his companion came to his box they came from the direction of the railway bridge.—P.C. Rogers, stationed at Wavertree, deposed that he apprehended the prisoner on the sth instant. He had the first witness with him, and on passing along Rathbone-road, the witness pointed the prisoner out as one of the men who had robbed him. He charged prisoner with having assaulted and robbed the boy, and he replied "I never saw the purse or anything of your boy either." He afterwards said "There was no one in com- pany with me on that day."—On being formally charged prisoner said he had nothing to say.—He was then commit- ted for trial at the Quarter Sessions. TUESDAY.—Before Mr. F. W. Earle, Mr. W. L. Evans, and Colonel Blackburne, M.P. A DRUNKARD COMMITTED TO Pnisq.pr.—Michael Walsh was charged with being drunk and disorderly.—On Satur- day night, the 10th inst., defendant was found in a drunken state, and behaving in a diaorderly manner in High-street, Prescot.—Superintendent Barker said defendant had been sixteen times previously before the court.—Defendant was sent to gaol for one month, with hard labour. BREACH OF THE PEACE.—Catherine Fitzpatrick was charged with committing a breach of the peace.—P.S. Dingley deposed that about eleven o'clock on the night of the sth inst., prisoner was making a great noise in Allen's- court, Preseot.—Superintendent Barker said that was the prisoner's 65th appearance. In December, 1879, in default of finding sureties, she was committed for twelve months; in January, this year, she was committed for a month for being drunk and disorderly; and in June this year, she was sent to gaol for two months for assaulting the police.— Prisoner said she had reared fourteen children, and had been a good mother to them. She had a bad husband. The police knew very well that they never saw her knocking about the streets in a drunken state. She was continually being twitted about her son who was convicted at the last Liverpool assizes of hav- ing caused the death of his wife and sentencsd to fifteen years penal servitude, and it was very hard. The Bench bound her over to keep the peace for three months, herself in £lO, and two sureties of £5 each, in default one month's imprisonment.—The prisoner became very noisy and was re- moved from the dock. On being taken out of the court-room and down the steps she screamed and yelled to the officers "Go away! go away " Poon REL'azroxs. —Joseph Parr and Thomas Parr, bro- thers, were summoned to show cause why they should not be ordered to contribute towards the support of their father who had become chargeable to the common fund of the Prescot Union.—Mr. S. H. Hartley, clerk to the Guardians, said the father of the defendants (Henry Parr) was 69 years of age, very feeble and infirm, and unable to leave his bed He had been in receipt of relief for seven or eight months. He had four sons, two of whom paid regularly towards his, main- tenance. Defendants had contributed up to within the last few weeks, but they now refused to pay unless an order was I made upon them. Thomas owed 10s. and Joseph 17s. The I Guardians asked for an order of Is. 6d. per week upon each, the same amount as the other brothers were paying, and an , order for that amount was made. RECKLESSNESS IN A WHISTON COAL MINE. James Goulding, a collier, was charged with failing to extinguish the light of a certain lamp which had become damaged, in accordance with the special rule in force at the colliery.— James Middlehurst, underground manager at Whiston Col- liery, said that on the 30th of Augut he visited that portion of the mine where defendant was working. He found de- fendant using a lamp which had become damaged and was unsafe to work with. He pointed this out to defendant, and he admitted that it had been done about half an hour pre- viously. Witness told him he ought to have extinguished the light, and taken the lamp to the place appointed to ex- amine and repair damaged lamps. Defendant's only excuse was that he did not think it was so bad as it appeared. A piece of the " protection " glass had been broken, and the flame was visible through the hole. The glass was used instead of gauze. The 32nd special rule in force at the col- liery set forth that if his lamp got damaged the collier should at once extinguish the light, and take or send the lamp to the place appointed for the examining and rerair- ing of lamps.—A fine of 201. and costs Was inflicted, in default one month's imprisonment. CILARGE AGAINST A RAINHILL INNKEEPER. Jane Little, keeper of the Red Lion Inn, Rainhill Stoops, was charged with selling intoxicating liquors during prohibited hours.—Mr. T. Swift, of St. Helens, appeared for the de- foe; tnntd. —a vT, ht he e c slot hfor twothe ppo rl iocsee ecuotni os tna ea ss wt heautt a to boutd elf eln-4do. ant's house and found nine men in the taproom, with pint cups containing beer before them. Five of the men resided within the limit prescribed by Act of Parliament relating to bona fide travellers, while the other four resided outside. Of the five men who lived within three miles of the public- ' -use, three resided at Appleton and the other two at Pres- , ..—For the defence Mr. Swift said that and tthheeydaytoilnd t question Mrs. Little was away from home End her daughter- in-law admitted the men after making the necessary in- quiry as to where they came- front. TRAVELS IN THE EAST., vn.i ore lae o g ho on the plain. I never witnessed anything strange Jericho eaend unearthly than the singing and appear- anceuponhairwhich of these women. They wore Arretab i he single garment of BY A SOUTH-WEST LANCASHIRE GENTLEMAN. blue serge common to the poor f twomen n country [SPECIA L. tattooed faces, piercing ,an No. XVII. places. the glare of the amdp mateteld \• flying about their shoulders, we had a picture before us that exceeded any witch-scenel had ever imagined. The leader of DOWN TO JERICHO. With these thoughts and feelings moving within us, we the dance had a sword in her hand, vele ich she also waved over her own head and that of the others as they fell stooping rode round the simi-circular ravine that leads along the on one knee in a circle, she uttering the while a sound in side of Olivet to Bethany, and soon had the once beautiful, her throat between a.screech and a warble, repeating the and waving the sword before one and another of the but now degraded and despoiled village sitting on the hill same. as she came whirling round the circle with hands up- behind us, as we began to descend into the long mountain Had we known the nature of the entertainment defile that divides Judah from Benjamin, and thence into the thus provided for us, Ido not think we should have enter- lifetmedp,any. postble, we concluded the evening by singing to them in wilderness of mountain and valley leading down to Jericho, tamed it; but to make the thing as agreeable and profitable apsarts our National Anthem, and one 'or two other; pieces, but the Dead sea, and the plain of Jordan. Through dreary de for our pains we discovered that the only effect our singing files and rocky paths we dropped from one elevation to had was to arouse the jealously of our audience. They another, until at the close of the day we found ourselves, instead of being.2,soo feet above the level of the sea, andabout had thought, poor things that we wanted to share the "back- aboutl,soo feet below it. A little more than half way down, noon, we came upon the ruins of the old khan. or sheesh " with them.' fortified [inn, called the "Good Samaritan." Here, sur- (To be continued next week.) rounded by scenery of the wildest description, we sat down to lunch within the crevice of a rock, which afforded a delightful shelter from the oppressive heat of the sun. To- day, as on all other days during our tenting out, the tink- ling of bells was heard ere we had finishedand oasusresnoloaniednaywirfeh f. past, and the long cavalcade of mules our baggage passed on the road a the aces pfrom us on the i way to prepare for our reception n he evening. Usually we sat in conversation, resting beneath some rock or tree for a couple of hours, and then, going forward, found our tents erected, and our little iron beds with their neat coverlets reads- to afford a lounge before dinner was announced. At a quarter to six, Aboo, the best natured fellow in the whole party, came round from tent to tent beating with an old pestle upon its equally antiquated mortar, and bawling out, " Firsht bell, shentlemen, if you pleash." Once only we got Aboo to in- clude the "Ladish;" but, like a true oriental, he insisted upon putting them last, and did it in such an awkward and faltering manner that he got laughed at, looked quite sheepish, and would never do it again. At six o'clock the pestle and mortar again sounded, and Aboo, with never fail- ing politeness towards his own sex, was heard calling, " Dinner ready, shentlemen, if you pleash!" Seven or eight nicely cooked dishes, besides dessert of oranges, figs, dates, and raisins, all very delightful in their freshness, made up our usual evening meal, crowned, generally,ivith a cup of teaswhich some ofus enjoyed most of all. But to return to our noon-day picnic beneath the shadow of the rock, and near to the ruins of the old Khan. From this point to Jericho is very wild; the region through which we travelled was grand, indeed. in its ruggedness; but the near and distant landscape was most painfully bare and parched. To our left one dreary mountain after another rose to view like great sand heaps, made up of smaller hillocks piled one behind another, sometimes with great regularity, and some- times without any order at all, and across those "withering heights," with the wild beasts skulking around Him by day, and yelling across the dreary wilds by night, the Son of Man must have wondered during the 40 days and nights of His temptation. Yet in calmness of thought He makes this region the scene of His beautiful parable of the man who fell among thieves, and was suc- coured by the good Samaritan. Doubtless the parable had a foundation in fact, and this Khan, the only place of enter- tainment between Jerusalem and Jericho, was the one to which the poor wounded traveller was brought. The char- acter of the region as a stronghold of thieves is still main- tained, and I have more than a suspicion that its evil report is kept alive for the purpose of extorting " back- sheesh," and of so doing the thieving in a gentlemanly way. It is romantic, you know, for the plundered Teuton or Anglo-Saxon to have an armed escort, mounted and on foot, and, moreover, so much more safe and pleasant for the thieves themselves to march before and behind, and do the plundering as an act of friendship, receiving the proceeds as a voluntary and well-earned gift, instead of jeopardising their race or their own necks by acts of violence. We had two stalwart Arabs striding on before us with immensely long guns slung over their shoulders, and two mounted ones, with guns equally long, bringing up the rear. We had almost ceased to wonder at all this formidable display of protection in a region apparently without an inhabitant, when, to meet all questioning by demonstration of the danger, three Bedouins of the desert had come forward, and were standing in a field a few yards from the road, about half-way down to Jericho. Of course, it was very conclu- sive, but very comical, reaching almost to the character of a I farce, when our dragoman galloped forward from the rear and placed himself between us and the threatened danger. To my mind the poor scarecrows in the field seemed far less capable of doing us mischief than the men by whom we were guarded. These wily Arabs make great capital out of the wicked deeds, few and far between, of their brigand brethren. They will tell you that ten or twelve years ago an Englishman was stripped on going up to Jerusalem, and had everything taken from him except a Times newspaper, which was left, in the absence of fig leaves, his only clothing until he got to Jerusalem. Stories such as these to an Englishman whose eyes and ears are f.miliar with the recital of horrid murders and crimes of every description, are, in comparison, "like tales that are told by an idiot, full of sound and fury, signifying nothing." As long as travellers can enjoy the security we felt in going down to Jericho, they can surely afford to be hoodwinked a little, and to smile at all those terror-inspiring contrivances, although they have to pay in hard cash for the performance. Three or four miles from the plains of the Jordan we saw the brook of I Cherith bursting from the bed of a ravine into a sort of pool or basin, overflowing which, it continued to follow our track through the deep gorges to our left. The mountain sides were peculiarly imposing; they sloped down in steps formed by decay of the strata until within a few yards of the base, when they fell almost perpendicularly into the bed of the river, of which we only get here and there a glimpse until the glorious plain of Jericho burst upon our view, then we saw it quietly winding its way across the plain towards the Jordan. We had to cross its sparkling waters soon after we issued from the mountain range, and after their hard and sweltering journey, our poor horses were de- lighted to cool their hoofs and mouths in the refreshing stream. Turning northward, with the noble plains to our right, and the Quarantursia mountains on the left, in a few minutes we crossed another brook at the "Fountain of Elisha," and soon found ourselves stretched on our couches upon the supposed mounds of ancient Jericho. How was it possible to realise that we were lying on the very spot over which the ram's horns had sounded, and which had shaken with the crash of its demolished walls? And how strange that, under such circumstances, we should be going, after a few minutes, in the most common-place manner, with our towels over our arms, to wash in Elisha's fountain The tropical heat, added to our toilsome journey, made us glad to have,our heads and hands in the refreshing stream. Two of our Arab muleteers were there before us, and were attending to their evening devotions, after their customary washing. One was kneeling and bowing on the stone ledge of the fountain, while the other was at his ablutions ; the latter gentleman very coolly asked us for the loan of a piece of soap, which, being scented, he put to his nose with evident delight. Seeing we regarded his companion with some in- terest, he pointed to him as he knelt bowing his head to -the ground, and said, " Good! geod Arab !" It was curious to see how, if anything attracted the attention of the wor- shipper, he could break off, engage in conversation with his companion, and then resume until he had gone through the prescribed forms and prayers. Looking from the site of ancient Jericho, the northern end of the Dead Sea can be seen eight miles distant to the right of the plain. We started next morning at nine o'clock to visit its shores. In a quarter of an hour we passed through the supposed site of Jericho of the New Testamant, now the most miserable-looking village in Palestine. The only in- habitants we saw were a few dark and dirty-looking women, with tattooed faces, and a swarm Of clamorous children, whom our attendants made it their business to keep out of the way as we passed. A house of larger dimensions than the rest has the honour of being called the house of Zaccheus, probably because it is the only one in the neigh- bourhood with the slightest pretensions to such a dis- tinction. In a few minutes the vegetation which flourishes so richly but so wildly opposite to our tents, becomes more and more bare, until nothing but thinly-scattered clumps of prickly shrub are to be seen. These entirely disappear as you come near the Dead See; then you ride between great heaps of soil, eighteen to twenty feet high, all of one level, and flat on the top, which the floods have left in washing away all the rest of the land. The soil is so impregnated with the salt deposits, caused by evaporation from the Dead Sea, that it is covered over the surface with -white crust. Most of our friende'bathed in the sea. The water, though acrid beyond all description, is perfectly bright and clear, very tempting to persons of bathing propensities in $o sultry a climate. It looked so aelightfully transparent and quiescent that I plunged right over head. An immediate smarting of the eyes and nostrils followed, and I found it no easy matter aiterwards to free my hair from the dummy substance that was left. From accounts I had read I almost expected to be able to walk upon the water, or float like a cork upon the surface, but the most real experience I had of that kind was some little difficulty in getting my feet down when they once left terra firma. It takes an hour to reach the Jordan crossing the plain diagonally from the Dead Sea. Most of the bathers got another dip when we got there. The Jordan is very muddy and rapid in its flow opposite to Jericho, It issiratea narrow river compared to many in England, which h ow is how much sacred associations and great historical events tend to elevate pla ces and things which are in them- selves mean and by the springing up ainsignificant. We were greatly favoured brisk, refreshingbreeze as we returned to our tents. by the way ef ancient Gilgal, which lies on the plain a little to the north of Jericho. A few loose stones lying about are the only remains of the town where Joshua first encamped after crossing the Jordan After winding through brushwood and tamarish trees' almost labyrinthine in the tortuousness of their paths, we reached our tents about four p.m. Scarcely had the dinner loth been removed in the saloon tent when an unearthly cloth was heard outside, and on issuing forth we found the tents illuminated, and about a dozen Arabs dancing and singing on the sward. The Arabs have only one dolorous ditty, compw,d of about three whines, slightly differing in sound. In dancing they merely stamp the ground and bend the knee to a monstrous clap of the hands. The leader of the performance waved a sword over his own and their heads, sometimes dropping on one knee and leaning forward, while thok rest, still singing and clapping their hands, fell also on orte knee in a circle around him. I found them improvis'-g compliments to our conductor, doubtless as the sheik of party, and to them the Bey of Backsheesh. In its w. .1 and demonical character, the performance of the men far surpassed by the women, who came from 1.1. e

WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS. At the fortnightly meeting, held at the Workhouse, on Wednesday, Mr. J. Harrison presided, the other members present being—Major Cartwright, Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, Messrs. Darbyshire, Blackhurst, Woolfall, Winstanley, Greening, Hall, Heaton, Woods, Cooper, Owen, Appleton, Humphreys, Greenall, Fairhurst, Houghton, Jeans, Bal. harry, Hunt, and J.C. Sutton kclerk. BILL OF PARTICULARS WANTED. On the accounts being read, Mr. WINSTANLEY said there was an account of IS 15s. from Dr. Watkins for expensive medicines, but no particulars were given. He did not sup- pose Dr. Watkins would do anything wrong but it would be much more convenient. The CHAIRMAN: It would be much better. Mr. WINSTANLEY moved that Dr. Watkins be iustructed to send the bills for the future to the Newton Relief COTII- - before presented to the Board, and that he give a de- tailed account of medicines dm., used. Mr. DARBYSHIRE seconded the motion. He thought it only right and fair that the Board should have the par- ticulars of the expensive medicines in a proper form. The CLERK said Dr. Watkins had previously sent in a bill of particulars. Mr. WINSTANLEY said Dr. Watkins extras had always been very moderate. The motion was carried. AN ECCENTRIC AND COSTLY PATIENT. Mr. DARBYSHIRE said he noticed in the Liverpool C,urier of Saturday that a man who had been an inmate of the Warrington Workhouse for many years, had cost the rate- payers £IOO ; and that he had promised to make a state- ment of where he came from, and how it was he went there, but that he had deferred his explanation until it was too late. He said the Guardians ought to be in possession of information as to anything that transpired in the Union as soon as the newspapers. He did not know whether it was customary for the Master to state the deaths of these people to the Board but it would have been information to them all, seeing that the inmate entered under very peculiar cir- cumstances, and had been a very peculiar character. Mr. WINSTANLEY said he asked the Master at the meet- ing of the Visiting Committee, on Wednesday last, if any endeavour had been made to obtain a statement from the man before his death, and he replied in the affirmative, but the man refused to make any statement is to his antece- dents. All requisite attention had been paid to the man. Major CARTWRIGHT said he did not think the Master had given any information to the reporters ; it was well known that the man was a celebrated character. The Rev. John Yonge had had an audience of half an hour with the man for the express purpose of getting to know something about him, but his efforts were fruitless. He never would tell, and he was some years in the House and the Guardians did not know whether he was dumb or not. Mr. WINSTANLEY : He simulated dumbness for four

years. The MASTER, in reply to Major Cartwright, said the man had been in the House nine years. Major CARTWRIGHT said the man had been in the Hospital all that time, and the cost of maintaining a person in the Hospital was Sc. 6d. per week, so that the deceased could not have cost the Guardians £4OO. The CHAIRMAN said the Master had made a report of the circumstances in his diary of September 10th, stating that deceased, Moses Woods, about 42 years of age, was admitted into the House on the 20th November, 1872. He had been in bed the whole of the time, and for nearly four years he never spoke. The subject then dropped. APPOINTMENT OF NURSE. Three candidates for the office of nurse appeared before the Board, and after some consideration Miss Diana Watkins, of the Nurses Home, Brownlow Hill, Liverpool, was unani- mously appointed. The other applicants were Miss Mary Annie Coleman, of the Chorlton Union, and Miss Annie E. Donough, of the West Derby Union. THE GRANTING OF SCHOOL FEES. Mr. DARRYSIIIRE said the School Attendance Committee had granted the renewal of the payment of school fees in 41 cases and also in 4 new cases. The number of cases kept increasing. He moved that the orders be confirmed. Mr. GREENING seconded the motion, which was carried. TENDERS. A number of tenders from tradesmen for the supply of provisions, Ltc., for the half-year ending March, 1882, were considered and the following were accepted :—Beer and porter, Wm. Bolton; flour and oatmeal, —. Caldwell; Wm. Fletcher ; glaziers' work, J. Gaskell ; brushes, Wm. Chester ; groceries, N. B. Percival ; cheese, Mrs. Eckersley ; straw, potatoes' and milk and butter, —. Houghton • butchers' meat, John Cross; and coal, Messrs. Evans. A' conversation occurred as to the heaviness of the of the stationery contract, and Mr. Hall stated that as it , was now tendered for the Board paid 150 per cent. more than was necessary. A committee was appointed to consider the matter and to draw up an improved system of tendering. NEWTON AND EARLESTOWN. ST. MARY AND Sr. Joll.N'S CATHOLIC CHURCH, NEWTON. —Special services were held at this church on Sunday, when sermons wee preached, and collections made, on behalf of the day schools. In the morning the Rev. Father Caldwell, Si., of Holy Cross Church, St. Helens, occupied the pulpit, and in the afternoon the Rev. Fathar Kavanagh preached. Good congreations wera present at both services, and the collections realised £35. EARLESTOWN STARR-BOWICETT BUILDING SOCIETY.— The Earlestown branch of the Starr-Bowkett Building Society has not proved such a success as was anticipated, and it has been determined to wind it up. On Monday night a meeting was held, when the manager and secretary attended in order to receive the balances and books for the period ending August 29th, 1881. Stnnaer DEATH AT NEWTON.—RaIph Davis, 74 years of age, died suddenly on Sunday, at Newton. Deceased had been unwell for some time, and he had been attended first by Dr. Watkins and subsequently by Dr. Broe. A week ago he became worse, and on Sunday his son found him lying dead on the floor of his bedroom. BILLIARD HANDICAP AT EARLESTOWN.—A billiard handi- cap has been played at the Earlestown Liberal Club. The first prize consisted of 65., and the second 3s. There were 13 entries, and the game lasted a fortnight. W. Clark won the first prize easily, and W. Calvert succeeded in carrying off the second prize.

YEbTERDAY'S MARKETS. LIVERPOOL COTION.—Spot : The business continues large, and prices are firmly maintained. Sales 1.2,000 bales, of which 2,000 are on speculation and for export. The sales for the week are 53,600 bales, or 7,660 more than the estimate. Spinners have taken 45 360 bales, including 5,380 forwarded direct. The import is 35,959 bales, and the export 5,296. The stock has decreased 12,400 bales. The visible supply is 370.180 bales more than at ihe_same time last year. Futures have been firm all day at a partial 1-32 d advance on last night's rates. MANCHESTER COTTON.—The market is in a worse position than ever, and no progress is being made. The fresh advance in cotton stops business, and advices from Calcutta are very ad- verse. Prices are firm, or even higher, except here and there where stock or the fear of stocking induces sales at low prices, and buyers confine themselves to such lots. CORK BUTTER.
