div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 24, 1881. I RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 24, 1881. I RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before Sir Richard Brooke (chairman), ant. Messrs. Jim. Brundrit, Chas. W. liazlehurst, Alfred Thomas, and R. M. Brooke. ADJOURNED LICENSING SESSIONS. This was the adjourned licensing day, and John Ogden, who keeps the Swan Inn, Shaw-street, Runcorn, applied for a renewal of his license.—The Chairman said that owing to some com- plaints having been made against Mr. Ogden by the police, the Bench had adjourned the granting of the renewal, and he warned him that next time anything of a like nature occurred his license would be withdrawn.—The renewal was granted. . IMPORTANT LODGING-HOUSE PROSECUTIONS. Luke Cavaney was summoned, by the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners for keeping a common lodging-house without having it registered.—Mr. W. H. Linaker appeared for the prosecution.—Mr. Parry, nuisance inspector, said he visited defendant's house on the 12th instant, and found one man and three women in addition to defendant and his wife and two children. He had several times inspected the house and found it in a disgraceful condition. Defendant had made application to have his house registered, but he had refused to do so.—Caveney did not appear, and a warrant was issued for his apprehension.—Owen Mullaney was also charged with not having his house registered.—Mr. Parry said he visited the place and found ten persons there, though it had only three rooms.—Defendant, who had been previously convicted of a similar offence, was fined £3 and 10s. 6d. costs.---Elizabeth Abbott was summoned for a like offence.—Mr. Parry said that on visiting the house he found defendant and another woman in one room; and the kitchen was occupied by a man and woman, who both slept on a sofa. Defendant, in reply to the charge, said that the woman who slept with her went with a fiat, and always made it a rule to come and sleep in her house when the vessel was in Runcorn. The Bench imposed a fine of £5 and Ils. 6d. costs or in default two months' imprisonment. Defendant ssid ;he should go to gaol.—William Hill was also charged with keeping an unregistered lodging-house. Mr. Parry said be found two men and two women in one room without any division; and the defendant, his wife and child, in a room downstairs. Defendant had applied for registration, but he (Parry) had refused to grant it. Super- intendent Williamson remarked that some time ago pro- ceedings were about to be taken against the defendant on the charge of keeping a brothel in Albert-street, but the de- fendant heard of it and left the house. Defendant was fined 40s. and 9s. 6d. costs, or one month's imprisonment with hard labour. TRESPASSING AT ACTON GRANGE.—William Stubbs and Thomas Parker, of Kingsley, were charged with trespassing on the ground of Aston Grange, and breaking the boughs of trees, doing damage to the amount of is—Samuel Light- foot said he was a gamekeeper in the emply of Mr. Daglish, of Aston Grange. On Sunday he saw the the two men getting nuts and breaking the boughs of the trees. On going up to them Parker ran away in the direction of the River Weaver.—Parker, in defence, said he was merely getting nuts, and did not break any boughs.—He was fined 55., is. damage, and 10s. 6d. costs.—Defendant Stubbs did not appear, and the hearing of the case against him was ad- journed for a week. ALLEGED Assant3.—Anna Thompson was charged with assaulting Mary Ann Igo on the 10th inst.—Complainant said she was sitting on her own door-step in Fryer-street, when the defendant came up and gave her a blow in the face. Several witnesses were called, but the evidence was so conflicting that the case was dismissed, the Chairman remarking that it was "six of one and half-a-dozen of the other." STREET FIGHTING.—MichaeI O'Harro and James Ather- ton were charged with fighting in the street OR the 10th inst.—P.C. Noden proved the case.—Superintendent Williamson said us was in the office at the time the defend- ants were brought in custody, and Atherton said that O'Harro had struck him on the face. They certainly had the appearance of having had a scuffle. o'-ilarro said they had not been fighting, but only had a few words, and it was a strange thing if a man could not walk through the town without being " ilsulted."—They were both bound over to keep the peace in sureties of £5 each, and had to pay us. 61. costs. A BEER-HOUSE KEEPER FINED 40s. AND COSTS.—Edward Hill, keeper of the Dog and Partridge beerhouse, Halton - road, was charged by the police with permitting drunken- ness on his premises, upon the 30th ult.—Superintendent Williamson said the proceedings had been taken in conse- quence of certain facts which came out at an inquest touch- ing the death of a man named Benjamin Jolly. On the night of the 30th August, several men, including the deceased, Benjamin Jolly, were drinking in the Dog and Partridge from six o'clock to a quarter to nine. He thought he should be able to show that these men were drunk, and that they were allowed to remain on the premises while in a state of intoxication.—Catherine Jolly, wife of William Jolly, of Canal-street, said that on the 30th August she went into defendant's house, at about half-past six in the-even- ing. There were present Charles Woodward, Mr. Holt, William Jolly, her husband; Benjamin Jolly, the old man who was afterwards drowned, and a woman. She went to defendant's in order to fetch her husband home, and remained until a quarter to nine. On leaving she asked her daughter to assist her home with her husband, who was very tipsy. Woodward was such a jocular looking man that it was very difficult to tell whether he was drunk or not; he looked just the same whether sober or intoxicated. (Laughter.) Holt paid for three half-gallons whilst she was at defendant's, and the company joined in drinking it.-Mr. T. W. Husband, of Widnes, appeared for the defence.—Defendant's wife was next called, and said that on the night in question her hus- band was away at Manchester, and she had charge of the place. She could not tell whether Woods was drunk or sober. Benjamin Jolly left the house directly , after his son, and after what she saw, she was of opinion "he was right enough."—ln reply to Mr. Husband, witness said her husband missed his train at Warrington, and did not get home until two o'clock in the morning. She and her daughter served three half gallons to the company between six and nine o'clock. There wer.3 seven or eight men to share it.—Mr. Husband, for the defence, contended that it had been clearly shown that the men had among them only three half-gallons. There were eight of them, and he main- tained that that quantity of liquor divided between them was nothing to hurt a British workman. (Laughter.) True, in Jolly's case the man had been drinking for a fortnight, but a man who had been doing that could drink a few extra glasses of beer without showing any effect therefrom that would justify the landlord in refusing to serve him.—Eliza- bath Cross said she saw William Jolly going home on the night in question. She said to him, "Well, Jolly, you are going home," and he replied, "Well, I am." He was not very drunk,--la reply to questions from Superintendent Williamson, this witness admitted that she did not take any very particularly notice of Jolly on the night in question when she passed him.—Thomas Bull said he went to defen- dant's on the evening in question, and was asked to have a glass out of the jug of beer that was on the table, and he had one. He went out, returned at a quarter-past seven and had another glass out of the same jug. Those in the room had three half gallons served altogether, and there were eight of them for it, He did not think any of those present were drunk.—Mr. Brundrit said the Bench considered the case clearly proved. They would:not endorse the defendantslicense as this was his first offence, but he would have to pay a fine of 40s. and costs, making £3 is. They hoped the conviction would act as a warning for the future—Charles Woodward was summoned for having been drunk on the same premises, on the 30th ult.—Mr. Husband again defended.—Defendant was fined ss. and costs, 11s. 6d. A FAMILY QUARREL.—Louisa Bostock was charged with assaulting Emma Bostock, on the 14th July, 1879; but complainant expressed a desire to withdraw from the case, and the Bench consented to this course being adopted upon her paying 6s. 6d. costs.—Defendant appeared much moved at what she characterised as her sister's untruthfulness in placing the facts before the magistrates. AN ADVENTURE IN THE MAGISTRATES' CLERK'S OFFICE.

- - A sharp-looking young man named Thomas Bromley, of Longton, Staffordshire, was charged with having, on the 17th inst., refused to show his certificate under the Pedlar ' Act, IS7l.—Mr. Frank Johnson, deputy magistrates' clerk, said he was employed in the office of Mr. Ashton (the clerk to the magistrates) at Runcorn. On Saturday morning he was in the office, between eleven and twelve o'clock, with Mr. Pownall, another clerk, when the prisoner came in. He noticed at once that there was something not quite right about him. The prisoner seemed rather taken aback when he saw the words "magistrates' clerk's office" upon the door. He said he wanted a lawyer's office, and Mr. Pownall said "This is the lawyer's office." The prisoner replied, "This is the magistrates' office." Pownall then asked if he wanted Mr. Barton, and prisoner again replied that he "wanted the lawyer's office." He then, after some further demur, came into the office, and, speaking in a confidential manner, asked witness if he wanted any tobacco, as he had some of first-rate quality which he and a chum of his had brought from Liverpool. At the same time 'le intimated that the matter must be kept quiet, as the tobacco in eines- tion was smuggled, and it would not do to let the Custom- house officers get on the scent. Witness then said, "I don't want any tobacco; I don't use it." The prisoner asked him if he would look at some splendid French tweed he had. He pretended that the tweed was of an extraordinarily fine quality, and said that unless he (witness) had been in Paris he could never have possibly seen such tweed. He declined to purchase any of the stuff, but told the prisoner that the other clerk might possibly do so. Prisoner went to fetch the cloth which he had outside, and he told his fellow clerk that he was going to fetch Inspector Hollingworth. He asked Mr. Pownall when the prisoner came back to detain him until he (witness) should return. On his way to the Police Station, he met the prisoner with the bag produced with him. The prisoner then again asked him if he would look at it. Ile said he did not want any as It was no use to him, but he might take it to the office and show it to Mr. Pownall, whom he had told to keep him there until the inspector came. On reaching the Police Station he found that Inspector Hollingworth was not in. He then returned to the office. The prisoner was already there, .And had got the cloth unpacked and was showing it to Mr. Pownall. He (witness) looked at the cloth, and at once said it was rubbish. Thereupon the prisoner became very impertinent, saying, "Oh ! you are one of those clever fellows who think they know everything but know nothing !" Witness thereupon told him to take up his cloth and leave the office. The prisoner became still more insolent and refused to go, on which he said he should put him out. Then it was that Mr..Pownall said, "But I shall want my ten shillings back ;" and intimated that he bad parted with t 10s. to the defendant. He (witness) then told the prisoner • he must give Mr. Pownall the half-sovereign back a,za:in. He replied that Mr. Pownall had bought the cloth and be

should stick to the half-sovereign. The prisoner then tried to quit the office, and a struggle between witness ensued. Mr. Pownall went to fetch a policeman. The struggle lasted some time. At last a constable came. The first thing he did was to ask the prisoner for his licence. He said he could not produce it, and pleaded in excuse that he Lead left it behind at Warrington Central Station.—The prisoner: Anything more to say ? (Laughter.) Didn't You strike me 7—Mr. Johnson: I didn't strike at you. I got hold of you and held you there; and in the struggle you broke my spectacles—Prisoner: Didn't you say if I had got any of that tobacco you would buy it ?—Mr. Johnson: ; I said I never used tobacco; I had made up my mind that it was a swindle. (To the Bench). When the prisoner came to the office he had a bit of gold braid on his cap, but I believe he has since taken it off. The braid was such as is worn by sailors.—Prisoner picked up his cap, and said he had not taken off the gold braid.- -Mr. Pownall said that between eleven and twelve o'clock be was in the office with Mr. Johnson when the prisoner came in. After Mr. Johnson went out to the police station prisoner returned to the office and began to talk about some grand French stuff from Parie. He took some stuff out of his bag, which he said was French cloth, of a quality not to be had in this country, and wanted 30s. for it. He asked him if he had ever been in Paris, and he told him he had not. He also declined to buy the stuff from him at the mice he demanded, and added that he had no money to throw away. The prisoner then asked him how much money he had, and witness went into the lobby and took half a sovereign out of his purse. Prisoner afterwards snatched the money out of his hand. A struggle, as had already been detailed, ensued between the prisoner and Mr. Johnson.— Superintendent Williamson: But you never bought the cloth ?—Mr. Pownall: No.—The Prisoner: You did.—Mr. Pownall said he had made enquiries, and he found that the cloth was not worth making up.—The Prisoner said the cloth was worth 10s.' and they might bring any tailor to prove it.—Sergeant McMichael proved apprehending the prisoner, and that he was unable to produce his license.— The prisoner was ordered to return the 10s. to Mr. Pownall, and to pay a fine of ss. and costs 10s., or in default be im- prisoned 14 days.—Superintendent Williamson (to the Bench): Gentlemen, this is a very old game, and one often adopted by men such as the prisoner, who by their cunning generally succeed in working upon the tender feel- ings of certain people. It is a systematic plan of swindling which has been in vogue ever since I became a policeman, and that is some years ago. Under the circumstances, and seeing the way iu which the prisoner carried on what he professed was a bona fide trade, I request the magistrates to cancel the pedlar's certificate possessed by him.— Mr. Brundrit said that considering the fact that it had been proved, the prisoner had not carried on his trade in a manner similar to a proper pedlar, his certificate would be cancelled. —The Superintendent : The prisoner is respectably con- nected, and I have no doubt that the cancelling of the cer- tificate would be to his advantage. If he wants to commence business, let him go to Staffordshire and begin it there in a fair manner.—The prisoner, who appeared very lively under such depressing circumstances, said he would sell the wonderful piece of cloth and BO raise the money, which be, after a short time, succeeded in raising, and was set at liberty.

AN INCORRIGIBLE YOUTIL-Wm. Harris, a youth about 17 years of age, was charged with haying, on the 6th inst., stolen a pair of trousers, two pairs of drawers, two singlets, two shirts, a pair of boots, and a bag, the property of Thos. Byrne, a seaman on the schooner William Berry. Prosecutor left the things in the forecastle on the night in question, and missed them in the morning, about six o'clock. The prisoner had conducted himself so badly whilst on the vessel that the captain said he would not pay him any wages for three months', was also found to have decamped. The Young fellow was seen to pass the Francis Dock at about ten O'clock, by P.C. Weedall ; and it was afterwards found that he had pledged the articles at Mr. Alexander Taylor's, Rochdale-road, Manchester, and Mr. Glister's, in the same thoroughfare. Prisoner was taken into custody by the Manchester police, and brought to Runcorn by P.C. Noden. —Prisoner -alleged that he had been treated with great unkindness on board the vessel, and deprived of his rightly earned wages, and had, therefore. decainped.—Mr. Brundrit said the prisoner was, first of all, sent to a reformatory and then put into a situation, but lost it through his misconduct. Then a place was found the prisoner upon the William Berry, and he had now stolen the clothes of his companion. It appeared he was incorrigible, and be would be sentenced to six weeks' imprisonment, with hard labour.

At the fortnightly meeting of this Board, which took took place on Tuesday, at the Dutton Workhouse, the Rev. Canon Barclay occupied the chair, and there were also pre- sent the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. Handley, Whittaker, Ashton, Norman, Fisher, Weir, Rigby, Darbyshire, Jackson, Mclntyre, Campkin, Henry Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk).

MR. LINAIER AND THE COUNTY RATE ASSESSMENT. The CLERIC read a letter from Mr. Roberts, Deputy Clerk of the Peace, Chester, stating that he saw by the report of a meeting of the Guardians that it had been stated they had been informed, and believed, that the whole of certain dis- crepancies were not due to the increase in the assessments to poor rates, or from new assessments, but to errors which in some way had crept into the basis as settled in 1873. As he (Mr. Roberts) was not aware what the supposed errors were, he wrote that he should be much obliged if the Board would inform him. Every care had been taken to secure a uni-'s formity of rating throughout the whole county in 1873, by adopting the assessment to schedule A of the property tax as the foundation of the County Rate Assessment, and as long as the different Boards of Guardians were not required to act on any uniform plan in their valuations, it was diffi- cult to see how the present county rate basis could be amended with a revaluation.—The Clerk remarked that he had prepared the following letter in reply:—" Yours of the Bth inst. duly received, and it was laid before the Guardians at a meeting to-day. In reply, I am directed to say that the discrepancies referred to in my letter to you of the 15th ult., as not being due to the increase in the assessments to poor rates, or from new assessments, but to errors which have in some way,crept into the basis, as settled in 1873,'are among the following : ' Union. Township.

Assessm't to Discre- Basis. Pool Rate 1880. pancy. 2 a Northwieh... Acton Northwich...Hartford ...... 7,406 10,679 3,173 Northwich... Moulton 3,350 ... 7,138 ... 3,788 Northwich...Wimboldsley 4,068 ... 6,810 ... 2,742 Northwich...Weaverham The Guardians also desire me to refer to 27 and 28 Vic., c. 39, sec. 9, by which the clerk of every assessment committee is bound to send annually, in the month of December, to the Clerk of the Peace of the County, copies of the totals of the year's estimated rental and rateable value in the several par- ishes within the union; and by a circular-letter issued by the Poor Law Board on the 17th August, 1864, the attention of clerks to the assessment committees is called to this pro- vision, and the Board say ',this information will facilitate the proceedings of justices at their quarter sessions when they make and assess the county rate.' By reference to the returns made by the clerk to the assessment committee, pre- vious to the basis being fixed, it will be found whether the discrepancies referred to then really existed, and by what or whose error they crept into the 'basis.' The Guardians have assumed that the returns referred to, with the schedule of deductions from the gross estimated rental allowed by the several assessment committees—and which were applied for when the basis was arrived at in 1873—would give a finance, or other committee, appointed by the justices, differhnt information to form a new basis with a revalua- tion."—Mr. HANDLEY : I think it is a very good letter, and should be adopted and sent by the Board.—Mr. MCINTYRE : They don't want to grapple with the questionjat all; they want to fence round it.—On the proposition of Mr. NORMAN, seconded by Mr. WEIR, it was resolved that the letter be adopted by the Board and forwarded to the gentleman in question.

MR. COLEBURN AND DR. MCDOUGALL. The CLERIC stated that he had received a reply from Dr. McDougall, of Runcorn to the complaints made by Mr. Coleburn, the registrar Of births and deaths to the Local Government Board, as to the signing of vaccination certifi- cates. TM, doctor said he could not add any thing to the explanation he gave some months ago.—The DEPUTY CLERE : Dr. McDougall may appoint his own deputy, ac- cording to the words of his contract. A GUARDIAN ON THE TITHE QUESTION. The CHAIRMAN remarked that this half-year they would not need any rate for educational or rural sanitary purposes. The poor rate would be ed. in the L.—Mr. Rionv I thought, Mr. Chairman, that some short time ago you said we should have no rate at all.—The CHAIRMAN : lam afraid that happy time has not come yet. That would, in- deed, be anticipating the golden age !—Mr. RIGBY No rate and no rent I—The CHAIRMAN : No rates and no rents, Mr. Rigby—(laughter)—and no tithes !—Mr. : Well, we shall not have to pay tithes very many more years; the legislature will stop that game just now. (Loud laughter.) The man who ever invented them wants putting on the top of a pole and burning!

div.head: ESTIMATES.
div.p: THE ESTIMATES.

Mr. HANDLEY presented the estimate for the half-year ending Lady-day, 1882. Special charges: School fees £l5, hospital loan and interest £lOB, total £123. Common charges : In maintenance £685, out relief £1,636, other charge £1,441—£3,762. Estimated sum to be repaid by Government and the collector £6BO, to be deducted, leaving £3,082. county rate .£1,568, contingency fund and balance £2,310, making the total sum required for the half-year .L 7,083. From this the sum of £2,127, the probable balance in Michaelmas this year, would have to be deducted, leaving the sum to'be provided by the various toWnships £4,956. The rateable value of the utnion on the 13th inst. was £200,995, showing an increase since September of last year of .£1,030. A rate of 6d. in the Lan this amount would produce £5,024 17s. 6d. The rate in the corresponding period last year was 71d. The report was a very satisfactory one. During the last few years he had heard Runcorn Union spoken of as a wonder in regard to the economical way in which the busi- ness was managed, as compared with other poor law districts. He thought that the publication of the statement would have the effect of showing other unions where savings could L. 3 effected. One of the principal causes of the state of finan- cial matters which existed in connection with that union seemed to be the manner in which the out-relief was ad- ministered. About one week's pay in thirteen weeks was now saved. It took something like £65 to pay the relief in each week, but in June quarter the sum was reduced to £63 odd, and this quarter it would be about the same amount. With regard to the county rates, they were a fraction over fourpence for all purposes over which the Guardians had control, and a fraction over twopence for county rate pur- poses.

RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY. The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday afternoon, the Rev. Canon Barclay in the chair. There were also present the Rev. John W. N. Tanner, and Messrs. Ashton (vice-chairman), Mclntyre, Darbyshire, Rigby, Weir, Henry Linaker (clerk), and W. Linaker (deputy clerk).

div.head: BOARD AND THE MEDICAL OFFICER,
div.p: THE BOARD AND THE MEDICAL OFFICER,

The CIARIC read a communication from the Local Govern- ment Board, dated the 12th inst., sanctioning, untii the 29th September next year, the reappointment of Mr. John Grant Bride as Medical Oficer of health to the Authority, at a salary cf £l2O per annum.

div.head: FRODSHAM AND FRODSHAM LORDSHIP-URBAN POWERS
div.p: FRODSHAM AND FRODSHAM LORDSHIP-URBAN POWERS
GRANTED.

A letter was also read from the Local Government Board expressing their willingness to invest the Authority with the urban powers contained in the second and third para- graphs of section 169 of the Public Health Act 1875, in respect of the contributory places of Prodsham and Frod- sham Lordship; and stating that they would also put in force there section 17% if the authority would make the necessary application. Before further considering the pro- posal that the authority should have conferred upon them powers under sections 112; 113, 114, and 115 with respect to offensive trades, the Board were desirous of being furnished with full particulars as to the nature and number of such trades. The CLERK said the only offensive works in the neighbourhood was the bone manufactory; and the Guar- dians gave instructions that a reply be sent to that effect.

div.head: FINANCIAL ESTIMATE FOR THE HALF YEAR.
div.p: FINANCIAL ESTIMATE FOR THE HALF YEAR.

The following estimate for the half year ending Lady Day, was submitted:—Balance in favour of the Union at Lady Day, this year, £259; calls Michaelmas this half year, £159; total capital for half year £4lB. Probable expendi- ture this Michaelmas half year, £219; probable balance at Michaelmas, this year, £199. Probable expenditure during Lady Day half year 1882, being the exact amount of ex- penditure in the corresponding half of last year, £169. No provision has been made in the foregoing estimate for a balance and contingency fund, as the sum of £l3O will be due from the Parliamentary grant in March next, on account of the salaries of the Medical Officer of health, and Inspec- tor of nuisances, and no calls will, therefore, be required from the overseers in respect of the ensuing half year end- ing Lady Day next year. Mr. RIGBY considered this financial statement capital. Mr. WEIR thought it was not bad news at any rate. Mr. IliGny : No rates at all this next half year, John. (Laughter). Mr. WEIR: I beg your pardon, there will be some rates.

The CLERK said the several claims made by Mr. Higham, of Warrington, for damage to an omnibus, the Warrington Corporation for damage to gas mains and loss of gas; and a claim made by the surveyor of highways, and the Daresbury Highway Board for repairs to road, were all in course of settlement between the contractors and the several claimants. Mr. RIGBY asked if any steps were being taken to improve the road from Tom Payne bridge to Wilderspool. The I CLERK replied that the road was undor the control of the Daresbury Highway Board. Mr. RIGBY observed that the road was in an abominable state of repair. FRODSHADI SEWERAGE.

div.head: WIDNES POLICE COURT.
div.p: WIDNES POLICE COURT.

WEDNESDAY.—Bef ore Mr. W. N. Heald (chairman) and Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, jun. A WOMAN'S QUARREL. Mary Power, an elderly woman, and her son, John Power, were charged with assault- ing Ann Riley, on the 12th inst.—Complainant said she was assisting a neighbour to remove some bed-stocks, when the male defendant, who is only about 17 years of age, used some very offensive language to another woman. She told him he ought to be asharnecl, as a mere youth, of using such filthy language, when he knocked her clown, and his mother caught her by the back of the head and encouraged her son I to hit her on the eyes, so that she had afterwards to go to Dr. O'Keeffe.—The youth was fined ss. and costs, or 14 days' imprisonment, and the case against his mother was ditmissed. COAL STEALING EXTRAORDINARY.—Mary Fitz.simmons and Hannah Smith, two women living in Bank-street, were charged with stealing a quantity of coal, the property of Messrs. Bournes and Robinson.—Mr. Swift, sen., appeared on behalf the firm, and said the coal was stolen from the firm's wagons upon the railway siding at Widnes dock, on the 13th inst. About three o'clock in the afternoon, the agent, who was near to the West Bank office, saw the two prisoners at the wagons. Fitzsimmons was upon one of them, handing the coal out to the other prisoner. When they had taken as much. as they needed, the prisoners coolly proceeded to put it into bags. The coal stealing in Widnes had become such an intolerable nuisance that he had been asked to press for a conviction in the case, as it was believed that nothing short of sending some of the gang to gaol would pat an end to their conduct. The woman Fitzsimmons had frequently been seen to take coal from the wagons, but the company had not been able to pro- ceed against her on the last occasion when she did so, be- cause their servants were not able to swear to the particular .ragon from which it was taken. Not less than two tons were stolen from the wagons on the previous Saturday and Sunday.—The Chairman said there was no doubt that such robberies as the one of which the prisoners had been con- victed, were carried out in a wholesale manner in, Widnes. Smith would have a fine of 20s. to pay (without costs) and the other prisoner would be sent to gaol ,14 days, without the option of paying a fine. A Noisy COUPLE—John Kennedy and Patrick Kennedy were summoned for causing a breach of the peace.—P.C. Clarkson gave evidence to the effect that on the 10th inst. he saw the defendants, who were drunk, fighting with a man in Lugsdale-road.—Patrick was fined 10s. and costs, or 14 days' imprisonment, and John ss, and costs, or seven days'.

div.head: TIIIIRSDAY.—Before Mr. Brock.
div.p: TIIIIRSDAY.—Before Mr. Brock.

SERIOUS Casn OF UNLAWFULLY WOUNDlNG.—Catherine I McCaffery, a married woman, was charged, on remand, with unlawfully wounding Mary McCaffery, of Nelson-street.— Mr. Swift, son., 'appeared for the defence.—Complainant said that on the night of the 17th inst., she was going home from a neighbour's house, about 11 o'clock, when she saw the prisoner in Nelson-street, at the door of a Mrs. Farrell's house. She had some words with the prisoner, but could not say who commenced the conversation. She walked on and the prisoner followed and overtook her before she could shut the door of her own house. Prisoner seized her by the hair, and they struggled for two or three minutes. She had a child in her arms at the time. When prisoner let her go she found she was bleeding freely from the right side of the neer. She afterwards went to the police office about the matter, and, in company with the inspector, proceeded to the pointed her out. She next went to Dr. prisoner'sm c L en flan, housewh d o and her. She was still suffering.—ln cross-examination the complainant said she was a sister-in- law of the prisoner. Before they struggled together she had called prisoner an hnmoral woman, on which prisoner replied in similar terms. She was married last Christmas, and her baby was now five months old.—Dr. McLennan said that on Sunday morning, about a quarter past twelve he was sent for to the police office, and examined the com- plainant upon the side of whose throat he found two incised wounds. The larger one went in a transverse direction, and expised ' the jugular vein. One of the wounds was a dangerous one. —ln cross-examination wit- ness said that on Sunday morning it was sug- gested to him that the wornds had been caused by the latch key of the door. He ex imined the door, and thought that the sharp edge of the latch might have made them. The larger wound was in the position in which it would have been if complainant had fallen against the latch.—lnspector Barnett proved apprehending prisoner, and said on the way to the police station she said complainant had sustained the injuries by falling against the latch.—Mr. Swift addressed the court for the defence, and argued from the discrepancies in the evidence that there was no case for a jury.—Mary McDermott, Nelson-street, said the complainant used very bad language to the prisoner when she cane up the street. Complainant struck prisoner with a jug on the head or face. There was no struggle before the blow with the jug. Prisoner had nothing in her hand. Shortly after the com- plainant's husband came out of the house with a poker in his hand.—Jane Forshaw, Nelson-street, was also called for the defence.—The prisoner was committed to Liverpool Quarter Sessions for trial.—Mr. Swift said as the case was not one of felony but of misdenieanour, he applied for bail. —Mr. Brock said he would grant bail on the prisoner enter- ing into sureties, herself in £2O, and two sureties in £lO each TIIEFT OF A GOLD WATCH AND CHAIN, VALUE £45. John Watson, a stranger, was charged with assaulting Wm. Henry Loveday, landlord of 'the Masonic Arms, Lark- lane, Sefton Park, Liverpool, and stealing a gold watch and guard, value £45 —The prosecutor said that on the 16th Inst. he visited the Farnworth Agricultural Show, and at about half-past six in the evening he went on to the Cheshire Lines station platform, and was getting into the train for Liverpool when he felt a tug at his watch chain, and then saw the prisoner had hold of it, and also had the watch in his hand. He seized Watson, and held him until Mr. W. 11. Hindle, Cheshire Lines' detective, came up and took him into the station master's office.—Sergeant Robin- son qaid the man was given into his custody, and, on charg- ing hint, be denied having stolen the articles, and said he of attempting to steal them.—Prisoner, who 9711.8 onlyhe3';egtiit serivPYd his defence, was committed to the Liver- pool Quarter Sessions for trial.

div.head: SIR R. A, CROSS AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: SIR R. A, CROSS AT WARRINGTON.

The Right Hon. Sit. R. A. Cross, M.P., on Weduesday opened a bazaar in the ill Hall, Warrington, which has been promoted with the iect of raising funds towards Di, purchasing a Workmen's CIO. There was a fair atten- dance at the ceremony which took place at one o'clock. Prayer having been offered by the Retetcr, Mr. REAMONT, addressing Sir Rishard ,Cross, said he had very willingly complied with the request en" the committee of the Workmen's Club, that he should reael to him the address which they proposed to hand to the eight hon. gentleman on the opening of the bazaar. A bazaar N,S they all knew was an Eastern institution, but it had imerroveel in its travels; for in its eriginal country no ladies would be seen at the counters, but here they saw the smiling faces of the Lancashire witches. (Applause.) The address was as follows: To the Right Honourable Sir R. Assheton Cross, G.C.B.— Right Honourable Sir,—We, the Committee of the Workmen's Club Bazaar, desire to express to you our hearty thanks for your kindness in coming amongst us this morning to open our bazaar. We remember your frequent assistance to us when you were our townsman, and we rejoice that time has not lessened your interest in Warrington, as we are sure that it has not abated your desire to elevate the working-classes In general, of which the venerable Earl of Shaftesbury spoke in such eloquent terms on a public occasion not long ago. Our object in holding the present bazaar is, as you are aware, to raise the necessary funds to purchase the Old Music Hall, a building which is associated with many pleasant memories In the minds of all the old inhabitants of Warrington; and we hope that the building, by being ours, will at all times be open to us as a warm, well-lighted, and comfortable workmen's borne during the day time, however the state of trade in general, or the condition of any workingman in particular, may be depressed. We have done a little ourselves towards itting up the club, and we would have done far more had the club been a new building at which we could have worked during our spare hours, each man in his own department. Many of our townsmen and neighbours have so far been very generous in their assistance, and we trust to be able to pay the cost of the building and its fittings by the assistance which we shall raise to-day, and on the next three days that the bazaar Is to continue open. We take this opportanity of referring to the sell-denying labours of the many ladies who for some months past have been teaching classes 01 young women to make and mend their own garments. We shall take precau- tions to secure the use of the hall of our club-room for similar classes in future, believing that amongst the ladies of War- rington teachers will at all times be ready to give the necessary Instruction. We refer with pleasure to one or two of our fun- , damental rules ; one of 'which is—" That the club-room shall I not be used for the sale of intoxicating liquors ;" the second is —" That any workingman who may have brought disgrace on himself and his order by misconduct shall not be permitted to enjoy the benefits of the club until be has given full proof of amendment ;" and the third and last fundamental rule to which we would avert is—" That the benefits of the club, sub- ject to any regulations which future committees may make, shall be open to workingmen free, or on a nominal payment. entirely irrespective of their religious creeds or political views, but under no circumstances shall anything inconsistent with religion or good government be permitted within its walls."— We are, on behalf of the committee, Right Honourable Sir, yours respectfully, A. VICKERS, T. EAUDE, J. W. Will TTLE. The object of the institution was described very fully in the address, but he might say that a cynic had said there was nothing so soon grew old as gratitude; but he was sure they would be very ungrateful indeed if they forgot the former services they had received from the right hon. gen- tleman to whom they were presenting the address. They none of them forgot it was not long ago since, with a golden key, he opened that noble place where sick people received relief. He hoped the result of the proceedings would be to produce a golden shower which would open another house where the workingmen might find a house under circum- stances which had been described in the address. (Ap- plause.) Sir RICHARD Creoss, in rep'y, said he could assure them that, after the heat of a somewhat anxious and very weary- ing session, it was the greatest possible pleasure to him to come to any meeting where they could forget differences of all kinds; and it was an unspeakable pleasure to him to be amongst them that day on absolutely neutral ground, where persons of all shades of politics' and persons of various opinions, so far as religious faith was concerned, met, at all events, for once, with a simple common object, that of fur- thering the work which the workingmen of Warrington had set up for their benefit. (Applause.) But it was a peculiar pleasure to him that this should happen in the town of Warrington, because he, as they knew, had had the pleasure of living amongst them for several years; and he could assure them the years he spent at Warrington were some of the happiest he ever passed in his life. (Applause.) It was a matter which gratified him more than he could express to find that the working men, in the address which had just been presented to him, still had it in their minds that he had once lived among them. (Hear, hear.) If his presence there could do the smallest good towards the great object which they had in view he should be more than gratified. (Ap- plause.) He had said they were united heart and soul that day, and probably in no matter were they more united than in an expression of opinion, which he was quite sure they I would join with him in giving, of the deepest possible con- dolence with -the great nation on the other side of the Atlantic—(applause)—in the terrible loss with which it had pleased Providence to afflict them, and also an expression of the deepest sympathy with the widow of the unfortunate President, and an expreseion of utter abhorrence of the great crime which had been committed there. (Applause.) He had listened with great pleasure to the rules which had been read out as part of the programme for the Workingmen's Club. One great advantage that it seemed to him to possess was that workingmen had taken it up themselves. (Hear, hear.) It did not do for people to do things for workingmen, and then trust that they would very gratefully receive them. Englishmen liked to do things for themselves, if they could. (Hear, hear.) They liked that spirit of inde- pendence, that spirit of self-reliance—that spirit which had made this nation what it was. They did not like to have things done for them, but liked to do them themselves, and therefore it was with great pleasure that he heard the workingmen had formed their own comerectee, I and had passed those rules. It was great pleasure to him to see that one of the main objects of these rules was entirely to and order. He was glad they had eeserve decency pa,cl that rule with regard to intoxicating liquors, because it would save them a. world of trouble in future years. eed he heartily congratu- lated them on the rules the had adopted. He was at a great distribution of prizes the other day in one of their neighbouring towns—Bolton—where a very large number of prizes had been wee by the pupils who had undergone ' examination—teelani cal exami net ion —in connection with an institution welch had been establiehecl by the City Guilds. In lookied over the books and the last report for that insti- tution, he was sorry to find that althoueh Bolton stood at the head of the list, and next to that Oldham, not much was said about Warrington, and therefore if they would allow him he would like to dxplain the objects of these examina- tions, because he was quite sure they would derive immense , benefit from them. They wanted to teach applied physics, applied chemistry, applied mechanics, and applied art. They I wanted to show them how they could get a knowledge which scientific persons had thought out themselves, and I how they could apply that knowledge to the particular trade in which they were engaged. They did not want to teach them trades, because the only place where trades could be I learnt was the workshop. They could not learn trades from books or lectures. They must work it out for themselves in the workshop or ' factory. The object of the institution was to place at their disposal the knowledge which scientific and wise men had thought out, in order that when they went into the work- shops and factories they might have the great advantage of all the knowledge which the world possessed on their par- ticular work or trade. Everybody must know that know- ledge was power, and they must also know at the present moment and feel that they no longer had the monopoly which England used to have in trade and manufacture, but had all the nations of the world competing with them in the keenest possible rivalry. But if they were pine- to beat them—and he knew they were—(hear, bear)—they must' sharpen all their weapons and use all the tools in their armoury they possibly could, and by the force of their own energy and skill, aided by technical education, they had such a power in their hands that he did:not care where the competi- tion came from, hewas quite sure in the long run they would win. (Applause.) He ventured, if he could do so without seeming to press any views of his own too strongly upon them, to ask them to enquire about these technical examina- tions, because there was no doubt whatever from all he could learn,—and he made strict enquiry when he was there —that the practical effectof this knowledge weaver)/ telling. But if they were beaten by America, don't be beaten by Belton. Therefore he should like the people of the town of Warrington to enquire for them- selves, and if they thought these technical examinations were worth the time and trouble, which no doubt they would take, let them take them up. In conclusion he wished them most heartily success in this great undertaking. He believed it would be a very great advantage to the town and the workingmen in order that when they were away from their work on wet, rainy days they might have some place to go to besides the public-house. (Applause.) Albums were then presented to Sir Richard, the Mayor, cf which Mr. Beamont, and the Rev. W. Quekett, as mementos of the o The Mason proposed a vote of thanks to Sir Richard Crossc occasion, ono , r a hisfte r kindness in coining to open the bazaar. He said he did not think they could have found a better man for the occasion' because they remembered when he was at the head of the Home Office how hard he worked for the benefit of the working classes of this country. His Artizans Dwellings Act, and other matters connected with the work- ing classes, would never be forgotten by them he was cer- , tam. He thought Dr. Mackie had very properly asked Sir Richard Cross to come down, and had put the right an in the right place. (Applause.) They in Warrington knew that Sir Richard Cross did all he could for them. He was proud to say he served with him in the local Volunteer Corps, anti theyall remembered him at the head of the Musical , Society, and in connection with every other movement to promote the enjoyment and innocent recreation of thbe Peeple. (Applause.) Warrington had good reason to e Proud of Sir Richard Cross when Her Majesty gracious y called upon him to take the office of Home Secretary. (Applause.) Mr. VICKERS, a working man and a member of the Com- mittee, seconded the motion. Sir R. A. RUNCORN IMPROVEMENT ACT, 1852.—PUBLIC HEALTH ACT, 1875. • DEPOSIT OF PROPOSED BUILDING BY-LAWS. NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that the Runcorn Im- provement Commissioners intend to apply to the Local Government Board to confirm by-laws :—With respect to the level, width, and construction of new streets, and the provisions for the sewerage thereof; with respect to the structure of walls, foundations, roofs, and chimneys of new buildings, for securing stability and the prevention of fires, and for purposes of health; with respect to the sufficiency of space about build- ings to secure a free circulation of air, and with respect to the ventilation of buildings: with respect to the drainage of build- ings, to water-closets, earth-closets, privies, ashplts, and cess- pools in connection with buildings, and to the closing of buildings or parts of buildings unfit for human habitation, and to prohibition of their use for such habitation ; with respect to notices, and the deposit of plans and sections by persons intend- ing to lay our streets or construct buildings. And Notice is Hereby Further Gives, that a copy of the proposed by-laws is now open to the inspection of the ratepayers at the Commis- sioners' Offices, Bridge-street, Runcorn, and will remain open for inspection for a period of one month before the aforesaid application is made. Copies of the proposed by-laws may also be obtained on payment of sixpence each copy.—By order of the Commissioners. W. BROOKES, Secretary. Public Offices, Runcorn, September 23rd. 1881.-

WIDNES SCIENCE AND ART CLASSES. TN connection with the Science and Art Department, Kensington, and City and Guilds of London Institute. —Session 1881-82.—The eighth Session will commence OCTOBER 3rd. SYLLABUS :—Mondays: Inorganic Chemistry. 6-30 to 8-0 p.m.; Alkali Manufacture, 14.0 to 9-0 p.m. Tuesdays: Art —Freehand Drawing, 6-30 to 8-0 p.m.; Machine Construction and Drawing, 8-0 to 9-0 p.m. Wednesdays: Art--Freehand Drawing, 6-30 to 8-0 p.m.; Building Construction and Draw- ing, 8-0 to 9-0 p.m. Fridays: Sound. Light, and Heat, 7-0 to 8-0 p.m.; Animal Physiology, 8-0 to 9-0 pm. The Technologi- cal Class (Alkali Manufacture) will include the manufacture of Sulphuric Acid, Sulphate of Soda, Soda Ash, Caustic Soda, Soda Crystals, and Bleaching Powder. Candidates eligible for the Technological Class (Alkali Manufacture) must be actually employed in Chemical or other allied works, and they must have passed, or peas during the coming session, in two of the following-named subjects :—Machine Construction, Building Construction, Theoretical Mechanics, Applied Mechanics, Acoustics, Light and Heat, and Inorganic Chemistry. Fee, 3s. per class, payable in advance. No class will commence unless a sufficient number of students join. Intending students will please send In their names to the Hon. Sec. on or before the 20th instant, JOSEPH MORRAON, Hon. Sec. Widnes, September 22nd, 1881.

----- RUNCORN UNION.—CONTRACTS for PROVISIONS and SUPPLIES for the half-year ending, 29th March, 1882.—The GUARDIANS of the POOR of the RUNCORN UNION are desir•us of receiving TENDERS from parties willing te CON- TRACT for the supply of Flour and Oatmeal, Groceries, Peas, Cheese, Salt Butter ; Cod Liver and Paraffin Oil ; Quinine ; good Beef, to consist of vein anel brisket pieces the price to include about 30lbs. per week of the In butcher's meat for the officers, and sides of Mutton; beat litie(lsts) American Bacon: Potatoes; Wheat Straw; Drapery and Clothing; Men's, Women's, Boys' and Girls' Shoes, of various sizes, as per samples, to be seen at the Workhouse, Dutton; House Coal (colliery to be named); good Deal Coffins, specifying size of each, to be delivered in the Union when and where required; Carting at per mile, and Funerals at per funeral. Parties tendering for the supply of the above-mentioned goods will be required to deliver the same at the Workhouse, free of cost to the Guardians, how and when required. Tenders to be accompanied with saoaples (except drapery goods) as far as practicable. The Guardians do not bind themselves to ac- cept the lowest or any tender. Persons desirous of tendering must apply by letter to my office, in Frodsham, for a panted Form of Tender (and none other can be entertained), where a schedule of the various articles required and further particulars may be obtained. Sealed Tenders, addressed to the Guardians, to be lomat ded to the Clerk's office, Frodsham, on or before SATURDAY, the Ist day of October, 1881, endorsed "Tender for ." The tenders will be opened and considered at a meeting of the Guar- dians to be held in the Board Room, Dutton, on the 4th October, 1881, at Two p.m. Parties whose tenders are accepted must enter into a written contract, and be prepared to enter into a bond with two sureties, if required by the Guardians. By order of the Board, H. LINA.BER, Frodsham, 6th September, 1881, Clerk to the Guardians
